## Paper Source: A Brazilian Sign Language Video Database for Automatic Recognition

## A Brazilian Sign Language Video Database for Automatic Recognition

Priscila V. Gameiro 1 , Wesley L. Passos 2 , Gabriel M. Araujo 1 , Amaro A. de Lima 1 Jonathan N. Gois 1 and Anna R. Corbo 1 .

Abstract -Communication is a basic human necessity, but the deaf community is still facing some barriers. In Brazil, there are about 9.7 million people with some degree of hearing impairment but most Brazilians do not know the Brazilian Sign Language (Libras). Wearable gadgets like gloves or bracelets with sensors are a good tool to help in communication, but these solutions are pricey or intrusive. On the other hand, computer vision solutions are cheaper but challenging mainly due to the absence of reliable video databases. In this work, we propose a video database compounded by different signs, with various backgrounds, and different speakers. We also developed a system to perform computer vision-based sign recognition using the k-nearest neighbors (K-NN) and random forest (RF). In our tests, we achieved an average accuracy of 65.81% in multiclass classification.

Index Terms -Sign Language, LIBRAS, Computer Vision, Gait Energy Image, Image Processing.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Communication is a human necessity and the spoken language is a more common way to establish a dialogue. Nevertheless, the communication of deaf people is based on corporal gestures, facial expressions, and the local culture. According to the most recent Brazilian Census [1], 5% of the Brazilian population has some hearing loss and only 15% of these are fluent in Brazilian Portuguese. Most of the deaf population has as the first language the Brazilian Sign Language (also known as Libras) and the Portuguese as a second language. Despite this, the deaf population has a lot of barriers to use written communication. They are very different in syntax and semantics [2].

The Libras brings together the position of hands, the facial expression, and the gestures performed by the speaker to translate a word or a sentence. Besides, the same position of hands and facial expression, but with slightly different hands trajectories may have various different interpretations [3].

Therefore, to create a dictionary or an interface to translate those symbols is a hard task.

To recognize gestures, the literature presented two main approaches. The first one uses some devices as colored gloves or sensors to easily track the movements and that is known as 'visual-based gesture with glove-markers' (VBGwGM). The disadvantage of this approach is that the sensors can limit the movements turning the communication uncomfortable. On the other hand, the second way to extract the information of the gesture movements is using computational vision [4], [5], as know as 'pure visual-based gesture' (PVBG). This type of approach is less intrusive using only cameras. However, the usage of computational vision could generate a lot of unrecognized gestures.

The sign languages are the main method used by hearingimpaired people. Each sign language has specific characteristics as grammatical rules and their structure. The base structure is compound by a collection of gestures, movements, postures and facial expressions that all together generate the equivalent of letters, words and sentences in spoken language [6]. The sign language follows the patria language of the users. Therefore, for each spoken language, we have a different sign language. In American English, we have the American Sign Language (ASL); in French, we have the French Signal Language. Portuguese is the 9 th language in number of users in the world and Libras is its respective sign language. Interestingly, although Brazil and Portugal use the same spoken language called Portuguese, their respective sign languages, Libras and Portuguese Sign Language (in Portuguese L´ ıngua Gestual Portuguesa, LPG) are completely different. The same occurs between USA and UK with ASL and British Sign Language (BSL).

Despite the Libras popularity and usage, the literature presents few databases with gestures. The Brazilian Government, through the National Institute of Deaf Education (INES), maintains an online dictionary containing 3,853 lexical signs/items [7]. Despite the vast amount of signs, the dictionary has only one speaker, one background, and only one repetition of each word, making its usage for gesture recognition applications a hard task.

In this work, we will describe in detail the CEFET Libras Database, compounded by 547 videos with different gestures, hand positions, backgrounds and speakers without the aid of gloves or wearable tracking devices. This database may be used to train intelligent algorithms that can be implemented in robotic systems. We also proposed a computer-vision based method to recognize Libras signs in this database to serve as baseline. The method consists in a feature mapping based on the squared residual video, so the feature space can capture important details for Libras like expression, hand configuration and orientation as well as the motion. The classification of the words in the feature space can be performed by two classifiers, K-Nearest Neighbors (K-NN) or Random Forest (RF).

## II. RELATED WORKS

In the literature, most of the works discourses about static symbol recognition. The posture is a static hand position configuration, no movement is considered. In this case, the database can be constructed using only images instead of videos.

Carneiro et al. [8] evidenced the static symbols topic tackling the the alphabet recognition for Libras using neural networks. The authors produced a database formed by 50 images for each of the 26 symbols made by 3 volunteers, making a total of 3,900 images. The gesture recognition for the alphabet achieves 90% of accuracy.

Souza et al. [9] used a database mixing static and dynamic signs to perform the translation from Libras to Brazilian Portuguese. The database is composed of 46 static symbols and 13 words corresponding to 13,810 images and 939 video sequences, respectively. Two separated classification structures were adopted: one for the symbol classification that uses Hidden Conditional Random Fields (HCRF), and the other for the gesture classification that uses Support Vector Machine (SVM). The work shows 80.19% of accuracy using a 10-fold validation strategy. It can be observed, as a primary conclusion, that the gestures strongly reduces the overall accuracy.

In order to exemplify the last comment, it will be described a classification framework for 61 static symbols presented in Costa et al. [10]. The hand segmentation was performed by using the resources of a Kinect and the video sequence. This work used Principal Components Analysis (PCA) and 1-NN reaching the best accuracy of 96.31%, which is a good result in despite of the increase in the number of symbols.

Using a different perspective, the newly published work by Rocha et al. [2] combined symbols to create gestures. Each symbol is represented by static sign or more than one static sign in the same video, which are recorded with Chroma Key as background. However the number of speakers and repetitions were not detailed. The whole database consists in 31 classes composed by letters, symbols and some words. The authors achieved 99.42% of accuracy using a model based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).

This similar occurrence of showing higher hit rate for static symbols recognition can also be observed for other sign languages. Considering the usage of ASL [11] for static symbols (alphabet and digits), the best accuracy result achieved 99.93% using a fine-tuned CNN.

Dias et al. [12] performed a gesture recognition applied to Libras. The proposed database is generated from the data of 4 speakers, two men and two women, repeating three times each gesture, making a total of 600 samples. Although no result is mentioned on the paper, the gesture recognition reported uses Hidden Markov Machine (HMM).

Yang et al. [13] recently published a work based on Leap Motion Controller (LMC) and Deep Learning to classify dynamic hand gestures. Although it was the aim of the paper, it shows clearly how difficult is to aggregate the dynamic signs to the recognition task and their impact into the systems performance. The position of each finger in the video is precisely obtained by using LMC and considering the usage of an external gadget, this approach can be classified as VBGwGM. The results for a mixed static (60%) and dynamic (40%) symbols database (namely as HandicraftGesture Database), for 10 classes, using 10-fold validation and two-layer Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Network was only 90% of accuracy. Despite the fact that each finger was marked in the videos.

A Libras database is presented in Escobedo et al. [14]. It comprises 37 signs performed by ten subjects: six women and four men, containing RGB-D and skeleton information collected using a Kinect device. The database is supposed to be public; however, as far as we know, no means to obtain is provided. Moreover, a detailed description of the database is not given, making a comparison with our database unfeasible. The work also proposed CNN-based models that are trained using multimodal information (RGBD) through texture maps and hand configuration descriptors. Their best model achieved 87.02% of accuracy on the proposed database. As they use depth information in their method, a direct comparison with our results is unfair.

As a whole showed in this Section, we can conclude the classification of dynamic hand positioning is still a very challenging problem.

## III. DATABASE DESCRIPTION

In this section, we present our database which consists of 547 video sequences and 24 entries (words or phrases). The video sequences have 640 × 480 pixels as resolution and 30 Hz as frame rate. The records were done in a controlled environment with three static backgrounds: simple (F1), intermediate (F2), and complex (F3). Each entry was performed by 20 non-deaf volunteers, 13 women and 7 men. This database is available under request 3 .

Fig. 1: Database screenshots showing different speakers and backgrounds. Each row represents video frames in which a volunteer is performing a gesture in a background. First row: volunteer ID04, in background F1, performing the word 'scaffolding'; second row: volunteer ID03, in background F3, performing the word 'ghost'; third row: volunteer ID04, in background F2, performing the word 'miracle'.



The gesture sequence is performed in a video that describes a word entry as an acronym. The Table I shows all entries presented in our database and their respective acronym. It is possible to segregate the entries into two classes: the first one is with horizontal hands movement, and the other one, with vertical hands movements, as shown in Table II.

All the information about acronym, background, and volunteer identification is contained in each filename. For instance, the video named as MIGR\_F2\_ID04.avi is the video for acronym MIGR (word miracle), in background F2 by the volunteer ID04. Some screenshots are shown in Figure 1.

Following, we present some statistics of our database named CEFET LIBRAS Database. Figure 2 shows the duration (in seconds) distribution of the videos in the database. It is worth mentioning that the longest and the shortest videos of the database have 134 frames (5.37 seconds) and 14 frames (0.93 seconds), respectively. The average length of the videos is 50.05 ± 22.18 frames (2.34 ± 0.74 seconds).

Figure 3 shows a general information about the number of occurrences of the words in the database. The frequency of the words spoken by volunteers is depicted in Figures 3a and 3b showing the total number of frames for each word. We also analyze the distribution of the volunteers in the database, as shown in Figure 4, which shows the occurrence of each volunteer in the database. It is possible to notice that most of the speakers were recorded at least 25 times for different words.

## IV. AUTOMATIC GESTURES RECOGNITION

In this section, we describe a proposed method to recognize Libras signs in the described database to validate our database and to serve as a baseline for future works that will use our database. It is important to highlight that each video (640 × 480) was resized to q × q ( q ≤ 480 ) using bicubic interpolation before each feature extraction method. The feature extraction, detailed in Section IV-A consists in mapping the video frames into a feature space that we call S-Residue. After that, we perform the classification as described in Section IV-B. This pipeline is illustrated as a block diagram in Figure 5.

## A. Feature Extraction using residues

In our previous work [15], performed feature space mapping through the absolute residue according to:



where I n is the n -th frame in the video sequence. To obtain a specific size of features, the residual image R n was split into cells and each cell is represented using the sum of their values. However, some movements were canceled using this approach and it has an impact over the accuracy of the system as can be seen in Section IV-C. In this work, we use a different approach to avoid this problem. We perform the feature space mapping, which we call S-Residue by summing the squared residual frames according to

## C. Results

We validate our results using k -fold ( k = 3 ) cross validation so that the results in this section are the average across folders. We performed experiments varying q (Section IV) in the range { 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 50 , 100 } . To better compare to [15], we ran our experiments in two versions of the database, one full and other with 12 words (following the same rationale applied in [15]).

Figure 6 shows the results when using K-NN as classifiers. One can note from the graphic that the accuracy drops significantly when the number words are increased. The KNN is a simple classifier, which probably could not handle with the increase in the problem complexity when more words are taking into account. For the full database, the KNN average accuracy is 53.90% for q = 50 .

Figure 7 shows the performance when using RF, varying the number of trees. It is a much more powerful classifiers, so it could handle better with the full database. In this case, the best average accuracy is 65,81% when q = 50 and the number of trees is 400 .

All results are summarized in Table III. The result in the first line was reported in [15]. When using K-NN, there is no significant difference between absolute and squared residue. In all cases, the accuracy drops when the number of word increases. However, when using S-Residue with RF as multiclass classifier, the accuracy remains satisfactory.

## V. CONCLUSIONS

Technological tools for sign languages are very important to diminish the communication gap between the deaf community and the majority of the people. Tools using computer vision can be very powerful since they can be less intrusive. However, computer vision solutions are extremely dependent on the available data. In Brazil, there are about 9.7 million people with some degree of hearing impairment, but there is not a large reliable database for computer vision

applications in Libras. In this work, we describe in detail the CEFET Libras database, which is a challenging database with 547 videos and 24 dynamic signs. To serve as a baseline, we developed a computer vision-based system to recognize the gestures (the first one using the full database). In the proposed system, the feature mapping is performed by summing the squared residual video. This feature space (which we call S-Residue) can capture the Libras details, such as the face, hand configuration, as well as motion.

The gestures in feature space were classified through K-NN and RF. In the k-fold cross-validation framework ( k = 3 ), we achieved an average accuracy of 65.81%. Due to the complexity of the database, we consider it a satisfactory result.

## Paper Source: American Sign Language Recognition with Convolutional Neural Networks A Gateway to Enhanced Inclusivity

## American Sign Language Recognition with Convolutional Neural Networks: A Gateway to Enhanced Inclusivity

Naoufal El-Marzouki ( B ) , Imane Lasri , Anouar Riadsolh,

and Mourad Elbelkacemi

Laboratory of Conception and Systems (Electronics, Signals and Informatics), Faculty of Sciences, Mohammed V University in Rabat, Rabat, Morocco

{naoufal\_elmarzouki,imane\_lasri}@um5.ac.ma,

a.riadsolh@um5r.ac.ma

Abstract. In the realm of higher education, where the right to inclusive education is fundamental, it is essential to address the distinctive challenges faced by students with disabilities, particularly those who are deaf. This study explores inadequacies in accommodating the needs of deaf students within a university setting through the implementation of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for sign language recognition. We conducted thorough testing of our model using three optimizers Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM), Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Nesterov's Momentum. Notably, the highest test accuracy of 96% was attained when employing SGD with Nesterov momentum on the Sign MNIST dataset. These findings underscore that our proposed approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

Keywords: Inclusive Education · Sign Language Recognition · Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) · Deep Learning

## 1 Introduction

In the continually advancing realm of inclusive education, there is a growing recognition of the need to address the unique requirements of students with disabilities, particularly those who are deaf or hard of hearing and rely on sign language as their primary mode of communication. Traditional educational methods often struggle to fully accommodate these students' communication needs, presenting barriers to effective learning and participation. Recent research has responded to this challenge by harnessing the progress in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning to offer tailored support for students with disabilities. Inclusive classrooms emphasize the importance of diverse communication modes such as sign language, communication aids, or augmented and alternative communication methods [1]. Nevertheless, many educators encounter difficulties in managing this diversity due to insufficient training and support [2]. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) emerges as a pivotal tool in fostering e-inclusion, necessitating accessible resources and teacher competencies for genuine inclusive education [2]. Highlighting the significance of adaptable teaching materials and localized approaches, Huang et al. [1] underscore the role of ICT in enabling successful education, particularly in marginalized settings like rural areas. Echoing these sentiments, Drigas and Ioannidou [3] emphasize how ICT can revolutionize special education, enabling comprehensive assessment and effective interventions to enrich the learning experiences of students with special educational needs.

Recognizing these challenges, this article embarks on an exploration of an innovative solution that seeks to revolutionize the educational landscape for individuals reliant on sign language. At the heart of this transformative approach is the integration of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) [4] technology. The choice of CNNs is strategic, as these neural networks excel in pattern recognition tasks, making them particularly well-suited for the intricate and nuanced nature of sign language interpretation.

The use of sign language as a primary means of communication stands out as an important feature within the deaf and hard-of-hearing community. This underscores the importance of developing tailored tools and approaches to cater to their unique communication needs. While conventional educational methods may struggle to adapt to these unique requirements, the infusion of CNN technology aims to bridge the communication gap. By leveraging the power of deep learning and neural networks, we aspire to create a more inclusive and effective educational environment for individuals with hearing and speech impairments.

The main objectives of this study can be outlined as follows:

- Introducing an innovative sign language model utilizing Convolutional Neural Network CNN.
- Assessing the effectiveness of the model in recognizing sign language through assessments using different pre-trained model optimizers on the Sign MNIST dataset.

The subsequent sections of this article are organized as follows: Sect. 2 presents related work, while Sect. 3 introduces the proposed methodology in the domain of sign language recognition. Section 4 outlines our proposed CNN-based methodology and discusses the obtained results. Finally, Sect. 5 encapsulates the conclusion.

## 2 Related Work

In the realm of inclusive education and assistive technology, several studies have investigated the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning algorithms to facilitate communication and learning for individuals with disabilities. Srivastava [5] emphasizes the importance of AI-driven Smart Learning Assistance tools in fostering inclusive education, ensuring equitable access, and efficient communication for students with disabilities in educational settings. Additionally, Jarbou et al. [6] demonstrate the efficacy of deep learning algorithms in forecasting school absenteeism among autistic students, potentially amplifying their access to crucial educational and therapeutic resources while mitigating the likelihood of dropout.

Jain et al. [7] utilized CNNs to recognize American Sign Language and highlighted the significance of filter size, demonstrating the potential for improvements. Mittal et al.

[8] designed a sign language recognition system using LSTM and Leap Motion. They applied a four-gated LSTM cell with a 2D CNN for sentence recognition, achieving 72.3% accuracy. Individual word recognition attained an accuracy of 89.50% with this system. Aparna and Geetha [9] propose a pioneering sign language recognition method, blending CNNs and LSTM networks. They use pre-trained CNNs for feature extraction, followed by LSTM layers, achieving a notable 94% accuracy on the Indian Sign Language (ISL) dataset, demonstrating its significance in deep learning-based sign language recognition.

## 3 Proposed Methodology

## 3.1 American Sign Language Recognition Using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

In our research, a customized convolutional neural network (CNN) [4] model tailored for image recognition was utilized. The first convolutional layer applies 128 filters, succeeded by max pooling for dimension reduction. A second convolutional layer with 64 filters is introduced, followed by another max-pooling layer. Subsequently, a third convolutional layer with 32 filters is implemented, along with a corresponding maxpooling layer. The output is then flattened into a one-dimensional array before traversing through a fully connected layer with 7 neurons and a ReLU activation. A dropout layer is strategically incorporated to mitigate overfitting, deactivating 25% of neurons. The final layer comprises 24 neurons with Softmax activation for multi-class classification. This comprehensive architecture aligns with our overarching goal of advancing sign language recognition technology and promoting inclusivity within educational environments. Figure 1 illustrates a flowchart of our proposed methodology, while Table 1 presents the model summary of the CNN model.

## 3.2 Models Optimization

In order to optimize the categorical cross-entropy loss function of our models, defined in the following equation:



where m is the number of samples, C is the number of classes, Yij is an indicator of whether class j is the correct classification for sample i , and pij is the predicted probability of sample i belonging to class j , we employed a range of optimization algorithms. This range included Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) [10], Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM)[11],andSGDwithNesterovMomentum[12].Thisdiverseselectionwasmade with the specific goal of thoroughly assessing and comparing the impact of different optimization methods on the performance in our study.

- Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) [10] : is a widely utilized optimization algorithm in the field of machine learning, particularly for training complex models like neural networks. Its fundamental principle revolves around iteratively updating model

- Consider a parametric model f(x; θ ) where x is the input, θ represents the model parameters, and f(x; θ ) is the model prediction. The objective is to minimize a loss function J( θ ) associated with the difference between the model predictions and true values. The parameter update with SGD can be mathematically formulated as follows:



where θ t is the parameter vector at iteration t, η is the learning rate, a hyperparameter controlling the size of the update steps, JB( θ t) is the loss function, and ∇ θ JB( θ t) is the gradient of the loss function with respect to parameters θ t.

- Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with Nesterov's Momentum [12] : is an optimization algorithm employed in machine learning, especially for training neural networks. It enhances the standard SGD algorithm by incorporating Nesterov's Momentum, a modification of traditional momentum. Nesterov's Momentum introduces a look-ahead mechanism, anticipating the next parameter update and adjusting the optimization trajectory accordingly. Mathematically, the update rules for Nesterov's Momentum within the SGD framework can be expressed as follows:



where, vt represents the velocity term, γ is the momentum parameter, vt -1 is the velocity at the previous time step, η is the learning rate, ∇ J is the gradient of the loss function, and θ t denotes the current parameters. The parameter update is performed using the velocity term vt , contributing to improved convergence speed and stability, particularly in scenarios with complex optimization landscapes.

- Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) [11] : is a commonly used method. The moment update is converted into an exponential moving average. The equation of the ADAM optimization algorithm is represented as follows:



where θ t+1 represents the updated parameters at time step t + 1 , θ t represents the current parameters at time step t , α denotes the learning rate, vt represents the average of squared gradients diminishing exponentially, /epsilon1 is a small constant (usually around 1 × 10 -8 ) for numerical stability, and mt represents the exponentially decaying average of gradients.

## 3.3 Models Evaluation

- Accuracy: defined in (5), represents the ratio of the number of correct predictions to the total number of observations in the dataset



- Precision: defined in (6), is a metric assessing the accuracy of a model in recognizing pertinent objects. Calculated as the ratio of True Positives (TPs) to the overall detections made by the model, precision essentially measures the model's capability to accurately pinpoint and categorize objects of interest within its predictions.



- Recall: defined in (7), assesses the model's ability to recognize all true instances, indicating the ratio of True Positives (TPs) to the total actual instances. A well-suited model is characterized by both high precision and high recall. A flawless model, where Precision equals 1 and Recall equals 1, implies the complete elimination of False Negatives (FNs) and False Positives (FPs). However, achieving such perfection is often a challenging task.



- F1-score: defined in (8), measures the harmonic mean between recall and precision.



## 4 Experimental Results

## 4.1 Setup Environment

Theexperiment was conducted using a system running Windows 10 with 16 GB of RAM, a 64-bit architecture, a CPU with a clock speed of 3.20 GHz, Nvidia GTX 1070 graphics card, and an Intel Core i7 processor. We employed the Python-based Keras library [13] to facilitate the integration of models featuring different layer configurations into the training procedure. Before being fed into the system, images underwent resizing to dimensions of 224 × 224 pixels. Our model of choice was the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The entire process was conducted within the Google Colab platform, utilizing GPUs to ensure consistent conditions across all four models. Throughout the training phases, vigilant observation of the model weights enabled us to pinpoint the stage of peak validation accuracy.

## 4.2 Sign MNIST Dataset

The dataset used in this study has been carefully designed to closely resemble the wellknown sign MNIST dataset [14], as shown in Fig. 2, providing a familiar framework for researchers and practitioners. Essentially, each training and test case, aligning with the inherent challenge of accurately capturing gesture nuances.

Regarding size, the training data consists of 27455 individual cases, each uniquely labeled and prepared for analysis. Similarly, the test dataset comprises 7172 cases meticulously curated for validation purposes. While slightly smaller than the traditional MNIST handwritten digit dataset, it maintains a comparable underlying structure, facilitating seamless comparisons and analyses. The dataset follows a consistent format, starting with a header row containing essential information such as the label associated with a particular case. Subsequent columns represent pixel values, numbered from pixel1 to pixel784. Each pixel value indicates the grayscale intensity of a single pixel in a 28x28 image, ranging from 0 to 255. This detailed pixel-level representation serves as the foundation for capturing the visual intricacies of the images in the dataset, supporting subsequent analysis and recognition efforts.

Fig. 2. Example of images from the sign language MNIST dataset



## 4.3 Results

Figure 3 presents the performance of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model in terms of various metrics. The 96% accuracy indicates that the model correctly classified 96% of the data. With a precision of 99%, the model is accurate 99% of the time when predicting the positive class. A recall of 98% means that the model correctly identified 98% of instances belonging to the positive class. Lastly, the 99% F-score represents a harmonic mean between precision and recall, indicating a high overall balance between these two measures. These results suggest that the CNN model demonstrates strong and balanced performance across the metrics, although evaluation should always be interpreted in the context of the specific nature of the problem and dataset characteristics.

Fig. 3. Performance metrics for CNN-based sign language model



In the evaluation of different CNN models, three optimization algorithms were employed,asshowninFig.4.StochasticGradientDescent(SGD)withNesterovmomentum achieved the highest accuracy at 96%, showcasing its effectiveness in converging to optimal solutions during training. The second model, utilizing plain Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), achieved a commendable accuracy of 94.70%, demonstrating the robustness of traditional SGD optimization. Lastly, the ADAM optimizer yielded an accuracy of 90%, indicating its slightly lower performance compared to the SGD variants in the specific context of the CNN models under consideration.

Fig. 4. Performance comparison of optimizers based on test accuracy



Table 2 provides a comparative overview of Sign Language Recognition Accuracy across different methodologies. The first approach, employing 2D-CNN and Modified LSTM with a Leap motion sensor [8], achieves an accuracy of 89.50% on a custom dataset with 3150 signs. In contrast, a CNN and 2-layer LSTM [9] model attain a higher accuracy of 94% on a smaller custom dataset of 6 signs. The third method, utilizing CNN [15], achieves an accuracy of 94.7% on the NUS hand Posture dataset and American Fingerspelling A Dataset. Notably, the proposed approach in the study outperforms all others, achieving a remarkable 96% accuracy, leveraging the MNIST dataset for evaluation.

Table 2. Comparison of sign language recognition accuracy among different approaches

| Methodology                                          | Dataset                                    | Accuracy   |
|------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|------------|
| 2D-CNN and Modified LSTM with Leap motion sensor [8] | Custom Dataset (3150 signs)                | 89.50%     |
| CNN and 2layer LSTM [9]                              | Custom Dataset (20 videos)                 | 94%        |
| CNN [15]                                             | NUS hand Posture dataset, American Dataset | 94.7%      |
| Our proposed approach                                | MNIST dataset (American)                   | 96%        |

## 5 Conclusion

In conclusion, our research underscores the pivotal role played by Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in advancing the domain of sign language recognition, especially within the realms of higher education and inclusive learning environments. The robust methodology we proposed, harnessing a meticulously curated dataset and customized optimization techniques, has yielded remarkable success, boasting a test accuracy of 96%. This surpasses the performance of other state-of-the-art methodologies. The precision, recall, and F-score of our model further accentuate its proficiency in accurately classifying sign language gestures, an important aspect for effective communication in educational settings. These results not only highlight the viability of our CNN-based approach but also underscore its potential to foster more inclusive educational environments by facilitating communication for students who are deaf or hard of hearing. The adaptability of our model, striking a balance between precision and recall, ensures reliable and consistent performance across various metrics. Looking ahead, our work contributes significantly to the ongoing discourse on leveraging artificial intelligence to enhance accessibility and inclusivity. The success of our methodology serves as a solid foundation for continued exploration and development, encouraging collaboration among academia, technology developers, and educational institutions to create a more equitable and accessible learning experience for all students, irrespective of their abilities or disabilities. Through ongoing research and implementation efforts, we envision a future where advanced technologies like Deep CNN play a pivotal role in breaking down communication barriers and promoting inclusivity in educational settings globally.

## Interactive Learning Environments







## An intelligent system to help deaf students learn Arabic Sign Language

Hosnia M. Mohammdi a and Doaa M. Elbourhamy



a Computer Science Department, Mansoura University, Mansoura, Egypt; b Educational Technology and Computer Department, Kafr-elshiekh University, Kafr el-Sheikh, Egypt

## ABSTRACT

This paper proposes a new system to translate an Arabic Sign Language (ArSL). The system consists of two sub-systems: the fi rst, Speech to ArSL translation Subsystem. This sub-system is mainly based on the speech recognition engine. The second is ArSL to speech translation subsystem to translate the images of signs into speech, mainly based on GTTS library. This system will be easily used by both groups (the hearing disabled and normal persons) who want to learn ArSL and will support more communication between them. Among the advantages of this system is that it is expandable by adding new signs to the database and can be accessed online at: https://sr.gravita-demo.com/. The proposed system was evaluated using several methods. The fi ndings show that the system can translate ArSL with a recognition rate of 99%. An experimental approach was used to evaluate the e ff ectiveness of the proposed system. Results show that the proposed system was e ff ective and the ability of Arab deaf students to learn improved signi fi cantly. In addition, the system ' s performance evaluation questionnaire revealed that system users preferred this approach to ArSL learning and teaching and acquired new concepts, which predicts a promising future for this system in academic environments.

## 1. Introduction

Based on WHO ' s statistics, more than 5% of the world ' s population (466 million approximately) are hearing disabled (432 Million adults and 34 Million children). More than 900 million people will be su ff ering from hearing loss by 2050. Moreover, around 10 million people in the Middle East are Deaf. According to the World Federation of the Deaf, there were more than 700,000 persons in the Arab world who were deaf and hearing impaired in 2008 (Alzohairi et al., 2018; Neiva &amp; Zanchettin, 2018; Salema et al., 2019; WHO, 2020). Those su ff ering from hearing and/or speaking disorders cannot communicate or interact orally with others, especially when they try to get interact in educational, social and work environments. Moreover, they often have di ffi culties in learning how to read and write texts (Alzohairi et al., 2018; El-Gayyar et al., 2016; Shukor et al., 2015). Hence, usually they are excluded from society and are deprived from their rights to equal educational and professional opportunities. This being the case, these people are in a dire need for a language to communicate with people around them. Here, comes the role of sign languages as an e ff ective alternative to express their ideas and thoughts, to fi ll the gap communication between them and others (Alzohairi et al., 2018; Suharjito et al., 2017). The gesture is one of the nonverbal and non-vocal communication forms in which di ff erent body parts are used to express certain sentences and messages



## ARTICLE HISTORY

Received 6 February 2021 Accepted 17 April 2021

## KEYWORDS

Arabic Sign Language; sign language recognition; speech recognition engine; Google text to speech; deaf



(Bairagi, 2014). Sign language is a set of hand gestures and movements, positions and facial expressions that correspond to letters and words in natural languages. So, the sign language has more than one form because of its dependence on natural languages (Al-Dosri et al., 2014; ElBendary et al., 2011; Kumar et al., 2017). In the twentieth century, Sign Language (SL) acquired increasing interest and global recognition by several linguists and computer scientists because it is regarded as the Native language of the deaf who can use it to voice their needs and form concepts (Ahmed et al., 2018; Almasoud &amp; Al-Khalif, 2011). Like spoken languages, SL is not universally uni fi ed as each country has its own SL that is used by its hearing disabled citizens. So, there are Chinese sign language (CSL), Arabic Sign Language (ArSL), French sign language (LSF), … etc. (Brour &amp; Benabbou, 2019; Cheok, 2019). In the Arab world, ArSL is the o ffi cial sign language for people su ff ering from hearing and speech impairment. ArSL was formally launched in 2001 by the Arab Federation of the Deaf (AFD). In spite of being one of the most spoken languages globally, ArSL is still under evolution (Abdel-Fattah, 2005; Alzohairi et al., 2018). Studies conducted by the National Association of Deaf indicate the need for using Sign Language to educate those su ff ering from hearing impairment (Amrutha et al., 2016). Many schools were opened speci fi cally to teach sign language to the Deaf in several countries. However, these schools still need to be more developed, especially in our Arab societies. Although ArSL is the most used method to teach the deaf in the Arab world, opportunities for qualifying and training SL translators/teachers are few, which adversely a ff ect the ability of deaf student to learn SL and create a strong need for the development of modern methods and technologies to teach SL to deaf students. On the other part, SL teaching lessons consumes a lot of money and time and usually are provided in formal oneto-many sessions with a teacher who train learners/trainees how to perform the signs (Foong &amp; Low, 2009; Ritchings et al., 2012). Hence, it is highly important to develop tools and techniques to improve and facilitate SL learning to include the hearing disabled in educational environments (Pontes et al., 2018). With the current advancements in information technology and communication, it has become essential to develop several assistive systems to support the deaf communities globally (El-Gayyar et al., 2016). Recently, there has been an increased interest in developing automatic Sign Language recognition systems (SLRS) to further the communication between normal and hearing impaired or deaf people (Yang et al., 2016). SLRS is one of the application areas of human -computer interaction (HCI). The main goal of SLRS is to recognize signs of hearing-impaired people and convert them to text or speech and vice versa (Al-Rousan et al., 2009; Ibrahim et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017; Tubaiz et al., 2015) which is the fi eld of our current study. Several studies, including El-Gayyar et al. (2016), indicate that assistive technologies targeting Deaf communities in the Arab world are very few and limited due to the complexity of both Arabic and ArSL (El-Gayyar et al., 2016). ArSL studies admit the need for developing technologies that can be used to meet the requirements of the hearing impaired or the deaf in the Arab world. They also aim at creating environments that can include those su ff ering from hearing loss. This fi eld of research is encouraged and supported in the Arab world by several social bodies in health, educational, transport and other sectors. However, few individual attempts were done to develop computer ArSL learning systems (Almasre &amp; Al-Nuaim, 2020). In view of this, the main motive behind the development of our proposed system is to try to supplement research e ff orts in the fi eld of ArSL recognition and attract the attention of the researchers of this fi eld to serve the interests of the Deaf. This paper presents an interactive web-based system that can support teaching SL in classrooms and enable users to use SL without supervision at their own pace at home. The system performs a two-way translation between SL and spoken language. The system is mainly designed to help students su ff ering from hearing impairment to learn ArSL, improve their interaction with the hearing world and acquire new concepts. It also plays an important role in assisting SL teachers. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: we outline related work in Section 2, describe the proposed system in Section 3, show experimental work in Section 4, describe system evaluation in Section 5, follow this by an outline of our fi ndings in Section 6 and fi nally present the conclusion and future work.

## 2. Related work

Sign language recognition has been an active area research and development in recent years. Many systems developed for sign language recognition targeting di ff erent sign languages Table 1 provides an overview of these studies. However, few of these systems were developed to recognize ArSL, mainly due to a lack of resources or the complexity of the Arabic language itself Table 2 provides an overview of these studies.

## 3. Description of the proposed system

This paper proposes an ArSL translation system. It is an educational application developed to support the deaf and the dumb community to facilitate their communication with normal people. It also helps learn and teach ArSL in academic environments. This system is used to convert user ' s speech into signs/text or convert the signs of the deaf user to speech/text, which makes it a two-way system and makes special communities closer to normal people. In general, this system enables users to choose one of two di ff erent systems: Speech to ArSL or ArSL to speech. This is shown in Figure 1, which presents an overview of the architecture of the proposed system.

In this section, we will describe and discuss the details of the proposed system and the used database. From Figure 1, it is clear that the system consists of two sub-systems, each of which will be discussed in detail in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 below.

## 3.1 Speech to ArSL subsystem

Speech to ArSL subsystem was developed to translate and convert natural speech into signs understandable by the deaf. The system works in several phases, as shown in Figure 1.

## 3.1.1 Speech input

At fi rst, the user ' s Arabic speech is input through the microphone. Then, this speech is sent to the speech recognition engine to be processed.

## 3.1.2 Speech recognition engine

The Speech to ArSL Subsystem mainly depends on a software component known as the speech recognition engine that has a somewhat complex job, that is, to receive speech input, recognize it and translate it into a recognized text understandable by the application. Speech recognition techniques can be divided into two categories: speaker dependent and speaker independent. In speaker-dependent systems, models are created for a particular speaker and subsequently are not intended to work for di ff erent speakers. Speaker-independent systems need to be more generic and consequently require more complex design. Speech recognition systems tend to be much more complicated because of the large variation of pronunciations, even from the same speaker, depending on the context and mood of the speaker (Kim et al., 2019). In this work, the Speech to ArSL Subsystem uses speaker-dependent and independent speech recognition system using Python-based Arabic speech recognition library.

## 3.1.3 Text tokenization

Tokenization is a process in which a text stream is broken up into words, phrases, symbols, or other meaningful elements that are called tokens (Vijayarani &amp; Janani, 2016). in this phase, the recognized text in the previous step is split into tokens consisting of words using the method split.



Figure 1. Architecture of the proposed system.



## 3.1.4 Searching &amp; matching

The database is an important part of the entire application development. In this phase, the database/ dictionary of the proposed system was built. It is noteworthy that a uni fi ed ArSL dictionary was published in two versions in 2008. However, due to the lack of a serious interest in ArSL recognition, there are no common databases available to researchers in this area. So, we built our own Sqlite database named ' Speech Database ' using SQLparse library, which is a database development library in Python. The Speech Database consists of two tables: Sdata, which contains the list of stored signs and their corresponding words, and SImage, which contains the images that will be selected to be converted into speech in the ArSL -To-Speech subsystem, which will be described in detail in Section 3.2 below. The Speech Database contains a list of about 500 signs for the following sections: letters, numbers, education and learning, school and its tools, animals, food and its tools, family, friends and people, money and quantities, sports and hobbies, time and seasons, travel, holidays and directions, home, clothes and colors, jobs, health and emergency, synonyms and antitheses, di ff erent things. These are the most used signs in communication between the deaf and hearing impaired and normal people in academic environments and life activities. These sections were used based on a discussion with students su ff ering from hearing/ speech disabled and their teachers. The speech database is characterized by being easily expandable through a webbased interface that allows the admin to add new signs to the database and delete other signs from it. Figure 2 shows the administration panel of the database, which allows controlling the database.



After building the Speech Database, the system searches in the speech database for the word/ sequence of words obtained in the previous phase. When a match with the words pre-stored in the database is found, the equivalent sign/sequence of signs are retrieved and showed to the deaf person to understand the speech of the normal person. The system uses still images with no motion to express the recognized speech, so, it is more suitable for educational purposes rather than for translation.

## 3.1.5 Output

As output, the system displays the image/images of the sign equivalent to the speech input, with its textual value displayed below the image. This system provides the output in one of two cases: The fi rst case, an image of a sign equivalent to a single spoken word. In the second case, the system presents a sequence of sign images equivalent to a certain sentence/sequence of spoken words. Figure 3 shows the pseudo code of the system developed for translating speech into sign image and text.

## 3.2 ArSL to speech translation subsystem

ArSL to speech translation subsystem was developed to translate sign images into natural speech understandable by normal people. This system consists of several phases, as shown in Figure 1.

## 3.2.1 Input sign image(s)

The input of this system is a sign image/sequence of sign images to be converted into natural speech that can be heard on a speaker.

## 3.2.2 Image store

After selecting the sign image/image sequence as inputs for the system, these images are stored in the ' image store ' (SImage table in the Speech Database), which is a temporary memory where recently identi fi ed images are stored to perform search and retrieval process, as will be shown in the following step, to obtain the right outputs. Note that all the images stored in the SImage table will be completely deleted once the required output is obtained by the system, and SImage will become ready for other new entries.

Figure 2. GUI of Django administration database panel.

Figure 3. Pseudo code for translating speech to ArSL.

## 3.2.3 Searching &amp; retrieval

The Speech-to-ArSL system also depends mainly on the same Speech Database mentioned above. In this phase, the system searches inside the ' Sdata ' table for the sign image/image sequence stored in the ' image store ' one after the other. If a match is found, the word/sequence of words corresponding these images are retrieved. In this way, the input sign image is converted into text, which is then sent to the Google text To speech (GTTS) and Google Text to Speech Token (GTTS-token) libraries. The basic idea upon which the search process is based is that the image is stored in the database under the same name of the image searched for. For example, if the word to be searched for ' ﻛﺘﺎﺑ ' , its corresponding image name will be ' ﻛﺘﺎﺑ ' hence, the search is done using the image name.

## 3.2.4 GTTS

In this phase, the text (word/sequence of words) received from the previous phase will be translated and converted into speech using GTTS library. This library has been used to achieve the highest accuracy and e ffi ciency by converting the text into speech so that a normal person can hear the speech corresponding to these signs through the microphone. Along with GTTS library, GTTStoken library was used to ensure the e ffi ciency of speech by dividing the input text into small parts each of which consists of one letter so that the output speech looks as closer as possible to the natural and continuous speech of a natural person.



## 3.2.5 Output

The output of the system is the equivalent speech of the input sign image/sequence of images with a display of the textual value of this speech input. This system provides output in one of two cases: the fi rst case, a speci fi c spoken word matching a single input sign image is output. in the second case, a sequence of words/spoken sentence is output matching the input sign images. ## 5. System evaluation

Expert evaluations were widely used to evaluate the outputs of the proposed system, validate it and ensure its applicability by presenting it to a number of ArSL experts, who selected a number of desired inputs and outputs for the purposes of evaluating the system. Evaluation was conducted in two phases: fi rst, they operated the system and input an ordered set of Arabic speech (isolated words, complete sentences) to see if the system will output the equivalent signs. Then, they identi fi ed a sign image/sequence of sign images to make sure the system will output the speech matching such inputs. The number of Correct and incorrect outputs were recorded. After that, the recognition rate was calculated using the following equation (Anggraini et al., 2018):



where RR is the Recognition Rate, Ncorrect is the number of signs/spoken words correctly recognized, and NTotal is the total number of signs/spoken words input to the system.

The fi ndings show that the proposed system was able to translate ArSL with a recognition rate of 99% whereas only 1% of the inputs were not recognized. This high accuracy rate mainly due to two major factors: the accuracy and quality of the speech recognition engine and the accuracy of GTTS engine. Those experts con fi rmed that the system is reliable and applicable and can be used as a practical and educational tool to recognize ArSL.

## 6. Results and discussion

The objective of this study is to develop a web-based ArSL translation system as a contribution to the automatic recognition of ArSL and an attempt to solve the di ffi culties and challenges faced by deaf students in educational environments in terms of interacting and communicating with normal peoples, and to facilitate their inclusion in the educational community more e ff ectively as well as to encourage and support the learning of ArSL. To achieve that goal, we divided it into sub-goals and phrased them as research questions. Here are the research questions we tried to answer:

Q1: What are the speci fi cations of the proposed ArSL learning system?

Q2: How e ff ective is the proposed system in teaching ArSL to the participants of the study?

In the following section, we will discuss in detail the experimental fi ndings of the study.

## 6.1 Participants

The participants were a representative random sample consisting of 60 male and female hearing disabled students aging 6 -8 years in hearing-impaired School cycle1, Al Mansoura City. Participants were divided into two equal groups, the control group ( n = 30) and the experimental group ( n = 30), as well as about 15 volunteers (teachers, specialists for the deaf and speech disabled, and normal persons).

Figure 10. Translating ArSL into speech and text as output.





## 6.2 Experimental results

After ensuring the system ' s applicability, it was implemented and used by the participants. But before implementing the system, the researchers prepared an illustrated test to measure the participant ' s acquisition of the signs included in the system. Test questions were objective and illustrated comprising two types of question: multiple choice questions and matching linked shapes. In its primary form, the test comprised 28 items. Test validity was veri fi ed by Arbitrators of instructional technology and special education arbitrators, who recommended some modi fi cations to the phrasing of certain vocabulary items. The reliability of the test was veri fi ed using Cronbach ' s Alpha, after implementing the test to a pilot sample. Reliability factor was 0.81, which shows that the test has an acceptable reliability. Di ffi culty and discrimination levels of each test items were calculated and three items were deleted, so that, in its fi nal form, the test consisted of 25 items with a maximum score of 25 and the available time for answers is about 25 min. Thus, the test became applicable to the research participants. After preparing the illustrated test and ensuring its validity and reliability, the research experiment was implemented as follows: the pre-test was implemented to the participants. After that, the experimental group studied the proposed system whereas the control group studied the same system content in the traditional way. The implementation took twelve weeks in the fi rst term of 2019/2020 school year. Finally, the post-test was implemented to the participants and data were collected for perform the appropriate statistical processing and then answer the questions of the study. To answer the fi rst research question, the proposed system was developed as described in detail in the above sections. To answer the second research question, the following three research hypotheses were veri fi ed:

Hypothesis 1 : There are statistically signi fi cant di ff erences between mean scores of the pre- and post-test of the experimental group in the illustrated test for the favor of the post-test. To validate Hypothesis 1, the T-test was used. Table 3 shows the signi fi cance of the di ff erences between the mean scores of the pre- and post-tests of the experimental group students in the illustrated test.

From the results shown in Table 3, the value of ( T ) calculated at the comparison of the mean scores of the pre- and post-tests for the students of the experimental group in the illustrated test is (11.096), which is statistically signi fi cant at level 0.01 for favor of the post-test. Thus, Hypothesis 1 is validated.

Hypothesis 2 : There are statistically signi fi cant di ff erences between mean scores of the control and experimental groups in the post-test of the illustrated test for the favor of the experimental group. To validate this Hypothesis, the T-test for both groups was used. Table 4 shows the signi fi cant di ff erences between the mean scores of the students of the control and experimental groups in the post illustrated test.

From the results shown in Table 4, the value of ( T ) calculated at the comparison of the mean scores of the students of the control and experimental groups in the post-test of the illustrated test, is equal to (3.045), which is statistically signi fi cant at the level 0.01 for favor of the experimental group, Thus, Hypothesis 2 is validated.

From Table 5, it is clear that the e ff ectiveness of the traditional method to teaching ArSL to the control group was 0.9416, which is relatively representative but less than the e ff ectiveness threshold (&gt;1.2), which makes the traditional method lower in terms of acquiring and learning sign language. However, the e ff ectiveness of the proposed system used to teach ArSL to the experimental group was 1.3624, which is greater than the e ff ectiveness threshold (&gt;1.2). This indicates that the proposed system is more e ff ective in acquiring and teaching ArSL. We should note that another method was used to test and evaluate the proposed system by the Deaf students, who interacted with the volunteers during two di ff erent evaluation sessions each lasted over 3 h in the presence of an ArSL specialist. During these evaluation sessions, for the purposes of the test, we carefully created several realistic scenarios and situations related to what these students learned, such as requesting di ff erent types of information or services or simulating di ff erent types of problems that require the interaction of the hearing disabled users with the volunteers. At fi rst, the volunteers looked at signs implemented the hearing disabled students, such as Where is the pen? After then, the volunteers were asked to convert these signs into spoken words. In addition, the deaf students looked at certain signs and were asked to identify them, such as ' ﺍﻧﻌﻄﻒ ﻳﻤﻴﻨ ّ ﺎ ' (Turn right) and the students did as they were told and so on. After that, certain questions were asked to the participants through the questionnaire prepared by the authors using Google Forms at the following link: https://forms.gle/dWecksaPtoGgCD2c6. Through this questionnaire, several aspects of the system performance can be assessed. The questionnaire was prepared in Standard Arabic and ArSL. The questionnaire contains six simple questions with a scale of fi ve answers (1 = Poor, 2 = Fair, 3 = Good, 4 = Very Good and 5 = Excellent). The questions were designed to identify whether the system is easy-to-use, helpful, has a low response time, gives correct translations and is suitable to learn ArSL. The objective of the last question is to identify whether individuals are ready to use it on a daily basis. Figure 11(a -f) shows the results of the questionnaire.

## 7. Conclusion

Teaching and learning Sign Language is one of the main challenges faced by the Deaf students, their teachers and normal people interacting with them. So, this paper proposed a two-way system to translate ArSL into speech and translate speech into ArSL. The system aims at teaching ArSL signs to the Deaf and also to normal people, which helps fi lling the communication gap between them. So, this proposed system may motivate parents, friends, teachers and normal persons to learn Sign Language to communicate with the hearing disabled in the family or in the society in general, and in classrooms in particular. The application supports several platforms. To identify the feasibility of this system in educational environments, tests and questionnaire were implemented to collect data from the Deaf students and their teachers in classrooms. Results show that the proposed system is accurate and e ff ective. Moreover, all system users found it

useful and suitable for learning ArSL. In addition, the system was evaluated by the experts of the fi eld and the results show that the proposed system was able to translate ArSL in both ways with a recognition rate of 99%. We intend to develop the system more in future to meet various teaching and learning scenarios and to provide it as an iPhone app.

## Paper Source: Application of Three-Dimensional Interactive Virtual Conference in Special Education
