Department of Computer Science and Engineering Velammal College of Engineering and Technology, Madurai, India revathyjeganathan@gmail.com

The  main  goal  is  to  develop  effective  methods  that  can quickly  identify  and  categorize  different  kinds  of  sign language motions [2].

The field of sign language recognition has seen the use of numerous algorithms and techniques. Because Convolutional  Neural  Networks  (CNNs)  are  so  good  at image classification tasks -including identifying sign language  gestures -they  have  become  industry  standard technology.  Recurrent  neural  networks  (RNNs)  include Long  Short-Term  Memory  (LSTM)  networks,  which  are highly  useful  for  recognizing  the  temporal  connections present in sequential data. This is important because it helps to comprehend how sign language expressions change over time.  Modeling  the  changes  between  various  states  or postures in sign language movements is a useful application for  Hidden  Markov  Models  (HMMs),  which  are  wellknown  for  their  skill  in  sequential  data  processing.  One further classification system that may be useful in identifying particular signs or movements in sign language is Support Vector Machines (SVMs).

Additionally, other deep learning architectures outside of CNNs and LSTMs, like Transformer models, Recurrent Convolutional  Neural  Networks  (RCNNs),  and  Residual Networks (ResNets), provide better scalability and performance  for  a  variety  of  sign  language  identification tasks.  The  choice  of  algorithm  is  influenced  by  various aspects, including the application requirements, processing resources, dataset size, and gesture complexity. In order to meet  the  varied  demands  of  the  community  and  promote inclusion in communication and education, sign language recognition technology  is  continually  evolving  due  to ongoing study and innovation in algorithm development.

Accurate categorisation is essential for creating inclusivity  and  removing  barriers  to  communication.  To accomplish our first goal, this makes use of state-of-the-art deep learning techniques, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and VGG19, which are well-known for their  proficiency  in  image  identification  tasks.  CNNs  are very good at extracting features from images, which makes them ideal for deciphering the intricate visual cues included in  sign  language  gestures  [3].  On  the  other  hand,  the complexity and depth of the VGG19 architecture improve our  classification  abilities  and  lay  the  groundwork  for  a sound  and  dependable  model.  A  major  improvement  in accessibility has occurred with the transition from anticipated  sign  language  movements  to  audio  output.  It guarantees  that  people  with  hearing  impairments  can  not only comprehend  but  also  actively participate in the messages  that  are  being  given,  furthering  a  sense  of inclusion and understanding [4]. The deep learning models are trained and validated using a large and varied dataset. The value of inclusive data that takes into account different sign languages, regional differences, and dialects.

## II. BACKGROUND

Ensuring that deaf children have equal access to literacy and  knowledge  is  vital  for  their  academic  and  social development. To create a conducive learning environment for them, teachers should focus on deaf-friendly strategies. Deaf students may have diverse communication methods, including sign language for those who are prelingually deaf, and some may use cochlear implants or hearing aids. Others might combine spoken language with sign language, while some rely on lip reading.

The lack of accessible auditory information remains a significant obstacle, posing challenges related to comprehension, information access, and communication for these children. A study conducted in Jordan highlighted the multifaceted difficulties faced by students with hearing loss, encompassing communication, academics, social interactions, emotions, and family dynamics. The significance of customized language, speech, and audiological rehabilitation programs  for  students  who  are deaf  or  hard  of  hearing  is  highlighted  by  this  study. Although the government provides essential support to help these  students  reach  their  full  potential  and  ensure  their optimal development, there remains a need for additional facilities and improvements [5].

## A. Sign Language as A Bridge

For  many  deaf  people,  sign  language  serves  as  their main form of communication, and it has enormous value in educational  settings.  Sign  language  has  its  own  syntax, grammar, and vocabulary. For many deaf individuals, it is their  first  and  most  accessible  language.  Just  as  spoken language  that  is  integral  to  the  hearing  population,  sign language is crucial for deaf individuals to express themselves, convey complex ideas, and engage in meaningful communication. They evolve naturally within deaf  communities,  reflecting  the  culture  and  identity  of those who use them. Sign language provides a way for deaf individuals  to  access  information  and  communicate  with others. It bridges the communication gap that exists between deaf and hearing individuals, enabling them to interact in various settings, including education, employment, healthcare, and social interactions [6].

Deaf  individuals  can  convey  their  emotions  through facial  expressions,  body  movements,  and  signs.  It  also empowers the deaf individuals to be more independent in their daily lives and enables them to make choices, express their needs and preferences, and navigate various situations. Sign  language  is  essential  for  deaf  children's  educational development. It allows them to access curriculum content, engage with teachers and peers, and develop language skills necessary for cognitive and social development. Many deaf individuals attend specialized schools where sign language is  the  primary medium of instruction. Proficiency in sign language  opens  up  career  opportunities  in  fields  such  as interpreting,  education,  and  advocacy.  Deaf  individuals who are fluent in sign language can pursue careers as sign language interpreters, educators, or advocates for the deaf community.

## B. Rise of Sign Language Recognition

For those who are deaf or hard of hearing, sign language (SL) is the primary means of communication. It consists of both  non-manual cues like facial expressions and manual gestures like hand and body movements. Expressions that communicate the meanings of words or phrases are made by combining and connecting these components.

The Deaf community places great emphasis on comprehending and recording these expressions and words. The  need  for  creating  sign  language  tools  to  help  deaf people communicate and be included  in  society has long been acknowledged by the scholarly community. The vast range of sign languages and the extensive annotated datasets provide challenges, but recent advances in machine learning and  artificial intelligence (AI)  have  been  essential to automating and advancing these technologies [7].

The resolution and discriminating capabilities of sensors, together with the difficulties presented by occlusions  and  fast  hand  motions,  are  currently  the  main limitations on  the  accuracy  of sign  language  capture technologies. The development of machine learning algorithms that can precisely classify human articulations as single signs or lengthy sentences is necessary for the process of sign language recognition (SLR). The absence of large annotated datasets, which has an impact on the accuracy and generalizability  of  SLR  techniques,  is  one  of  the  present limitations of SLR. Success in machine learning algorithms responsible  for  reliable  sign  recognition  depends  on  the precise extraction of hand and body movements, along with facial expressions [8].

## III. SIGN LANGUAGE RECOGNITION TECHNOLOGY

## A. Overview

In  order  to  identify  and  comprehend  sign  language motions, sign language recognition technology uses computer  vision  and  machine  learning  algorithms.  This makes  communication more efficient  and  inclusive.  Sign language  recognition  begins  with  the  detection  of  sign language gestures [9].

Fig. 1. Sign Language Architecture.



Fig  1  shows  the  technical  structure  of  systems  that automatically  recognize  and  translate  sign  language  into spoken language or text. These systems typically follow a pipeline involving:

- 1) Sign  Detection: Employing  sensors  or  cameras  to record the sign language movements.
- 2) Feature Extraction: Analysing the hand positions, movements, and other visual cues from  the captured signal.
- 3) Recognition: Utilizing machine learning techniques, such  as  neural  networks,  to  categorize  the  elements  that were retrieved and determine the associated sign.
- 4) Translation: Converting  the  recognized  sign  into spoken language or text.

This can be achieved through different types of sensors, including cameras, gloves with built-in sensors, or depthsensing devices like Microsoft Kinect.  These  sensors capture the movements and positions of the signer's hands, facial expressions, and body gestures. The system collects data on sign language gestures, creating a database of signs and their corresponding meanings. In order to train machine learning models, this data is necessary. The  data is processed  using  machine  learning  methods,  namely  deep learning neural networks, which are used to identify sign language  gestures.  The  data  is  processed  using  recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The recorded data is subjected to feature extraction algorithms in order to emphasize important aspects of sign language motions, like hand shape, motion trajectory, and face expressions. Once the system has learned to recognize sign language gestures, it translates them into text or speech [10].

## B. Recognition Techniques

- 1) Real-Time: Real-time captions involve the conversion of spoken language into text, which is displayed on a screen or device in real-time. Captions are typically generated by a trained captioner or using automatic speech recognition  (ASR)  technology.  Real-time  captions  are suitable  for  a  broad  range  of  situations,  including  media and virtual meetings, providing universal accessibility [11]. 2) Sign Language Interpretation: Sign language interpretation involves a trained interpreter who translates spoken language into sign language using gestures, facial expressions,  and  body  movements.  They  are  trained  not only in language but also in the cultural nuances of the Deaf community,  promoting  effective  communication.  Sign language is a two-way communication method that may be used  for  interactive  conversations  and  dialogues  since  it can express not just words but also emotions and tones [12].

## IV. IMPLEMENTATION IN EDUCATIONAL SETTINGS

## A. Data Acquisition

Collect a dataset of sign language gestures or signs. This dataset should include video or image sequences of people signing  various  words  or  phrases  in  sign  language.  It's important to have a diverse dataset with different signers, lighting conditions, and backgrounds.

## B. Recognition Process

Preprocess the collected data to extract relevant features. This involves process such as video or image normalization, removal of background, and tracking of hand to isolate the signing hand or hands. Extract meaningful features from the pre-processed  data.  Common  features  for  sign  language recognition include hand shape, hand motion, finger positions, and facial expressions. These characteristics are necessary  for  machine  learning  model  training.  More complex  models  for  sign  language  recognition  can  be created using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). For instance, you can use 2D CNNs for image-based sign recognition and RNNs for sequences of signs. Implement the recognition logic that takes the output of the machine learning model and maps it to the corresponding sign or word in the sign language. This may involve post-processing and context-aware algorithms [13].

## C. Display and Delivery

Make the system's interface easy to use so that users can communicate with it. This interface can be in the form of a mobile app, desktop application, or even a hardware device like a glove or camera-based system [14].

## D. Benefits and Impact

Sign language recognition technology plays an effective role  in  promoting  inclusive  learning  environments.  By accurately translating sign language into written or spoken language, it breaks down communication barriers for deaf students,  ensuring  they  have  equal  access  to  educational content

An  important  benefit  of  sign  language  recognition technology is that it facilitates better  communication between teachers and students who are deaf. Educators can effectively  convey  information  through  sign  language, which the technology then translates in real-time [15].

The integration of sign language recognition technology creates a level playing field for deaf students in mainstream education. It ensures they can actively participate in class discussions, ask questions, and express their thoughts and ideas without any communication barriers. This technology, by providing real-time translation, helps educators understand  and  respond  to  the  needs  of  deaf  students promptly

## E. Algorithm

Deep  learning  tasks  are  the  main  application  for  the VGG19 algorithm, a model that uses picture classification. While it's a powerful architecture for recognizing objects in images,  it  may  not  be  the  most  suitable  choice  for  sign language recognition, which involves video data and sequential patterns of hand movements  and  gestures. Recurrent  neural  networks  (RNNs),  convolutional  neural networks  (CNNs),  or  hybrid  models  that  can  analyse sequential  input  and  capture  temporal  dependencies  are usually needed for sign language recognition.

A model built for video data or sequences, such as a 3D CNN  (Convolutional  Neural  Network),  an  LSTM  (Long Short-Term Memory) network, or a combination of the two, may be used for sign language recognition. These models can effectively capture the dynamic nature of sign language gestures and recognize signs based on the order and motion of hand and body movements. While VGG19 is not directly suited  for  sign  language  recognition,  you  can  adapt  its principles  for  feature  extraction  from  individual  frames within  a  sign  language  video  and  then  combine  these features  with  a  suitable  sequence  modelling  network  to build a more appropriate system for sign language recognition.

Fig. 2. Sign Language Recognition System.



Fig 2 the diagram outlines a system that translates sign language  gestures  into  text.  It  is  divided  into  four  main stages:

- 1) Input: This stage captures the sign language gestures using a camera or sensor.
- 2) Feature extraction: The system extracts key features from the captured video, such as hand shapes, movements, and relative positions.
- 3) Recognition: A  machine  learning  model  analyses the extracted features and classifies them into the corresponding signs.
- 4) Output: The recognized signs are converted into text and displayed on a screen or sent to another device.

It also includes a feedback loop, suggesting the system can learn and improve its recognition accuracy over time. The "database" refers to a collection of sign language data used to train the machine learning model. The "processing" might involve additional steps like noise reduction or hand segmentation before feature extraction.

## F. VGG19 Architecture

1. The VGG network takes an RGB image with a fixed size of 224x224 pixels, represented as a (224, 224, 3) matrix.
2. Each  pixel  is  preprocessed  by  deducting  from  it  the mean RGB value computed throughout the training set.
3. It uses 3x3 kernel sizes with a stride of 1 pixel to cover the  entire  image  while  maintaining  spatial  resolution through padding.
4. The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation is used to increase  classification  accuracy  and  introduce  nonlinearity.
5. The architecture includes three fully connected layers, with the first two having 4096 units and the third being a softmax layer for 1000-way ILSVRC classification.
6. A Model Checkpoint callback function is used to save the model's weights to disk at the end of each training epoch, ensuring that the best model is saved based on validation loss improvements.
7. The callback monitors 'val\_loss' and saves weights only when there is an improvement in validation loss.
8. The model is  trained  for  ten  epochs  using  the  Adam optimizer,  with  'categorical\_crossentropy'  as  the  loss function, a learning rate of 0.001, and a batch size of 64.

## V. CONCLUSION

The achievement of VGG19 in sign language recognition,  boasting  an  unprecedented  accuracy  rate  of 99.97%, represents a significant leap forward in technology's role in education. By harnessing the power of deep learning and convolutional neural networks, VGG19 has demonstrated its prowess in understanding and interpreting the intricate gestures and movements inherent in sign language. This application of VGG19 revolutionizes education by enhancing accessibility for deaf and hard of hearing students. It bridges the communication gap that has long  hindered  their  engagement  with  educational  content and interactions in traditional classroom settings. With sign language  recognition  technology,  these  students  can  now fully  participate  in  lessons,  discussions,  and  collaborative activities,  ensuring  that  their  educational  experience  is inclusive and equitable.

Moreover, the real-time translation capabilities afforded by  VGG19  create  an  inclusive  learning  environment  not only  for  students  but  also  for  educators.  By  facilitating seamless  communication  between  teachers  and  students, this  technology  fosters  more  meaningful  interactions  and facilitates a deeper understanding of the subject matter. The importance of VGG19  in  this application cannot be overstated. Its unparalleled accuracy and efficiency pave the way  for  a  future where  educational  opportunities  are universally  accessible  to  all  students,  regardless  of  their abilities.  By  leveraging  the  transformative  power  of  sign language  recognition,  we  are  breaking  down  barriers  and opening doors to a more  inclusive and  empowering educational landscape.

## VI. CHALLENGES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

## A. Challenges

- 1) Accuracy of Recognition:
- a) Challenge: Achieving high accuracy in recognizing  various  sign  language  gestures,  considering the complexity and nuances of sign languages.
- b) Solution: Utilize deep learning techniques, extensive datasets, and  continuous  model  training to enhance the accuracy and robustness of recognition
4. systems.  Collaborations  with  the  deaf  community  for dataset creation can also improve accuracy.
- 2) Scalability:
- a) Challenge: Adapting the technology to different sign languages and dialects, making it scalable for widespread adoption.
- b) Solution: Invest in research to develop languageagnostic models and systems that can adapt and learn from diverse  sign  languages,  allowing  for  broader  usability without significant retraining efforts.
- 3) Cost of Implementation:
- a) Challenge: High costs associated with implementing  hardware,  software,  and  maintaining  the infrastructure needed for sign language recognition.
- b) Solution: Focus on cost-effective hardware solutions, cloud-based services, and open-source software to reduce initial investment. Collaboration with tech companies  and  academic  institutions  can  further  drive down costs.
- 4) Data Privacy and Ethics:
- a) Challenge: Safeguarding the privacy and ethical use of the data, especially considering the sensitive nature of sign language communication.
- b) Solution :  Implement  strict  data  anonymization protocols,  informed  consent  processes,  and  compliance with privacy regulations. Transparent communication with users about data usage is vital to build trust.
- 5) Real-time Processing:
- a) Challenge: Achieving  real-time  processing  to ensure instantaneous translation during live interactions.
- b) Solution: Leverage  advancements  in  hardware capabilities and optimize algorithms to achieve real-time processing, reducing latency.
- B. Future Directions
- 1) Multimodal Approach: Develop systems that combine  video,  audio,  and  linguistic  context  to  improve accuracy and context awareness in sign language recognition.
- 2) User  Interface  Enhancements: Focus  on  creating user-friendly interfaces that integrate  seamlessly  with existing  educational  tools,  making  the  technology  more accessible and intuitive for both educators and students.
- 3) Mobile Integration: Optimize sign language recognition  technology  for  mobile  devices  to  promote learning  outside  traditional  classroom  settings,  allowing students to access educational resources anytime, anywhere.
- 4) Collaborative Research: Encourage interdisciplinary collaboration between researchers, educators,  and  the  deaf  community  to  foster  a  deeper understanding of sign languages and create more effective recognition  systems.  Addressing  these  challenges  and pursuing these future directions will not only enhance sign language  recognition  technology  but  also  contribute  to creating a more  inclusive and  accessible educational environment for deaf students.

## Explainable Machine Learning Prediction for the Academic Performance of Deaf Scholars

N. R. RAJI 1 , R. MATHUSOOTHANA S. KUMAR 2 , AND C. L. BIJI 3

1 Department of Computer Applications, Noorul Islam Centre for Higher Education, Nagercoil 629301, India

2 Department of Information Technology, Noorul Islam Centre for Higher Education, Nagercoil 629301, India

3 Department of Analytics, School of Computer Science and Technology, VIT University, Vellore, Tamil Nadu 632014, India

Corresponding author: N. R. Raji (rajinrsreelakam@gmail.com)

This work was supported in part by the Centre of Excellence for Disability Studies (CEDS), Kerala, India, under Grant R21F3.

ABSTRACT Deaf and Hard of Hearing (DHH) students encounter obstacles in higher education due to language and communication challenges. Although research aims to improve their academic performance, the potential of Machine Learning (ML) remains underutilized in DHH education. The opacity of ML models further complicates their adoption. This study aims to fill this gap by developing a novel ML-based system with eXplainable AI (XAI), specifically utilizing Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explainer (LIME) and Shapley Additive Explainer (SHAP). The objective is twofold: predicting at-risk DHH students and explaining risk factors. Merging ML and XAI, this approach could positively impact DHH students' educational outcomes. A dataset of 454 records detailing DHH students is collected. To address dataset limitations, synthetic data and SMOTE are used. Students are categorized into three performance levels. The data is modeled with different ML models, transfer models, ensemble models, and combination models. Among the models, the stacked model with XGBoost, ExtraTrees, and Random Forest exhibited better performance with an accuracy of 92.99%. Results highlight the model's significance, providing insights through XAI into crucial factors affecting academic performance, including communication mode, early intervention, schooling type, and family deafness history. LIME and SHAP values were found to be effective in deriving insights into DHH student performance prediction framework. Communication mode, notably, strongly influences at-risk students. The major contribution of this study is the development of a novel ML-based system and the XAI interpretations whose value lies in its social relevance, guiding stakeholders to enhance DHH scholars' academic achievements.

INDEX TERMS Artificial intelligence, deaf education, explainability, machine learning.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The academic progress of DHH scholars is essential in achieving sustainable economic development in the community. Constructive feedback at an early stage can help scholars to improve their productivity. Though deliberate efforts were initiated to address the challenge, DHH scholars needed to be provided with opportunities in the right direction. Quality feedback and action are essential for this self-regulated learning. There are 388 government-funded schools for DHH students in India [1] but the colleges that offer undergraduate programs for this population are only six [2] as per the



The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Gustavo Olague .

available information. Policymakers in India are eager to create early detection and intervention programs for DHH youngsters. The stakeholders of education [3] -students, teachers, and policymakers- need valuable insights that can be used to improve the educational conditions of DHH students.

The factors affecting the academic performance of a DHH student are different when compared to his hearing peer. [4] states that hearing loss of any type or degree can be a barrier to learning. In India, hard-of-hearing students usually prefer an inclusive setup in regular schools, and deaf students generally prefer special schools. As per the Rights of Persons With Disability (RPWD) Act, 2016, a person with 60 DB to 70 DB hearing loss in both ears is considered Hard of Hearing. Though deafness is not a barrier to learning, the inaccessible environment makes learning a challenge for a DHH student. The difficulties faced by DHH students are studied in [5] which identifies the need for communication access, classroom modifications, and other accommodations that are needed to improve the success rate of DHH students. The studies show that students even with minimal or mild hearing loss suffer from poor speech recognition which eventually results in poor academic performance [6]. A regression model with variables related to education, hearing devices, sign language proficiency, and home language was suggested in [7] which shows that sign language proficiency has a significant effect on the academic performance of DHH students. The sign language proficiency of teachers is also important in delivering the content effectively in a classroom with DHH students [8].To maximize the academic potential of these students early intervention and usage of assistive devices like hearing aids are also important [9].



The challenges faced by DHH students are very different from those of hearing students. This calls for the need for studies that specifically focus on the performance of DHH students. The low academic performance of DHH students has been attributed to several issues. Low academic performance has resulted in poor employability, low salaries, and substandard quality of life in India, hence research into this performance and the causes associated is critically needed [2]. In various studies the factors affecting the academic performance of DHH students are identified as parent influence, availability of facilities, teaching, reading, and learning materials [10], [11], Mode of communication, the usage of sign language or speech [7], Grades, demographics, geographical region, school, course type, and course score [12]. In addition to these factors, deafness-related factors also need to be identified which can be an influential factor in their academic performance. From the above discussion, the deafness-related factors identified for this study are communication mode, family history, type of schooling, type and degree of hearing loss, usage of hearing aids, and intervention through speech therapy and cochlear implants.

This paper explores the role of explainable AI (XAI) in improving the performance of DHH scholars in education. The significance of this study includes in its social relevance. As reported by World Federation for the Deaf 80% of the 32 million deaf children worldwide do not have any access to schooling. Only 1-2% of deaf youngsters receive instruction in sign language even when there are educational options. The possibilities to enhance the education condition of DHH population using ML techniques is under-explored and this study is a stepping stone towards achieving this goal. The major contributions of this study include:

- Novel ML System with XAI: A novel ML system integrates eXplainable AI (XAI) using LIME and SHAP techniques. It predicts at-risk DHH students and explains academic risk factors
- Enhancing Education: This study aims to improve DHH students' academic achievements. Identifying
- factors like communication mode, early intervention, and family history guides effective support..
- Addressing Data Imbalance: Synthetic data and SMOTE mitigate DHH dataset limitations, boosting model robustness
- Algorithmic Comparison: Comparative analysis highlights the stacked model with XGBoost, ExtraTrees and Random Forest superior accuracy (92.99%) in predicting at-risk DHH students, aiding algorithm selection.
- Interpretability and XAI: Incorporating XAI explains predictions, enhances model transparency and offers insights into academic success factors.

This paper is organized as follows: Section II highlights the related works in academic performance prediction of students using Machine Learning techniques. Section III explains the method followed in this work. Section IV discusses the results obtained and Section V concludes by summarising the contributions and future scope of this study.

## II. RELATED WORKS

Machine learning (ML) is revolutionizing education and altering teaching, learning, and research in profound ways. MLisbeing used by educators to identify at-risk students earlier and take steps to increase their achievement. Researchers are using machine learning to speed up research and uncover new findings and insights. The ML models are often considered black boxes which do not provide explanations for the predictions made. The emergence of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) made these black boxes more transparent. In 2016, Roberto et al. suggested an algorithm called Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME), a unique explanation technique that learns an interpretable model locally around the prediction to explain any classifier's predictions in an interpretable and faithful manner [13]. In 2017, a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is introduced [14]. These methods justify the prediction made by the ML model by giving an appropriate explanation for it.

In today's world, AI systems and Machine Learning algorithms are widely used in a variety of fields. Data is used in different ways to assist humans in solving issues. Theadvancement of machine learning, demands transparency in its prediction. Explainable AI, or XAI, is a set of techniques for better understanding and validating machine learning models. Models must be understood not only by data scientists who are building them but also by end-users who want explanations for why certain decisions are made.

In the education domain, the stakeholders of education highly benefit from the use of machine learning models. The classifications and predictions made by these models help the stakeholders to get insight and help them to make more effective decisions. In [15], the major stakeholders who use the models are classified into four. The students are represented as the affected users, the advisors or teachers are represented as the end-users who trust the model, the regulatory bodies who obtain insights from the model, and the AI system builders who train and evaluate the model and ensure its performance. Some of the major applications in the education domain using ML techniques are the classification of students according to their academic performance [16], [17], [18], identification of at-risk students [19], [20], [21] prediction of marks [22], [23], [24] and identification of factors affecting academic performance [25], [26].

The predictions made by machine learning models indeed give valuable insights to the students and other stakeholders of education. Unfortunately, the current approaches usually give only predictions, not the actual explanations of the predictions to the students [27]. An attempt is made to overcome this major limitation by adding explainability to the developed model. The scope of explainability can be local or global. Global-level explanations explain the complete model and local-level explanations provide explanations at an instance level [15]. Local explanations illustrate how the outcomes of the model change when the values of specific features change within a specific interval [28]. This makes the prediction made by the model more trustworthy and useful.

The pilot study of this research [29] revealed that deafness-related factors have a strong contribution to the academic performance of students with hearing loss. According to a thorough study done in Saudi Arabia using data of DHH students, there is a strong correlation between student grades, demographics, geographic region, school, course type, and course score when predicting academic outcomes. Religious curricula, Arabic language, and Mathematics also function as important predictive indicators of success or failure in the outcome [12]. A time series model was proposed in this study to predict the academic performance of DHH students. Another significant study in analyzing the predicting the academic performance of DHH students was in 2009 [30]. Statistical methods are used in this study to predict the academic performance of DHH students. The datasets used in both these studies are not openly available.

The power of XAI is effectively used in many applications like credit risk prediction [31], Network Intrusion detection [32], medical diagnosis [33], and student performance [34]. The papers on using XAI methods in the academic performance analysis of DHH students are very limited. A framework, XAI-ED is proposed in 2022 using which educational AI tools can be designed and developed [35]. It is observed that the development of dashboards that use the XAI techniques can give valuable feedback to all the stakeholders of education [27].

## A. DATA ACQUISITION

The data for this study is collected from the higher education institutes for the deaf in different parts of India. The data sources are admission, academic and clinical records of students. The data is also collected through an online survey with their consent. Specially made signed videos were also included in the survey to ensure accessibility. The signed videos were made with deaf signers and the validation is done with another two Sign Language experts who are deaf. A total of 454 students gave their consent and their data is collected. The limited higher education opportunities for DHH students explain the small size of the dataset.

## E. SYNTHETIC DATA GENERATION

The dataset size is one of the crucial factors that affect the performance of a model. In this case, the size of the dataset is small. There are synthetic data generation methods to increase the size of data. The similarity score gives an idea of the similarity between real data and fake data. In this paper, conditional generative adversarial networks from open-source Python libraries called CTGAN and Synthetic Data Vault (SDV) are used for generating fake data. A similarity score of 0.6 is obtained which shows that the dataset is ready for production. After synthetic data generation, the size of the data became 1500.

## F. DATA SAMPLING USING SMOTE

The obtained dataset was imbalanced with uneven distributions of target class observations. As shown in Figure 4, the instances of classes are distributed in the training dataset as class A-18.1%, class B - 72.9%, and class C-9.0%.

Here it is observed that class C and class A are the minority classes whereas the majority class is class B. That is, the class distribution is not equal or close to equal. This is a challenging problem that appears in classification problems and leads to poor performance. One of the most important factors in improving model performance is resolving the issue of an imbalanced dataset. This problem leads to the majority class dominating the minority class during the classification. When the dataset is imbalanced, the classifier may get biased toward the prediction.

To overcome the problem of the imbalanced dataset, the oversampling Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is considered a benchmark solution [30]. In this study, this method is used to handle an imbalanced dataset problem. SMOTE examines minority class instances and uses k nearest neighbor to choose a random nearest neighbor, then creates a synthetic instance in feature space at random.

## G. DATA MODELLING

After balancing the dataset, it is modeled using different machine-learning classification algorithms. The algorithms used are classic ML models -Support Vector Machine (SVM), K Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Naïve Bayes(NB), TreeBased models-Decision Tree(DT), Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XG), ExtraTrees Classifier(XT) and Combination models -Stacked model of XG, RF and XT. The performance of models is then compared. It was found that the performance of the Stacked model is superior when compared to others. Further, the evaluation of the model is done using a classification report considering the values of accuracy, F1 score, precision, and recall. The performance of the model is further improved by using the k-fold validation technique. Since the dataset is balanced, this method is suitable for model evaluation. The k-fold validation technique is used to generalize the model. That is, to reduce the variability, crossvalidation is performed using different subsets of the same data. The model evaluation is done with accuracy, F1 score, and precision. The sensitivity and specificity scores are also considered for evaluating the performance of the model. The parameters are calculated with True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP), and False Negatives (FN) from the Confusion matrix.



FIGURE 4. Distribution of grades in dataset.



Cross-validation is used for a robust evaluation of the model's effectiveness. A machine learning model's performance and capacity for generalization are assessed using the cross-validation methodology, which divides the dataset into many subsets systematically This process is performed several times, with a new subset being used for testing each time. The model is trained on a subset and tested on the remaining data. To reduce the possibility of bias or overfitting that comes with a single train-test split, the results are averaged to offer a more reliable evaluation of the model's performance. By averaging results over multiple iterations of training and testing data subsets, this method evaluates the overall performance of the model. Crossvalidation maximizes data utilization and identifies potential issues like overfitting and underfitting.

## H. EXPLAINABLE AI COMPONENT

To make the model transparent, an attempt was made to include Explainability to improve the student's experience in learning. Two methods are used to add explainability to the model

- 1) Explainability with SHAP values.
- 2) Explainability with LIME

## 1) EXPLAINABILITY WITH SHAP VALUES

SHAP is a more comprehensive and interpretable method for evaluating feature importance in machine learning models, while feature importance is a quick and simple option. SHAP provides a unified and consistent measure of feature importance, accounting for complex relationships between features and the model output. It assigns a contribution value to each feature for a specific prediction, whereas feature importance only provides a single value per feature across the entire dataset. feature importance is based on a linear approximation of the model's output while SHAP can account for non-linear relationships and interactions between features. Being model agnostic, SHAP can be applied to any model regardless of its type, while feature importance is specific to certain types of models, such as decision trees.

TABLE 2. Method to calculate shapley values.

Using SHAP, the reliability of the model can be enhanced by explaining the model behavior. SHAP has explainers and model-agnostic methods on how the features used in the model influence the outcome predicted by it. SHAP uses Shapley values to explain to what extent each input features contribute to every model prediction. The average marginal contribution of a feature value across all possible coalitions is referred to as the Shapley value. The Shapley value is calculated for the feature f out of the set of input features F as in the method described in Table 2.

Mathematically Shapley values can be calculated using the formula [31],



where f is the model, x is the available features, and x are the selected features. The quantity fx ( z ′ ) -fx ( z \ i ) expresses, for every single prediction, the deviation of Shapley values from their mean: the contribution of the i-th feature.

SHAP can give both global and local explanations for the model. The summary plot, force plot, and waterfall plot in the SHAP package are used to give explanations for the predictions. The summary plot combines the relevance of features with the effects of features. A Shapley value for a feature and an instance is represented by each point on the summary plot. The feature determines the position on the y-axis, while the Shapley value determines the position on the x-axis. The color denotes the feature's value, which ranges from low to high. Overlapping points are jittered in the y-axis direction to give us a sense of the Shapley value distribution per feature. The features are ranked in order of importance. The force plots in the SHAP package can give both global and local interpretations. The SHAP waterfall plot visualizes how individual localized predictions are made.

## 2) EXPLAINABILITY WITH LIME

The LIME zooms into the local area of the individual prediction and creates a simple explanation that makes sense in the local region. LIME creates a linear model in the local area which helps to make simple explanations for the prediction. That is a local approximation of a complex model. Using the prior knowledge about the domain, the explanations can be validated and trust can be built. The explanations using LIMEarevalid locally, in the global perspective, they may not be faithful. The working of the LIME algorithm is shown in Figure 5.

The algorithm of LIME assumes that every complex model is linear on a local scale. LIME seeks to fit a basic model around a single observation that simulates the behavior of the global model at that location. For the instance to be explained, perturb the instance n times to create replicated feature data with slight modifications in values. This perturbed data is created around the instance used to build the linear model locally. Based on the range of possible category values and how frequently they appear in the training dataset, random values are selected for categorical variables. Samples from a normal distribution are used to perturb data for continuous variables, and the perturbed value is added to the original. On the perturbed data, predictions are made using the predictor function of the black box model. These forecasts are utilized to train LIME's local linear model. The original and perturbed data points are compared for each data point, and the Euclidean distance between them is found. A sense of the point's distance from the initial observation can be obtained using Euclidean distance. A smaller distance implies the data point is closer to the observation. LIME typically uses a kernel function to assign weights to the perturbed data points based on their distance, and these weights or similarity scores are then used in the weighted linear regression model. The closer the point to the observation, the higher the similarity score. The model could be run with n features which are selected using feature selection methods like highest weights, forward selection &amp; lasso path. With all the input data prepared, LIME creates the local linear model that can be used to explain the predictions. The coefficients or the weights from the linear regression model, combined with the features of the perturbed instances, are used to explain the local behavior of the instance.

LIME and SHAP have different strengths and weaknesses, and the choice between the two depends on the specific use case, the complexity of the model, and the trade-off between computational cost and interpretability.

The steps involved in the LIME algorithm are shown in Table 3.

The algorithm of LIME assumes that every complex model is linear on a local scale. LIME seeks to fit a basic model around a single observation that simulates the behavior of the global model at that location.

The optimization used in LIME can be represented as



x - Input data point f - Complex model g - Simple interpretable local model such that g ε G, where G is the family of interpretable models L (f,g, 5 x)- Denotes approximation of complex model f by the simple model g in the neighborhood of data point x (g) - regularization term

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS

The features included in the dataset can be classified as Socioeconomic features, prior academic features, and deafness-related features. EDA on the collected data showed that the distribution of semester 1 marks is normally distributed around the mean value of 408. The majority of students have 100% of disability and they fall in the profound or severe type of hearing loss category. The graphical representation is shown in Figure 6.

Figure 7 shows that there is no significant variation in the distribution of semester 1 marks based on hearing aid usage. The communication mode seems to be an important factor in academic performance. The students who use both sign language and speech scored more than those who depend on sign language alone for communication. Though the number of speech users is very low, their performance is much better than others. There is not much difference in performance based on the type of hearing loss.

It is observed that the majority of students studied in special schools and the majority received speech therapy below the age of 5. The early intervention can be a factor that the majority of students used both sign language and speech for communication which in turn helped in their academic performance. As the majority studied in special schools, there are high chances of them using sign language as the primary mode of communication and speech as a supporting mode of communication. The result is graphically represented in Figure 8.

The feature Grade is added depending on the semester marks. The distribution of features with the grades is shown in Figure 9. It is observed that the majority of students are middle-level performers. Though the mean semester mark is almost the same for male and female students, the high performers are more male students when compared to female IEEE AccesS'

students. The majority of high-level performers use sign language as a communication mode. The majority of students do not have a history of deafness in the family. The number of students who have undergone cochlear implants or use hearing aids is very low. There is no significant improvement in performance with the ensemble of SVM and KNN. This shows that the individual weakness of the individual classifier persists. It is observed that the performance of the majority of ensemble models combining different classifiers is better, which indicates that combining these models enhances the predictive capabilities and combines the strengths of individual classifiers. The stacked ensemble of XGBoost, Random Forest, and Extra Trees achieves the highest performance, indicating the effectiveness of combining diverse models. This ensemble model is likely to capture a wide range of patterns in the data.The best parameters of each model in the stacked classifier obtained with GridsearchCV are specified in Table 5.

The accuracy of this stacked model is found to be 92.99% and ROC AUC is .9781. The high accuracy indicates that the model is performing well in terms of overall correctness. The high precision indicates that when the model predicts a positive class, it is often correct. The high recall indicates that the model effectively captures a large proportion of the actual positive instances. The F1 score, being a combination of precision and recall, provides a balanced assessment of the model's performance. The confusion matrix, sensitivity, specificity, and ROC of this model are shown in Figure 11. The performance of this model is further evaluated with Mean Square Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), MeanAbsolute Error (MAE), and R-squared (R2). The values obtained are shown in Table 6.

The average squared difference between the expected and actual data is represented by the MSE (Mean Squared Error). A smaller number (0.16) denotes better model performance. The square root of the mean square error, or RMSE (0.39), shows better model accuracy. With a mean absolute error of 0.12, the accuracy is also better. The R-squared (R2) value, which ranges from 0 to 1, represents how well the model explains variation. A score of 1 denotes a perfect fit. With an R2 of 0.77, the model is deemed to be satisfactory as it accounts for 77% of the variation. All things considered, the model works effectively, capturing a significant amount of data variation with minor errors.

To evaluate the generalizability of the stacked model, the k-fold cross-validation technique is used with 10 folds. The average accuracy is found to be 92.95 with a standard deviation of 0.012 among the folds.

## Clinician's recommendation -

- The degree of hearing loss alone is not a direct predictor of academic performance; the area and extent of damage to the auditory system play a crucial role.

- Prioritize the use of assistive devices, such as hearing aids or cochlear implants, for rehabilitation, considering the individual's characteristics of hearing loss.
- Implement intensive speech and language stimulation to aid the participant in acquiring age-appropriate communication skills.

## V. CONCLUSION

In this paper, an attempt is made to propose a model that can classify a DHH student according to his academic performance. Unlike the students with hearing, the factors related to deafness have a significant role in the academic performance of DHH students. This leads to many decision-making policies that will result in more opportunities for the higher education of these students. This work also examines the possibility of multi-label classification interpretability. By adding explainability, the model is made transparent. The stakeholders of the education domain can get trustable predictions using this model. An interactive dashboard development can be considered as a scope of future work for this research. As the next phase of this work, more domain experts can be involved and the modification of the dashboard can be done. The model interpretations can be evaluated with more domain experts and can be compared to see the validity of interpretations.

The contribution of this study includes the development of a dataset comprising details of students with deafness. From the results, it is observed that the existing gap identified which includes the small data size -imbalance problem can be solved to an extent by synthetically generating data and SMOTE technique. It is found that the proposed stacked model along with XAI can give valuable insights to the stakeholders of deaf education which can improve the education opportunities and conditions of students with hearing loss. The ML model which is usually considered as a black box can be made transparent using XAI techniques. Individual predictions can be evaluated and analyzed which can help the stakeholders to make better decisions. In the deaf education domain, such models are rarely used. This study is a stepping stone to introduce possibilities of ML and XAI in deaf education which can change the lives of many students with deafness.

## Exploration of Automatic Speech Recognition for Deaf and Hard of Hearing Students in Higher Education Classes

## Janine Butler

National Technical Institute for the Deaf Rochester Institute of Technology Rochester, NY, USA jmbdls@rit.edu

## ABSTRACT

Automatic speech recognition (ASR) programs that generate real-time speech-to-text captions can be provided as supplemental  access  technologies  for  deaf  and  hard  of hearing (DHH) students in higher education classes. As part of a pilot program, we implemented ASR as a supplemental access service in biology, statistics, and other courses at our university. To identify the benefits and limitations of ASR as an  access  technology,  we  surveyed  26  DHH  students  and interviewed 8 of these students about their experiences with ASR in their mainstream classes. Participants believed that ASR was beneficial despite the errors that ASR continued to generate; however, the accuracy and readability of ASR need to improve  so  that students can  better  access spoken information  through ASR. This  paper reviews  points for researchers to consider when designing and providing ASR as a supplemental access service in educational settings.

## Author Keywords

Human-centered computing~Accessibility technologies; Human-centered computing~Accessibility design and evaluation methods; Human-centered computing~Empirical studies in accessibility

## ACM Classification Keywords

Deaf and Hard of Hearing; Automatic Speech Recognition; Real-Time Captions; Feedback.

## 1. INTRODUCTION

Real-time speech-to-text systems, also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR) engines that generate captions, can be  provided  as access technologies  for  deaf  and  hard  of hearing (DHH) students  in mainstream  classrooms.  Other captioning services, including C-Print and CART (Communication Access Real-Time Translation), are provided by human  captionists  who  may not always  be

available  for  hire  at  different institutions.  ASR  generated captions  provide students  with an additional  means  of accessing  spoken  language,  especially  when  other  access services are not readily available. While ASR is becoming more widely used across different platforms in more settings, researchers need to optimize the readability and accuracy of automatically generated captions for students.

As part of a pilot program, we continue to implement ASR as a supplemental access service in biology, statistics, and other  courses  at  our  university.  Automatically  generated captions  appear  next to  course  slides  in  combination with other access  services  in  the  classroom, including  sign language interpreters, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. ASR shown below PowerPoint in a biology course



In order to understand students' responses to reading ASR generated captions in their biology and statistics classes, we surveyed 26 DHH participants and interviewed 8 of these 26 participants.  This  qualitative  study  is  unique  in assessing DHH students' experiences with using ASR as a supplemental access service in classrooms with sign language interpreters  and human captionists.  Our findings suggest that while DHH students seem to benefit from ASR engines that supplement other access services, students are concerned with the accuracy and readability of ASR. Their perspectives inform future research studies that should aim to improve the  readability  and accuracy  of ASR  before providing ASR as a primary access service for students.

## 1.1 ASR in the Classroom

As  ASR  becomes  more  viable as an access service, researchers have studied the use of real-time speech transcription in various classroom settings for  a variety of

## Paper Session 1: Speaking and Signing

learners [1, 8, 15, 23]. These studies reveal the benefits of ASR for  students  and  particularly for DHH students  who receive access to real-time spoken information.

While ASR can be beneficial, the residual rates of inaccuracy and  latency,  or  delay,  of  automatically  generated  captions indicate  that  ASR  still  needs  to be improved before being used as the primary  access service in the  classroom. Researchers have been working  for years  on  humancomputer collaboration to raise the accuracy rates of ASR, particularly through human supervision or editors [11,  16, 17,  21,  22]  and  through customizing ASR  for  speech variability  [2].  Fujii  et  al.  [10] presented  a method for improving the readability of ASR by using an algorithm to help edit transcripts in order to support readers' understanding of course material. Their review of readability included disfluencies as well as unclear sentence boundaries, punctuation  marks,  and missed  or repeated  words. In addition to these  points,  our  interviews  with participants revealed that students' ability to read and understand ASR generated captions can also be  influenced  by the rate  at which words appear on screen in real time, how words are spelled, and the accuracy of course-specific keywords.

Other researchers have made progress with predicting and improving the Word Error Rate (WER) of ASR so that ASR can more accurately recognize and transcribe spoken words [4, 5, 19]. While improving the accuracy of ASR is crucial, WER  has been critiqued for not correlating with or predicting the performance  scores of participants, and researchers  have tested other  metrics  for  predicting  the usability  of  ASR  [7,  12] or  supplemented WER  with Semantic Error Rate [13].

Qualitative  studies  can compensate  for  the  limitations of WER metrics by investigating human subjects' responses to ASR [20].  Kawas  et  al.  [14]  responded to  the  scarcity  of qualitative studies on ASR and developed design requirements  and  features  for  human-based and  machinebased captioning services. Among other points, the authors' design  requirements  called  for  accurate  real-time captions with minimal lag that could be read and understood easily. They also mentioned key features, including using dictionaries  to  increase  captioning accuracy for different subjects and providing guidance to instructors. While they reviewed  a range of  human  and  automatically  generated captioning services,  our  current  study  provides  additional implications on improving ASR as an access service.

In a larger study on ASR that included qualitative methods, Berke et  al.  [3]  found  that accuracy  was  one  of  the  most important concerns for DHH users. In addition, DHH users were concerned about the reliability of the technology and the potential loss of sign language interpreting services. To provide additional strategies for supporting DHH students' access to speech in real time, we discuss our qualitative study in the following sections.

## 2. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS

For the purposes of this specific study, we recruited DHH students who took one of three mainstream courses at our university: General Biology I,  Evolutionary Biology,  and Introduction  to  Statistics  II.  ASR  was  used  in  conjunction with other support services in these courses, including sign language interpreters and TypeWell, which is similar to CPrint, a speech-to-text transcription system in which a human captionist condenses and organizes important information so that the meaning, rather than the verbatim, of what was said is conveyed  [6]. In  contrast to  human  captionists  who condense  information,  ASR  engines  can  create  verbatim transcripts-with exceptions that  the  program may  have been programmed to disregard, such as disfluencies. The rate at  which  ASR  transcribes  words  on screen  may  vary depending on the speed and complexity of spoken speech; for  instance,  words  might  appear  one-by-one  relatively quickly or appear in chunks with some latency.

Prior to embedding ASR in these classes, researchers at our institution  developed  custom language  models  of  ASR through  Microsoft  Custom Speech  Service by  feeding  the system with course-specific vocabulary  and key  concepts from glossaries in course textbooks, transcripts from prior semesters created by human captionists, and related sources. Without these custom language models, ASR would often transcribe keywords such as 'atom' and 'SQL' as 'Adam' and 'sequel.' Such transcription errors can be minimized in the  custom language  model, and  the  accuracy rates that students  saw  in the three  courses in our study typically ranged from 85% to 90%.

During  each  class  session,  the  instructor  wears a  headset microphone that is directly connected to the ASR service to ensure  the  best  audio  stream possible. The automatically generated  captions  appear in  real time  in  the  course's PowerPoint slides on screen in the front of the classroom and on DHH students' personal devices, as indicated in Figure 2.

Figure 2. Custom language model of ASR



Instructors briefly mentioned in the courses in our study that course materials were used to improve the accuracy of ASR and notified students that there would still be mistakes, but students  did  not  receive  detailed  knowledge about  the backend. While a custom language model can improve the accuracy of keywords, our qualitative analysis revealed that

## Paper Session 1: Speaking and Signing

punctuation, delay, and other factors can affect the readability of ASR and students' confidence in ASR. In the following sections, we investigate students' perspectives on the benefits and limitations of ASR in order to demonstrate that the readability and accuracy of ASR needs to improve prior to providing ASR as an primary access service.

## 2.1 Research Goals

We aimed to understand how DHH students  responded to ASR in their classes  so that  we  could  work  towards improving the use of ASR as an access service in mainstream courses.  In particular,  we  were  interested in the  following research questions:

1. What do students perceive as the benefits and limitations of ASR in class?
2. What is the role of ASR in helping students understand and attend to the instructor and class material?
3. What are students' levels of confidence with using ASR in class?
4. What are students'  preferences for  the  accuracy  and latency/timing of ASR in class?

## 2.2 Procedure

To collect information  from a range of students, we contacted DHH students who were enrolled in one of three biology or  statistics  courses  in the  previous semester.  We asked that they complete an online questionnaire about their experiences with ASR. After 26 participants completed the questionnaire, 8 consented to be interviewed once in person about their experiences with ASR. Questionnaire participants were eligible for a drawing of one of three gift cards and interview participants were compensated for their time. The questionnaire and interviews occurred during the first  few  weeks  of the spring semester so that  participants could reflect on and discuss their comprehensive experiences with ASR  throughout  the  fall  semester,  including any possible changes in their responses to ASR.

A member of the research team who is a nationally certified sign language interpreter conducted separate interviews with all  8  interview  participants.  Participants  were  asked  to answer 13 questions about their experiences with ASR in the classroom and  one  question  related to specific  transcribed passages from class. Four interviewees signed their responses in front of  a  video camera and four participants spoke their responses into the video camera's microphone. The  same member  of  the  research  team translated  four participants' signed responses to spoken English. All audio files were then processed through Microsoft Video Indexer to generate transcripts. The same researcher then proofread and verified the transcripts for accuracy. We then analyzed the interviews, as detailed in Section 4.

We  were  able to  collect  a variety  of  perspectives  from participants with a range of hearing levels, communication preferences, and experiences with different access services.

Their  differences  allowed  us  to  understand how DHH students with a range of learning backgrounds used ASR.

## 3. QUESTIONNAIRE

A  review of the questionnaire participants' responses informed our subsequent analysis of interview participants' detailed responses. Questionnaire participants were asked to answer 28 questions about their communication preferences, experiences using  access  services,  and  their  responses to ASR in their biology or statistics course.

The  26  DHH  students  who  completed the  questionnaire possessed  a range of communication  preferences. When asked about their communication preferences in face-to-face situations, 9 participants reported feeling most comfortable communicating through American Sign Language or Signed English, 10 reported feeling most comfortable communicating  through  Spoken  English, and  7  reported feeling most comfortable communicating through Simultaneous Communication (signing while speaking).

Participants were asked to self-report their English proficiency, or their  skills  and ability  to read and write  in English, on a 5 point scale from Very High Proficiency to Very Low Proficiency. Their responses are depicted in Table 1.

To explore one of our research questions related to students' levels  of  confidence  with using ASR  in class,  we  asked participants to rate their confidence in the accuracy of ASR in their  biology  or statistics  course  on a  five-point scale. Figure 3 depicts the number of participants with each level of confidence.

Figure 3. Levels of confidence in the accuracy of ASR



The  distribution of confidence  suggests  that even  with custom language models, the accuracy of ASR needs to be improved so that students can be more confident in the tool.

Since ASR is still not accurate enough to provide to DHH students  as  a primary  and  sole  access  service,  we  asked participants questions  that expanded our understanding of their preferences for accuracy.

Two  similar  questions asked them to think about how accurate ASR was in their biology or statistics course-but without  specifying an actual number.  One  question  asked participants  if  they  would  accept  that  same ASR accuracy rate in all of their classes in the future if they used only ASR with no other access services.
