The session was conducted at the weekly Deaf Club meeting in Kingston, Jamaica with 14 of the leaders in the Deaf community (five females and nine males, all of whom were in the age range 21-60), one hearing individual - a graduate student, who is also a trained interpreter - and an interpreter selected by the members of the Deaf community. Six of the participants were tertiary educated - one was enrolled in university at the time of the meeting. The others were educated to the secondary level. None of the participants had an assistive device.

## Sampling

Convenience sampling was employed, as the focus group was held during the height of  the  COVID-19  pandemic.  Recruiting  for  the  focus  group  was  done  indirectly, through the Jamaican Association for the Deaf (JAD). Owing to the closed nature of the Deaf community in Jamaica, the JAD was approached to act as a go-between and to seek an invitation for the researcher to attend a meeting of the Deaf Club to present the idea of the closed-loop system to the attendees and collect their feedback. Thus, the sample consisted of the members of the club who attended the meeting on that night. Additional sessions were planned with other members of the club, but the country went into a series of restrictions,  including  lock  downs,  which  prevented meetings of the Deaf Club. Given the exploratory nature of the study, the small sample size was deemed to be justified, as there was no intention to generalise the result -ing responses to the wider Deaf community.



## Table 1 Guiding questions for Focus Group

1. Did you use technology for education and was your experience with technology a positive one?
2. How would you feel about having a device in the classroom that would replace an interpreter?
3. Is there a general reluctance among the Deaf community to use technology in the classroom?
4. How would you feel about a software tool that allows for two-way communication between a hearing teacher and a deaf student in a mainstream classroom?

## Methodology

The session was facilitated by the first author with the assistance of the interpreter. The facilitator stood at the front of the room and spoke orally, while the interpreter signed the presentation of the facilitator to the Deaf participants. When the Deaf participants signed their feedback, questions and comments, the interpreter spoke orally, so that the facilitator could hear and respond. The facilitator's responses were then signed to the Deaf participants. Video and audio recordings of the session were made and transcriptions were produced after the session for future analysis. The session was divided into two parts; it began with engagement on the use of technology for education and the barriers to technology use in Deaf education (Coy, 2022). Next, the participants' views on the use of technology for Deaf education were elicited. As a part of this discussion, the facilitator introduced the notion of the closed-loop system described in Sect. 4 and then played a video of a signing avatar 2 for the participants, as an example of what a signing avatar could do. The format of the focus group session was to have an open discussion with the participants and to only intervene when clarification was requested. Guiding questions were used to stimulate discussion (see Table 1).

The resulting exchanges were analysed for themes and sentiment. ChatGPT-3.5 (OpenAI, 2023)  was  employed  for  the  thematic  analysis  -  the  results  of  which were verified by all three authors - while sentiment analysis was performed using a transformer-based sentiment analysis toolkit, the pysentimiento toolbox (Pérez et al., 2021). For the thematic analysis, a transcript of the session was generated. The authors worked independently to identify the key themes by reading through the transcript and extracting sections that followed a coherent theme. The separate analyses were shared and overlapping themes identified. Where themes could be merged, a decision was taken to do so. Additionally, the sections of the transcript that contained the  utterances  of  the  Deaf  participants  were  passed  to  ChatGPT3.5  and  a  prompt to generate a thematic analysis was given. The resulting themes aligned with those determined by the independent analyses of the authors.

2 The demo was one of Dutch Sign Language using an avatar developed using JASigning:   h t  t     p s :   / /  v h g   . c  m p .  u   e a . a  c . u  k /  d e  m  o /  m  o v  i e  / W  e  l k  o  m  N  G  T .  m  o  v .



## Results

## Thematic Analysis

Five main themes were extracted from the transcript. The themes were: avatar effec -tiveness  and  realism,  resource  and  cost  concerns,  language  and  cultural  considerations, real-time translation challenges and community involvement and feedback.

## Avatar Effectiveness and Realism

The  participants  had  two  major  concerns  regarding  the  potential  effectiveness and realism of the avatar. Firstly, they mentioned that it was not human-like in its appearance.

… and also the color of the complexion is just poor. And it seems like it' s a robot for real. It' s not human-like. I wasn't impressed of the [sic] complexion of the person when the person was signing. [Participant 3]

Secondly, the Deaf participants of the focus group had real concerns about the potential of the avatar to effectively represent their language. Here, the participants had two  primary  concerns,  the  multimodal  nature  of  signing  and  whether  the  avatar would be effective in situations where a Deaf relay interpreter would be required. The participants made the point that accurate signing involves facial expressions as well as gestures.

That's not effective. Let me explain why I say that. For example , prefix like prefix are some other words where you can add… UN.

For example , you have different form of prefix[sic]. We don't have a sign for those .

prefix. It' s how we express , by using our facial expression. So how would you do .

that with the avatar when it comes on to the prefix part of our language? [Participant 6]

Deaf relay interpreters (DRIs) are experienced Deaf interpreters that provide broker -ing services to other Deaf individuals (Adam et al., 2014). Their roles vary, but they often provide support for Deaf signers with mental challenges, home signs or vision challenges. In some instances, they work alongside hearing interpreters to assist the Deaf where unfamiliar concepts are being discussed, and where the sign being used by the hearing interpreter needs clarification. Given that the contexts within which signing avatars will be used (education, healthcare, transportation, etc.) may require clarification of some concepts, a system that employs an avatar for communication with the Deaf should consider how these clarifications will be provided.

… I have two things. It comes with interpreters and DRI. Deaf relay interpret -ers. For interpreter purposes , you have to sign naturally and sometimes persons don't understand. So that's why we need a deaf relay interpreter in between the hearing  interpreter  and  the  deaf  person.…  Possibly  a  deaf  individual  won't understand. For example , a deaf English word comes down to different words. A deaf person may understand that. For example , idiom.… How will the system incorporate those idioms , those prefix and so forth into the sentence , into Jamaican Sign Language? Because in English it is very easy. [Participant 4]



## Language and Cultural Considerations

The  participants  expressed  concerns  about  the  avatar's  ability  to  understand  and translate multiple languages and the importance of cultural and linguistic sensitivity. This concern arose from a discussion of the assumption that the teacher in the classroom would be using Jamaican Standard English for instruction.

So my concern , suppose the teacher is speaking patois with your program or whatever , you are able to understand clearly and translate it to JSL. [Partici -pant 4]

So will your program be able to understand the three languages , English , patois , and JSL? [Participant 5]

This thought led to the questioning of the motives for developing the avatar, as it related to Deaf culture. One participant asked if the avatar was being developed to replace interpreters - a common concern among the Deaf (European Union of the Deaf, 2023 ; World Federation of the Deaf, 2023, Kipp et al., 2011).

I'm just curious , what's the reason behind the development of that avatar? Do you have a problem with interpreters or what's the reason behind the develop -ment of the avatar? [Participant 12]

Another significant concern expressed, was that hearing parents of Deaf children may not find it necessary to learn sign language, if they think that a signing avatar can be used for real-time communication. This approach, they thought, would lead to hearing parents not interacting directly with their Deaf children.

And  for  young  children , I  think  this  system  can  be  a  bit  negative  for  them because their parents don't learn to use sign language to communicate with them one-on-one. [Participant 3]

## Resource and Cost Concerns

The participants wanted to know if the system would come at a cost to them. They recognised that there would be a cost to develop the system and to provide the classroom-based infrastructure  required  for  successful  deployment. Their  concern  was that the Deaf students, or their parents would have to pay a premium for access to the system. There was fear that, as they had experienced before, the Deaf community would be used as a way to get project funding, which was misappropriated and the community received no benefit from the project. Participants were keen to ensure that cost would not be a barrier to access for Deaf children.



… will that app be free?… , when you develop an idea for the deaf community , it' s  fantastic.  I  like  it.  But  most  times , the  deaf  person  feels  robbed  and  feel neglected and the person benefits from us. So , they go out , they start project and benefit from us , but we as deaf people don't benefit at all. So , they use the deaf community as a name to get funds for themselves. So… And that is not right. So , the deaf community , most times , they write to our views. I understand. So , before you finalise the development , make sure that the deaf club can have full access. [Participant 1]

One participant expressed the view that the money would be better spent on training interpreters, or training hearing teachers in sign language, who could be deployed in the various schools. A discussion ensued about the comparative benefit of spending on system development as opposed to interpreter training. Most participants seemed to accept the logic, if not the substance, of the argument.

Okay , no problem. We're talking about costs when it comes to employing inter -preters. That is true. And we have to save on costs. I agree. But we can save , we can spend costs on other things. For example , when it comes on to the hearing school from primary to high school , they must learn how to sign. That would be good. All the teachers. So , in a deaf school , teachers aren't skillful in those areas. When it comes on to the hearing school , the teachers are good in speaking and communicating. But for the deaf individual , they don't have so many skilled teachers. Teachers have their degree in primary school. So , I think when it comes on to our native language , it should be invested in that area and quali -fied teachers to communicate with us as deaf individuals. [Participant 5]

## Real-time Translation Challenges

The technical challenges were raised by the participants; they had concerns regarding real-time translation and its impact on classroom interactions and learning experiences. The proposed approach consists of a number of integrated sub-systems working together to facilitate classroom-based communication between Deaf students and hearing  teachers.  It  was  pointed  out  that  each  of  the  sub-systems  would  have  an associated time lag. When combined, they feared, the total system lag would hinder real-time participation of the Deaf student.

When the teacher is talking in… English , then translate[s] to Jamaican sign language… So it will be five minutes lagging , ten  minutes , one minute , 15  s because that would be a problem because when the teacher talks , the hearing person , they get it quick quick but for the deaf persons to benefit from what the teacher says. It depends on the waiting time for that , for the voice to be trans -lated to text and then to sign language , so what's the lag time? [Participant 3]



Participants pointed to other fora, such as plays, where interpreters were used. Often, the lag in signing caused them to be behind the rest of the audience, getting the punch line when the hearing audience had already moved on. They pointed out that in an educational setting, the student would have bigger issues than the mild annoyance they feel at the theatre; they made it clear that there could be real harm, frustration and disengagement.

The same challenge with questions for example deaf and hearing are in the class the teacher is there talking… the hearing students always answer first because the deaf person is always lagging behind when it comes on to a physical interpreter. So when the deaf person stand[s] up to sign or to ask a question. The deaf person understand[s] [and] answer[s] same time and the hearing person is lagging behind so it' s the same thing when it comes on to the two parties involved. [When the] Hearing [person is] talking , the deaf person is lagging behind and [when] the deaf person is signing and the hearing person is logging behind. When it comes on to hearing they're talking to the mic and when they speak the hearing person claps and the deaf have to wait until the interpreter reaches that applause phase and then they give a round of applause. So it's always lagging behind. [Participant 3]

## Community Involvement and Feedback

Finally, participants emphasised the importance of involving the Deaf community in the development process.

Will  it  constantly  involve  the  community  in  the  development  of  the  project? [Participant 4]

## Sentiment Analysis

Sentiment  analysis  was  performed  using  the pysentimiento toolbox  (Pérez  et  al., 2021). The sentiment analysis tool is trained with the SemEval 2017 corpus (Rosen -thal et al., 2019 ) using a pretrained RoBERTa model, BERTweet, which is trained on 850 million English tweets (Nguyen et al., 2020). The text of the participants' statements  was  tokenised  into  units  of  topical  coherence,  to  ensure  that  part  of  a thought was not separated into unrelated chunks. These were then input to the sentiment analyser, which output one of three labels, 'POS', 'NEU' and 'NEG', indicat -ing whether the input was positive, neutral or negative in sentiment. Along with the label, a percentage certainty was output by the tool. If the percentage certainty fell below 80%, the response was manually examined and the label corrected, if it was erroneous.



Figure  2 shows  the  result  of  the  sentiment  analysis.  Almost  50%  (49.61)  of the  statements  were  neutral,  while  45.76%  and  4.6%  were  negative  and  positive, respectively.

## Discussion

## Thematic Analysis

The focus group results raised many issues related to the design of a closed-loop system for  inclusive  education  of  the  Deaf.  One  of  the  most  striking  is  the  issue of cultural responsiveness. The appearance of the avatar proved to be an important concern for the participants. This is a common concern for the Deaf when they are introduced to the use of avatars for signing (Quandt et al., 2022) - Kipp et al. (2011) found that the Deaf thought naturalness to be the second most important feature of an avatar. It has been shown that the Deaf showed a preference for natural-looking avatars over more cartoonish anime-style avatars (Brock et al., 2018). However, there seem to be limits to this preference. Adamo-Villani et al. ( 2015) found that a realistic, human-like avatar was less acceptable to users than a stylised one - as pointed out by Quandt et al. (2022 ) this preference may be due to the uncanny valley effect (Mori et al., 2012 ; Shin et al., 2019 ; Wolfe et al., 2021 ). Users can, therefore, be significantly impacted by the appearance of an avatar; if the impression is unfavourable, then the interest in the avatar will be low, even if the signing is intelligible (Adamo-Villani et al., 2016). This may even lead to an overall rejection of the avatar (Naert et al., 2020). This speaks to the need for cultural responsiveness in the design. The requirement that the avatar be representative of the population resonates with the issue of representation and potential bias in AI-based systems for the Deaf (Kaffle et al., 2019).



Fig. 2 Sentiment analysis of the deaf participants' statements



A related  concern  is  that  the  avatar  should  effectively  represent  their  language ).  Despite the challenges, significant progress has been made in recent years to improve the synthesis of the non-manual elements of signing ). Additionally, there are novel approaches

- This issue has been one of the most challenging aspects of signing avatar development (Wolfe et al., 2021 (Wolfe &amp; McDonald, 2021 ; Johnson, 2022 to facial animation that have potential application in the development of signing avatars (Hussen et al., 2021 ; Laine et al., 2021 ; Vougioukas, 2019).

These concerns aren't simply cosmetic, they speak to the very heart of Deaf culture.  Many  Deaf  individuals  define  themselves  by  their  language  (Andersson  &amp; Adams Lyngbäck, 2022 ) thus any inappropriate representation of it is an affront to them. This is where UDL comes into play in the design process. As posited by Sil -vesti and Hartman (2022) a culturally responsive design of the proposed closed-loop system must respect the sociocultural backgrounds, identities (linguistic and cultural) and preferences of the Deaf student, if a desirable outcome is to be achieved.

The issue of Deaf Relay Interpreters, to the best of the authors' knowledge, is an area that has not been discussed in the literature. It is possible that this has been overlooked because the focus has been on generating an avatar to produce accurate, natural-looking signs and less on the deployment of that avatar in a real-world application. As the technology improves and more avatar-led communications systems are developed, attention should be given to how the role of the Deaf Relay Interpreter will be replicated, as stated in World Federation of the Deaf and the World Associa -tion of Sign Language Interpreters statement 'Translators and interpreters take time to prepare in order to fully understand a message and to give consideration to their target audience. An automated translation will not be able to take other sociolinguistic and sociocultural factors into account in order to ensure that the intent of the message sender, and the goals of the message receiver, are achieved.' (World Federation of the Deaf, 2023 , p. 1). This is where an AI-based system could be developed to model the appropriate sociolinguistic and sociocultural elements of deaf relay interpreting in order to enhance the utility of the proposed system for a wider range of Deaf learners.

When the  participants  pointed  out  the  need  for  supporting  bilingual  Jamaican speakers, it brought up the relevance of Vygotsky's concept of polyglossia in the system design in an unexpected way. The idea of support for multiple languages, in the context of inclusive Deaf education, is usually focused on providing language support for the Deaf who have access to both spoken and signed language. The fact that Deaf individuals are aware of the language needs of hearing teachers of the Deaf is a revelation. The Jamaican context is one in which most speakers are either monolingual speakers of the local English-based creole (referred to as Jamaican by linguists, but colloquially called Patois) or bilingual Jamaican/English speakers (Farquharson, 2013 ). While English is the official language of instruction, it has been found that most teachers selectively use Jamaican in the classroom (Nero, 2022). This raises the issue of the ASR system being able to effectively recognise what the teacher says - the hearing students would understand, but the avatar would not be able to sign it. This, the Deaf participants, linked to the culture of the teacher and the apparent effort to stifle the culture, by limiting the teacher to speaking one language over the other. This issue is distinctly a problem in the Global South, as creoles were developed in post-colonial societies, which is also where their use is still mostly seen as problematic (Krämer et al., 2022). Thus, the MPT aspect of the framework becomes relevant to both the hearing and Deaf users of the system - an aspect of the design that can be facilitated by the use of AI-based technological advancements in speech and language technologies.



Participants were in general agreement that it would be better for all teachers in mainstream classrooms to be taught sign language, so as to accommodate Deaf learners - this is echoed by some in the literature (Skyer, 2020). The rationale given was that there would then be enough teachers with the language skill to help the Deaf directly in the classroom and there would be no need for a signing avatar. The primary concern being expressed here, seems to be the fear of cultural marginalisation, which developers of signing avatars have to take seriously and address with the community (Wolfe et al., 2021). However, even the staunchest advocate for signing (even Deaf-only) teachers of the Deaf recognise that the concept is somewhat idealistic (Scott et al., 2023). While the reception to signing avatars may not be ideal, based on the view that signing humans, the logistics and cost implications (Gamal, 2022 ; De Meulder &amp; Haualand, 2021) suggest that the best option for inclusive Deaf education in the Global South is to have a system that allows for the use of signing avatars.

Despite the potential value of having a signing avatar, participants were sceptical. In particular, they felt that hearing parents of Deaf children may not find it necessary to learn sign language, if they think that a signing avatar can be used for real-time communication. This would be quote harmful, given the importance of early sign language learning to the overall development of the Deaf individual (Lieberman et al., 2024). This is a similar concern to that expressed about the rise in popularity of the cochlear implant (Wolfe et al., 2021). This cannot be ignored, but it should not be a barrier to technological innovation in inclusive education. One approach being taken, is to provide early interventions and support for hearing parents of Deaf children to learn sign language (Humphries et al., 2019 ; Terry &amp; Rance, 2023 ; Lieberman et al., 2024).

The  cost  implication  of  inclusive  education  is  significant  for  countries  in  the Global South (Coy, 2022). These concerns came out strongly in the focus group session. So much so, that past experiences of exploitation of the Deaf came up. It was indicated that, in the past, the Deaf community has been taken advantage of by individuals who got project funding and did not deliver, while engaging the deaf, raising their hopes, using them to gather information and ultimately, wasting their time. This non-tangible cost was seen as significant and weighed heavily on their minds. The cost to use the system was also a question that was raised - one participant suggested it might be better to spend the money that might be used for system development, on training new interpreters. The cost of assistive technology to facilitate inclusive education has always been a concern (Borg &amp; Östergren, 2015) especially  in  the Global South (Lynch et al., 2024). This is an important consideration for developers and policy makers who would have to ensure that any system developed using the proposed framework, is accessible, in cost terms, to the Deaf.

The focus group participants  were  sceptical  of  the  speed  and  efficiency  of  the proposed closed-loop system. While advances have been made in the various com- ponents of the proposed system (Kannan et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ; Waldow &amp; Fuhrmann, 2020 ; Wolfe et al., 2022) it is certain that much work will have to be done to ensure a seamless experience for all users.



Community involvement was highlighted as being important - the Deaf participants wanted to ensure that they were integrally involved in the development of the proposed system. Previous work aimed at the community did not include them in the design process, which led to a feeling of distrust of any solution claiming to be for the Deaf (Coy, 2022). This is not a new phenomenon, as other researchers have found the same limitation in systems aimed at inclusive education (Gersten and Edyburn, 2007 ; Stinson, 2010). The partnership model should see Deaf individuals brought into the process at the level of project conception, as their unique perspective can only make intended systems better. Wolfe et al., (2021) go even further, to encourage hearing researchers  to  get  involved  in  the  Deaf  community,  immersing  themselves  in  the language and culture, as much as possible, so that they gain perspective on the needs, concerns and expectations of the Deaf. This will go some way in developing trust in the developers and ultimately the solution.

## Sentiment Analysis

The positive statements highlighted the participants appreciation for what they saw as the inherent value of the proposed tool and its potential application in domains other than education:

'I was thinking this solution is a very good proposal and I appreciate it so much. And knowing that you all want to support the deaf community , I really appreciate it. But [also for] personal use , I think it will help me. Not only [for] education , but when you go out for business purposes and other business. [Participant 5]

The  neutral  statements  were  broadly  indicative  of  interest,  encouragement  and caution:

I'm not stopping you working. Please continue with it. Because maybe you'll surprise  us  with  it.  So , do  your  thing  and  we  will  see  what  happens  in  the future? And if you're successful with the signing at all , we will let you know. We can update you and see what's going to happen. We can help you to be success -ful in the system. [Participant 3]

Here the participant is expressing a certain level of scepticism, while at the same time, leaving room for the outcome to be positive and offering to help. The major -ity of the neutral statements took this form, identification of some value and sharing some concern. This is indicative of a willingness to give the approach a try.

Almost  half  of  the  comments  were  negative  in  nature.  Some  were  openly dismissive:



But for the school students , I  think it can be of assistance , but for the young ones , I don't think so. Nothing beats being natural , the interaction between the two humans. So , I don't see how it will be of any great assistance to the deaf community. [Participant 5]

Other statements reveal issues with how the Deaf have been treated in the past, when others have proposed solutions for helping the Deaf:

You have noticed , but first , when you develop an idea for the deaf community , it' s  fantastic.  I  like  it.  But  most  times , the  deaf  person  feels  robbed  and  feel neglected and the person benefits from us. So , they go out , they start [a] project and benefit from us , but we as deaf people don't benefit at all. So , they use the deaf community as a name to get funds for themselves. So… And that is not right. So , the deaf community , most times , their rights are abused. [Participant 1]

The lesson here is that the trust deficit can hamper acceptance of any solution, regard -less of its merits. Thus, working with the Deaf community from conception to completion is not only recommended, but critical to success.

## Limitations, Challenges and Possible Solutions

While there are obvious benefits to be gained from the proposed system, there are also potential pitfalls that need to be outlined and addressed. Firstly, the Deaf are often  wary  of  technological  solutions  being  proposed  for  their  education,  as  they often take the view that hearing teachers should simply learn sign language, or that the school should provide interpreters. With the use of signing avatars, this reluctance to engage with technology-based solutions may be exacerbated, given some of the concerns expressed in the focus group. An avatar could be seen as a translator, of sorts, because it would be taking input directly from the teacher and presenting it to the Deaf student in their own language. This approach would be more feasible in  mainstream classrooms, where the attempt by the teacher to sign and speak at the same time would be immensely challenging and would likely disadvantage both hearing and Deaf students. However, as pointed out in Sect. 7.1, there is recent evidence that signing avatars are seen as acceptable to the Deaf, though this is heavily dependent on the look of the avatar and the naturalness of the signing (Quandt et al., 2022 ). Another important finding of the study was that users who had been signing for  a  long  time  were  less  forgiving  of  the  perceived  unnaturalness of the avatar's signing,  while  younger  users,  and  those  who  acquired  sign  language  later  in  life, were more forgiving. This has implications for where signing avatars would be most effectively employed, with the evidence pointing to younger users being, potentially, the greatest beneficiaries. This chimes with the use of the proposed solution in the K-12 classroom.

Secondly, the technology would have to work well enough to ensure that it does not harm the Deaf learner. A hearing learner in a mainstream classroom that is exposed

## Abstract

The communication gap between deaf and non-deaf communities arises due to the use of distinct mother languages. A deaf student, who used to communicate in sign language, cannot read fluently materials written in spoken language. This fact causes serious  difficulties  to  deaf  students  since  most  didactic  materials  in  higher  education  are  available  exclusively  in  spoken languages. In this paper, we propose a pedagogical model to deliver educational materials in sign language aiming to provide deaf students the same conditions to succeed as the others, i.e., didactical materials avai lable in one's mother language. Our approach involves the integration of automatic translation technology between spoken and sign language pairs into MOOCs. As  a  proof  of  concept,  we  used  this  methodology  to  design  a  course  addressing  digital  literacy  for  schoolteachers.  The evaluation  of  the  inclusive  MOOC  and  its  underlying  model  reveals  its  potential,  even  though  further  improvements  are required, especially regarding evaluation and usability features.

Keywords: educational content; inclusive MOOC, pedagogical model; assistive technology; automatic translator.

* ADDRESS FOR CORRESPONDENCE: Paula Escudeiro, Games, Interaction and Learning Technologies R&amp;D Center, ISEP, Rua Dr. António Bernardino de Almeida 431, Porto, 4200-072, Portugal

## 1. Introduction

According to the last data of World Health Organization (WHO, 2018) there are about 466 million of people with hearing impairment in the world, and it predicts that hearing impaired conditions will rise to 630 million. When it comes to accessibility in education, deaf students face serious communication barriers  which  hinder  their  integration  within  the  wider  intellectual  communities  and  limit  their opportunities and chances to succeed.

The communication gap between deaf and non-deaf arises naturally since these two communities use distinct mother languages. Sign languages and spoken languages are distinct from each other in all their dimensions, from phonology and morphology to vocabulary and syntax. Spoken languages are linear;  sign  languages  are  visual  and  explore  spatial  dimensions.  A  deaf  student,  who  used  to communicate in sign language, cannot read fluently a spoken language, as much as people used to communicate in a spoken language cannot understand its sign counterpart. Digital information and most -not to say all -didactic materials are available in spoken languages, either in written or audio forms and naturally remain inaccessible to deaf students. Ziadat &amp; Al Rahmneh (2020) research showed the  educational  challenges  facing  deaf  people  are  'the  need  for  sign  language  translator,  lack  of comprehends scientific subject, and lack of teachers' competencies and knowledge to teach properly'.

Technological  developments  enable  the  emergence  of  tools  and  services  to  translate  between spoken and sign languages; however, they are expensive and seldom available in education settings. The  most  common  solutions  rely  on  hiring  interpretation  services  with  expert  sign  language interpreters. These challenges, together with the fact that sign language natives are a minority, may force educational institutions to offer no solutions for deaf students thus blocking their integration in higher education.  Nevertheless, the number of students with specific needs completing high school and enrolling  in  higher  education  has  been  rising  therefore  bringing  to  discussion  the  need  for  devising strategies  of  actual  inclusiveness  that  enable  access  to  the  educational  content  and  knowledge, improving communication and digital literacy.

Currently available technologies can be explored to develop digital content suited for the deaf, based on  an  inclusive  learning  approach,  empowering  deaf  students  with  minimal  computer  expertise  to acquire, enlarge and improve knowledge in a certain topic.

In this paper we propose a pedagogical model to deliver inclusive educational materials for the deaf, through Massive Online Open Courses bundled with sign language automatic translation technology. As a  proof  of  concept,  we  describe  a  course  addressing  digital  literacy  for  schoolteachers  that  was developed using our proposal.

This course was assessed by a group of users with regards to its inclusion features and its added value for deaf students. The results of this evaluation are encouraging and show positive impact.

At the remaining of this paper, we discuss the state-of-the-art of digital educational content available to the deaf, followed by the description of the inclusive MOOC we propose, highlighting the specific needs of the deaf. The process of translating digital learning material for deaf people from written or spoken  Portuguese  into  sign  languages  is  detailed.  The  specifications  needed  to  structure  the educational content for the deaf -underlying the two-way communication enabled by the automatic bidirectional translation -and how it can be used to promote integration and inclusive learning model (Escudeiro, et al., 2019) are also discussed.  Moreover, an example of the development methodology when designing, structuring, and producing multilingual learning objects for the deaf, which may also be used by non-deaf individuals, is considered. This methodology, first designed to work with Brazilian Portuguese and the Brazilian sign language (Libras) -which differs from Portuguese sign Language (LGP) -also includes content in LGP. Finally, the evaluation approach to assess the quality of the inclusive MOOC is explained. Evaluation results  are  presented  and  discussed.  In  this  evaluation  process,  the performance indicators from the Quantitative Evaluation Framework (QEF) (Escudeiro, &amp; Bidarra, 2006) were applied, and two questionnaires for gathering the users' perceptions were produced.

## 1.1. Conceptual or Theoretical Framework

The first institutions offering courses on Po rtuguese sign language (LGP) were based in Setúbal. This has recently changed  and, from  2005, higher  education degrees concerning translation and interpretation of  LGP  started  to  be offered  at the  Polytechnic  Institute of  Coimbra  and  Polytechnic Institute  of  Porto.  The  existing  offer  comprises  mainly  undergraduate  degrees  in  education  and pedagogical sciences available at higher education institutions, focusing on sign language teaching and educating  sign  language  translators,  interpreters  and  teachers  (Bento,  Claudio  &amp;  Urbano,  2014). According to Moraes et al. (2013), a significant part of the bibliography on technical subjects has been developed in Portuguese only, and deaf students rely on the exposition of the interpreted class, without being able to review the content and study materials produced in sign language.

The  participation  of  sign  language  interpreters  in  the  classroom  results  from  a  lack  of  adequate didactic materials and bilingual teachers. This contributes to the effective exclusion of deaf students in the academic community. Most interpreters do not have the same academic degree as the teacher and face difficulties with the concepts addressed in the classroom.  This can directly affect the translation process from Portuguese into sign language, distorting understanding of the content by deaf students (Sousa  &amp;  Silveira,  2011).  In  addition,  schools  and  universities  have  neither  the  adequate  physical infrastructure for this audience, nor teaching methods based on sign language and deaf culture (Galasso et  al.,  2018).  It  can  thus  be  seen  that  public  policies  of  inclusion,  when  poorly  executed,  result  in ineffective deaf education as they do not allow access to learning through these students' first language (sign language).

## 1.2. Related Research

In recent years, there has been significant progress in the accessibility of education. According to Iniesto's recent work, very few authors provide an overview of the process of developing a MOOC having the question of accessibility as the centre of analysis (Iniesto et al., 2022).

Looking from a deaf perspective, we find that only the work of Gupta and Fatima (2016) proposes ideas towards the development of MOOCs for people with hearing disabilities. When it comes to the barriers imposed on deaf learners when accessing e-learning environments, McKeown and McKeown (2019)  point  out  the  learning  management  system  (LMS),  which  are  not  usually  designed  in  Sign Language, as well as barriers in the communication requirements and in course content and materials.

Finding other studies in e-learning systems with accessibility for deaf and hard of hearing has shown to be a complicated task. Some examples are worth describing here, such as the ones by Alcazar et al. (2016), Batanero et al. (2019), Esdras and Galasso (2020), and Batanero-Ochaita et al. (2021).

Alcazar et al. (2016) introduced a speech-to-visual approach e-learning system as a supplementary tool for teaching English in the Philippines. This system includes an English lesson management module, a speech recognition module, and an assessment module. They found that introducing a speech-tovisual  approach  e-learning  system  had  great  advantages  when  teaching  deaf  students  because  it enabled their comprehension of content and addressed their individual needs.

The study by Batanero et al. (2019) redesigned a Moodle platform to include accessible Learning Objects for deaf, deaf-blind, and blind engineering students. Their work was empirically tested with pre/post-test method, content before and after the adaptation of the learning platform, which resulted in an improvement of the academic performance of deaf and deaf-blind students by 46.25% and 87.5%, respectively.  They  concluded  that  accessible  online  education  helps  the  learning  improvement  of students with different capabilities in telecommunications and computer engineering.

Esdras  and  Galasso  (2020)  designed  the  first  bilingual  virtual  learning  platform  which  includes learning tools such as Mental Map, Bilingual Forum, Personal Learning Environments, Digital Repository, among others.

Batanero-Ochaita et al. (2021) evaluate the accessibility and usability of a learning platform prototype and its content for deaf, deaf-blind, and blind. Their work found that all students had a positive response towards the adapted Moodle Learning Platform.

These are all examples within the field of digital accessibility for deaf students.

## 1.3. Purpose of the Study

Deaf students used to communicate daily using sign language, face serious difficulties to read content written in spoken language; this fact has a negative impact in their academic performance. Offering digital content in sign language will be of significant added value for deaf students who will then be able to study and learn using materials in their mother language, like the rest of the students. In this paper we propose a pedagogical model to deliver inclusive educational materials for the deaf, through Massive Online  Open  Courses  bundled  with  sign  language  automatic  translation  technology.  As  a  proof  of concept, we describe a course addressing digital literacy for schoolteachers that was developed using our proposal.

## 2. Methods and Materials

The  development  of  an  inclusive  MOOC  involves  multidisciplinary  teams,  so  that  an  educational environment is built which comprises accessible, and innovative pedagogical settings.

The  inclusive  MOOC  presented  in  this  article  was  devised  for  the  participation  of  deaf  people. Portuguese-speaking countries together with Portuguese and Brazilian people all over the world are the target audience for the post-graduation degrees structured in these MOOCs.

Each MOOC follows a common model grounded in a specific pedagogical structure supported by adapted technology, devised to guarantee the postgraduation degrees' homogeneous features. Within this  format,  any  content  production  must  consider  five  key  factors:  structure,  length,  pedagogical design,  content  production  and  validation (Sousa,  2018;  Queirós,  2018) .  Each  course  is  a  single homogeneous  unit,  of  short  duration,  based  on  online  learning,  which  complies  with  a  set  of specifications to ensure the MOOCs' coherence.

These  specifications  comprise:  (1)  the  prerequisites  and  learning  objectives;  (2)  the  content supporting  the  lesson;  (3)  evaluation  strategies;  (4)  the  interaction  model  to  be  adopted  including pedagogical tools for the deaf; and (5) an introductory welcoming video (Marques et al., 2017). Table 1 presents the specifications, scaffolding the structure of the course and the lessons within it. Continuous and active learning is enabled, with appealing, creative and up-to-date content, and the tasks to be accomplished according to each participant's knowledge and pace.

Table 1. Specifications to ensure coherence in the MOOCs

| Elements in a course                                                                                                                                                                                                | Elements in a lesson                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Promotional video Theme Prerequisites Learning objectives Course description Complementary material Video lessons Lessons summary Title and subtitle Course promotional image (in every lesson) Trainer's biography | Title and subtitle Lesson outline Learning objectives Presentation of appealing content Questions to lead participants to apply/ demonstrate acquired skills and knowledge Reference to the interaction model Bibliography to be used Lesson conclusions and next lesson theme Last lesson presents the evaluation strategy |

The  authors  have  embraced  the  challenge  of  applying  the  pedagogical  model  to  inclusive  and innovative MOOCs. The aim is to promote the inclusion in higher education of deaf individuals with the development  of  technical  equipment,  software,  and  strategies  to  extend  the  MOOC  model  to  a multilingual environment, including Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, LGP and Libras.

All the professionals are involved in the planning and development to meet the objectives and enable a consistent development process, to produce a course suitable for deaf people (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Stages in the inclusive MOOC approach and respective roles.



The sign language is made available through the VirtualSign technology that includes a 3D avatar who translates spoken to sign language.

The  computer  team  is  responsible  for  developing  the  sign  language  application -VirtualSign -(Escudeiro et al., 2013; Norberto et al., 2015) which enables the deaf to access the digital content and learning objectives, and likewise creating the sound environment, to allow the same digital content to be accessible for the non-deaf people.

VirtualSign is the bidirectional translator that translates LGP into written Portuguese, and the written text  into  LGP.  The  translation  from  spoken  to  sign  language  uses  a  3D  avatar  to  reproduce  the animations  mapping  the  corresponding  text.  This  supports  the  intended  interaction  model  for  the MOOCs.

The MOOC design is the responsibility of the Graphic Design Team who employ storyboards to guide the lessons' recordings to avoid flaws in the task performance. The design team also oversees video recording,  image  editing,  animations,  and  graphics  integration,  following  the  content  input  by  the teacher.

The provider is responsible for disseminating the MOOCs through their network, and the 'students' are the users of the final educational product. The teachers are responsible for planning and developing the content, including written texts, images, and videos. The UC Coordinators team validates lessons, with the design team overseeing any corrections and adjustments required to the audio. The research team ('investigators') is responsible for researching the specific needs of the d eaf people to enable intuitive  interaction.  Finally,  the  project  management  team  supervise  the  planning,  while  providing technological and scientific support for successful development.

## 2.1. Research Model

The MOOCs include an automatic translation system from text to sign and sign to text -based on the VirtualSign technology -to enable bilingual content and interaction.

Figure 2 details the pedagogical model, which integrates the content to be used by deaf students, and identifies each element: the digital content repository (DB), where the digital materials for a course are stored; the content experts (teachers), who may use diverse tools to provide the content (Word, PowerPoint, video, sound); the Kinect and the Sensor gloves, which enable the LGP specifications to be read by the computer; and the avatar, which allows the written text to be translated into sign language The educational content is translated automatically for both teachers and students without requiring them to master programming skills or be familiar with non-natural communication channels.

Figure 2. Design solution of the MOOC for the deaf



An audio add-on that converts text to speech was also included, aiming to integrate a simple interface empowering blind end-users to also benefit from the MOOCs. Although this is not core to the current work, this feature is a proof of concept that we are also interested to evaluate.

The MOOC must be clear and user-friendly for all deaf students. The participants are provided with an environment that enables them to interact with the content and succeed in accomplishing the tasks. The architecture of the sign language components is outlined in the next section.

## 2.1.1. Sign language translation component

It is widely known that deaf people rely on visual and spatial representations. to communicate while non-deaf are used to linear languages. These differences require distinct ways of communication for each group. The  Assistive  Communication  for  Education  (ACE)  architecture  (Escudeiro  et  al.,  2018), shown  in  Figure  3,  matches  these  two  distinct  communication  settings  especially  in  educational scenarios, by using a model that considers the specificities of both the deaf and the non-deaf.

Figure 3 shows the two main modules that perform the steps needed in the translation process. The text recognition module converts the written text into signs, which are animated by a 3D avatar. The second module translates the sign language into text. In this process, two devices are used: the Kinect for motion recognition and the data gloves for the recognition of static hand configurations.

Figure 3. Translator architecture.

## 2.3. Data Collection Tools

The  assessment  procedure  was  implemented  in  two  stages  aiming  to  test  the  efficiency  of  the proposed  architecture  and  the  effectiveness  of  the  MOOC  content,  its  usability  and  accessibility features. We have used questionnaires to collect end-user feedback and generate the inputs required by QEF.

Our  goal  was  to  find  out  how  the  proposed  model  might  enhance  access  to  educational  digital content, and whether factors in the performance indicators facilitated or limited its effectiveness.

## 2.4. Data Collection Process

We have been applying  QEF  to  assess  the  quality  of  educational  software  products  during  their development  cycle  for  the  last  30  years.  QEF  has  proved  to  assure  consistency  and  coherence throughout assessment procedure that compute product quality and its evolution during the product development cycle. It enabled to assess the compliance of the proposed MOOC to the needs of the deaf students. Blind students were also involved in this process aiming to grasp the adequacy of the course for this group, although we are aware that the blind-oriented features of the MOOC are still at an early stage of development.

QEF  uses  performance  indicators  based  on  the  standard  ISO  9126  and  SCORM,  that  provide  a quantitative  representation  of  product  quality  in  an  orthogonal  space  (Escudeiro  &amp;  Bidarra,  2006; Escudeiro et al., 2017). For educational software products, we are using three dimensions: pedagogical, ergonomic, and management (Table 3).

Each one of these dimensions impacts the performance of the final product (Escudeiro &amp; Escudeiro, 2012). QEF is grounded on a quality scenario that must be designed for every product.

## 2.4.1. QEF performance indicators

The Pedagogical dimension determines the interrelationship between the subject, the participant, the object and the technological instrument. The evaluation verifies which technological procedures are valid for the educational objectives (Bloom et al., 1956; Bloom, Madaus &amp; Hastings, 1981; Eisner, 2000; Krathwohl et al., 1964). The pedagogical dimension aggregates two factors: learning and evaluation.

The Ergonomic dimension handles the scientific knowledge (Falcão &amp; Soares, 2011; Fialho, 2018; Wisner, 1987), ensuring the conditions that directly affect a learning scenario in its technical, ergonomic, and social features. The ergonomic dimension aggregates three factors: usability, video/audio, and text.

The Management dimension reflects the quality from the functional and implementation points of view. This dimension aggregates two factors: adaptability and content management.

QEF computes the quality of a product based on the Euclidean distance between the real product, and a hypothetical ideal product. The coordinates of the real product is a weighted average of the values of  the  corresponding  factors.  The  value  of  each  factor  is  a  weighted  average  of  the  percentage  of fulfilment of the product features that contribute to the factor. The percentage of fulfilment of each feature is assessed using appropriate techniques for each measure, such as questionnaires or direct input  from  specific  sensors.  The  quality  of  the  product  perceived  at  each  evaluation  is  inversely proportional to the distance between the coordinates of the real product and the ideal product.

The QEF results for each one of the dimensions under analysis are presented in Figures 5, 6 and 7, corresponding to the Pedagogical domain, the Ergonomic domain and the Management domain. These results aggregate the inputs provided by twenty-nine users including 6 blind users, 8 deaf users and 15 users  with  no  sight  or  hearing  impairment.  These  users  were  also  asked  to  answer  evaluation questionnaires that will be discussed in the sections following Section 3.3.

Figure 6. Results of the factors in QEF's ergonomic domain.



Figure 7. Results of the factors in QEF's management domain.



The evaluation of the learning factor in the pedagogical domain was 82 per cent, while the evaluation factor quality results were 32 per cent (Figure 5).

As to the ergonomic domain, the evaluation results on the three factors -usability,  video/audio integration, and text integration -reached 100 per cent (Figure 6).

In the management domain, both the content management and the adaptability factors pointed to 100 per cent (Figure 7).

## 2.5.1. Testing user satisfaction

The MOOC prototype was tested with a sample of twenty-three users including 8 deaf respondents and 15 non-deaf (Figure 8, 9). Two different questionnaires were prepared using a five-point Likert Scale (Russell and Cohn, 2012) to measure the users' satisfaction. One of these questionnaires focused on deaf users and the other on blind users. The participants were also required to provide their education level so that it was possible to infer the results on the content quality. Twenty-three questionnaires were collected, including eight by deaf users which focused on the usability and adaptability of the model (Figure 8).

The survey procedure was the same for both questionnaires. The users had access to a lesson within the inclusive MOOC, and after interacting with it, filled in an online questionnaire structured according to the Likert Scale, concerning usability, adaptability, and content quality, in which 1 corresponds to 'strongly disagree' and 5 to 'strongly agree'.

Figure 8. Questionnaire focusing on deaf users' satisfaction.



Figure 9. Questionnaire focusing on blind users' satisfaction.

## 4. Discussion

The overall product quality of 82% -QEF results -is very encouraging and suggests that our approach has potential to create more inclusive didactic materials. There are still some improvements to be made, for example in the evaluation factor of the pedagogical domain (Figure 5), and in the usability factor in the ergonomic domain (Figure 6).

Regarding  the  users'  perspective,  both  approaches  were  considered  positive,  with  features addressing both bl ind and deaf people's needs when accessing digital content. Most respondents more than 57 per cent -'strongly agreed' with the items 'The lesson content is formally prepared to be accessed by a blind individual' and 'The lesson content is formally prepa red to be accessed by a deaf individual'. Previous research highlighted the importance of developing virtual learning models for the deaf.

Regarding  the  main  objective  of  the  research,  it  was  found  that  several  studies  suggested  the development of strategies and tools for web-based education for the deaf In addition, there was a need to develop an e-learning system with a pleasing user interface. Despite these types of models, including assessment, system, architecture, and design, implemented in previous studies, just one LMS was found for communication between deaf and non-deaf people, developed at the National Institute of Education for the Deaf, in Brazil (Esdras &amp; Galasso, 2020).

The  process  of  creating  multilingual  (Portuguese/Brazilian  Portuguese  and  the  respective  sign languages) courses explores the visual-spatial aspects of sign language in a digital process. A team of lecturers, educational designers, graphic designers, screenwriters, interpreter-translators, and specialized  studio  staff  creates  the  digital  learning  objectives.  The  staff  use  project  management methodologies which list specific tasks and organize the role of each member in the development of the activities. The visual language used is designed to touch deaf students conceptually and amusingly. Thus, the role of the educational designers is to make the learning experience effective while meeting the lecturers' aims for each course (Galasso et al, 2018).

The  combination  of  these  findings  has  encouraged  researchers  and  practitioners  to  design  and develop specific models with bilingual tools that will benefit both Deaf teachers and Deaf students.

## 5. Conclusion

This article presents an innovative MOOC developed to enlarge the digital educational offer for deaf people, also including a simple approach to blind learners. Deaf people are at clear disadvantage in education  as  their  condition  restricts  communication  with  others  and  limits  their  access  to  digital content and information which is a critical factor in education. The inclusive pedagogical model and the proposal  presented  are  designed  to  promote  the  development of  inclusive  and  interactive  learning environments. The intention is to minimize the barriers to access knowledge and education, enabling individuals with diverse needs to work together using the same educational materials.  This will allow bidirectional  communication  in  any  language,  which  can  be  used  in  classrooms  to  create  inclusive learning environments.

To control the quality of the MOOC and its potential to provide access to digital educational content, QEF was used. This is a framework that follows the development of the digital content and controls its production throughout the whole cycle. The results of the evaluation showed the positive potential of this model, even though further improvements are required, especially regarding the evaluation and usability  features.  To  conclude,  the  proposed  pedagogical  model  breaks  the  traditional  inefficient process of communicating with/between people with various types of disabilities, to foster inclusion.

## 6. Recommendations

The model proposed in this paper as well as the methodology that was settled to create inclusive educational materials are a step forward to promote equity and inclusion in higher education. This approach  addresses  those  students  facing  communication  issues  that  prevent  them  to  assess  the content available in the majority language and channels and empowers them to benefit from a more effective learning experience by having access to digital content in a way they can swiftly explore. The core of  the  work  performed  so  far  was  focused  on  deafness  and  sign  languages;  nevertheless,  the features addressing blindness, although simplistic, have proved to be valuable and this line of work should be continued.

The MOOC developed as a proof of concept is just the first of a set of courses that will be delivered following this same approach.

## Intelligent Learning Systems for Inclusive Education in Ghana: Towards an Effective Engagement with Hard of Hearing Students

Petra Mensah Abosi 1 , Hephzibah Emereole 2 , and David Ebo Adjepon-Yamoah 3

1,2,3 Computer Science and Information Systems Department,

* Ashesi University

* Berekuso E/R, Ghana

* Ghana

1 petra.abosi@ashesi.edu.gh, 2 hephzibah.emereole@ashesi.edu.gh, 3 dadjepon@ashesi.edu.gh

Abstract -This research attempts to address some challenges faced when facilitating an inclusive classroom experience for Deaf/Hard of Hearing students (D/HH) in Ghanaian schools and universities by proposing an intelligent learning system. Hence, this research contributes an Intelligent and Inclusive Learning System (IILS) with two main components: signWithMe subsystem and audio-visual transcription system (AVTS) subsystem.

The signWithMe subsystem presents a Ghanaian sign language learning management system (LMS) that is motivated by the limited sign language literacy in Ghana. This subsystem consists of a sign language dictionary, an E-resource, an E-forum, and an E-payment system. It supports inclusive learning of the Ghanaian sign language for both Deaf and Non-Deaf students to interact with the system. This ensures improved diversity and inclusion in our Ghanaian society. Also, the AVTS focuses on improving the teaching and learning experience of Deaf students in Ghanaian schools. The AVTS contributes a novel artificial intelligence approach that uses a counter-checking of Google speech-totext and lip-reading-to-text transcriptions of the Ghanaian sign language in inclusive university lectures. These two subsystems provide services in line with the mandate of the tenth and fourth Sustainable Development Goal (S.D.G.) of ' Reduced Inequality ' and ' Quality Education ' respectively.

Finally, the IILS was analysed per the two main components (i.e., signWithMe and AVTS) and are considered to have high level of usability by 20 Deaf and 5 Non-Deaf users.

Index Terms -Inclusive education, Deaf/Hard of Hearing, Sign Language, E-learning system, Text-to-speech, Transcription, Translation

## I. INTRODUCTION

## A. Background

According to the World Health Organisation [1], over 1 billion people live with some form of disability. Out of that populace, about 430 million people, including children, have complications with their hearing ability [2]. The World Health Organisation defines hearing loss as someone who cannot hear within the hearing thresholds of 20dB or better in both ears. Some of the causes of hearing loss and Deafness include genetic factors, childhood diseases and infections [2]. Hearing loss conditions result in one becoming hearing-impaired, Deaf or hard-of-hearing (D/HH). In Sub-Saharan Africa, there are about 8.9 million [3] Deaf children. The census report from the Ghana Statistical Service showed that as of 2010 [4] in Ghana, with a population of 24,658,823 people, 737,743 were hearing impaired. Most African societies stigmatise the Deaf and refer to them as 'deaf and dumb' [5]. However, some literature [6] indicates that assistive technologies can help students with disabilities to enhance and improve their independence in academic and employment tasks. However, such technologies could vary significantly in cost from one device to another and sometimes can be too expensive for families or schools to afford. Hence, the speech recognitionbased operation of devices such as prevalent smartphones should be leveraged on for accessibility and inclusion in our schools and communities [7]. Also, some of the students in one of the Ghanaian public universities, complained about the interpreting style when a 'new' sign language interpreter takes over from an 'old' sign language interpreter [8]. This reveals the need for government bodies to standardize the Ghanaian Sign Language at all levels of educational institutions to avoid confusing the D/HH students.

There is a communication gap between sign language and oral language [9], [10], and members of society must support families with Deaf children by learning how to communicate with the Deaf children to promote inclusion, and diversity in the society. Furthermore, the illiteracy rates among the Deaf in most countries are above 75 per cent [11], and very few get into higher education. As stated in [12], Deaf children who learn sign language during the childhood stage or schoolgoing period have higher analogical reasoning skills than those who acquired sign language at an adult stage. Hence, there is a need to educate both the Deaf and hearing on sign language to ensure smooth communication and hence, harness the growth of the Deaf community. In addition, main stream educational institutions should make provisions for inclusion of at least their hard of hearing students.

## B. Research Aim, Objectives and Question

This research aims to first provide educational software that will help the teaching and learning of Sign Language and bridge the communication gap between the hearing and the Deaf students. This would be achieved by developing signWithMe system that is composed of a sign language dictionary, a translator, an e-resource, an e-forum and an epayment system. The second aim of the IILS is to improve the speech-to-text and lip-reading-to-text transcriptions and translations in inclusive education environments with the audio visual transcription system (A VTS). To achieve the stated aims above, five objectives are provided below:

- 1) OB1 : Development of a Sign Language Dictionary which consists of videos of the sign language alphabet, numbers, days of the week, and a few phrases.
- 2) OB2 : Development of a Sign Language Translator for the Ghanaian sign language.
- 3) OB3 : Development of a Sign Language E-payment System which enables the purchase documents for their learning.
- 4) OB4 : Development of a Sign Language E-Forum which enables users to interact and share information about the Deaf and Sign Language.
- 5) OB5 : Build a system that incorporates existing technologies that supports the classroom experience of D/HH students, i.e., to access course materials, participate in class discussions, and attend an in-person class.

The aim and objectives outlined above lead to the research question: ' How can an inclusive e-learning system improve classroom engagement for D/HH students in Ghanaian educational institutions? ' This research is motivated by the Sustainable Development Goals 10 (Reduced Inequality) and 4 (Quality Education) [13].

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Assistive technologies enable individuals with disabilities to perform functions that might otherwise be difficult or impossible [6]. Hearing assistive technology helps individuals with hearing needs in listening, comprehending, or recognising sounds and enhancing sound frequencies, making them much clearer [14]. Some researchers explained that Deaf students fail to express their feelings and views to the hearing due to the communication barrier [8]. We discuss the related work in the following groupings: Deep learning and computer vision, OCR Web applications for inclusion, Speech-to-Text applications, and Mobile/Web E-Learning System.

## A. Deep Learning and Computer Vision

In five peer-reviewed papers from IEEE, three researchers [8], [15], [16] used deep learning and computer vision in developing sign language systems.

Moreover, researchers in some of the reviewed papers included Support Vector Machine [8], [15] in their implementation. Although, it could be expensive and lack processing power. Their research aim was to focus on recognising the fingerspelling of the manual alphabet and manual numeric digits. They performed this research using three different classification models. Thus, the log-sigmoid neural network, Elliot neural network and the SVM.

## B. OCR Web Applications for Inclusion

Other researchers from the reviewed papers [15] used OCR and Web 2.0 features that supported several sign languages. OCR makes use of optical character recognition. The process involves converting the scanned image into a binary image and then doing a connected component analysis for extracting character outlines. A case study in Japan demonstrated how a centralised-based learning e-system increased interactivity between the teachers and D/HI students [17].

## C. Speech-to-text Applications

An inclusive classroom requires the use of real-time captioning using a Computer Assisted Real-time Translation (CART) captioner to support D/HH. A captioner (either a person or through a system) is usually present during class and produces an exact transcript of everything heard in the classroom in real-time [18], [19], [20]. CART requires the use of a good microphone in the classroom so that the captioner can listen to the lecturer's voice and transcribe accurately. However, a core limitation to the development of a captioning system is in its ability to recognise and transcribe multiple voices in a classroom discussion where the students do not have individual microphones [18].

In spite of the cutting-edge nature of AI today, the average word-error-rate (WER) for speech-to-text is far from 100%. As per benchmarks published in March 2020 [21], Amazon had an accuracy of 73% (i.e., 27% WER), Microsoft was 78% accurate, Google came in at 79%, and Rev.ai (a dedicated speech-to-text engine provider) scored a slightly better 84%. That said, Google Speech API has the largest text database.

## D. Mobile/Web E-Learning System

Researchers have proved that E-learning systems in the form of mobile and web platforms can support the classroom experience of D/HH. An E-learning system was implemented in Malaysia for D/HH between 7 to 8 years old who wanted to learn alphabets and words using text and sign language [22]. The researcher designed the system using storyboards to describe the customer journey when using the system. They incorporated various sections to help guide the system's users and measured it with different HCI system principles such as consistent colour-coding, accuracy, and performance.

Based on the insight obtained from the related works above, a web application that can also be accessed on mobile phones would be implemented to make it convenient and accessible. Here, some technologies like HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Ajax, MySQL, PHP and frameworks like Bootstrap will be used in developing the web application system.

## III. METHODOLOGY

The methodological approaches used include:

Fig. 1. Audio-Visual Transcription Methodology



## A. Consent of Participants

The consent requirement of the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Ashesi University is essential for this research in order to meet the standards of conducting ethical research which respects the privacy of the disabled. This is in accordance with the international standards for the protection of human participants in academic research. The IRB clearance forms obtained were distributed and read to the participants before engaging with them.

## B. Data Gathering

1) Online Survey: An online survey was created and distributed to specific stakeholders and disability organisations in Ghana. The survey was created to gain more information from PWD on some assistive technologies they use to carry out general and education-specific activities. The survey also targeted school administrators to find out how they promote an inclusive education of PWD and non-disabled persons in their educational institutions.

- 2) Focus Group Interviews: In addition to the online survey, several focus group sessions were conducted to get qualitative data on the experiences of persons with disabilities. First the interviewees were asked for their consent and assured of privacy of the information shared during the focus group session. Thereafter, interviewees were asked questions and they gave their responses which were recorded and translated into themes.

## C. System Performance and Usability Metrics

This is to measure how efficiently a D/HH student can perform tasks on the system through the system functionalities. It includes aspects such as task response time which measures how long a D/HH can complete a task efficiently. Also, the system will be evaluated using Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) principles such as simplicity, consistent colour schemes, and free from errors.

## D. Audio Visual Transcription Methodology

The Audio Visual Transcription system captures both the audio and visuals of lips of the instructor during a lecture (refer to Figure 1). The audio input undergoes audio feature extraction (based on the Google Speech Translation model), in a component called Audio Speech Recognition with particular emphasis on African accents. Also, the visual input undergoes visual lip feature extraction (based on the RNN and LSTM model [23]) in the Visual Speech Recognition component with particular focus on African skin tones. Then, the audio and visual features are synchronised in the Multimodal Fusion component. Finally, a text transcript is generated.

## IV. DATA COLLECTION AND SYSTEM DESIGN

The duration of the data collection process spanned a period of two months. Additionally, one-on-one interviews and focus group conversations with 106 Deaf persons were conducted with D/HH students and other stakeholders in the disability space in Ghana. The contact institutions for the primary research include The Special Needs Department at the University of Ghana Legon, Deaf Congregation of Church of Christ, Circle and Demonstration School of the Deaf &amp; Blind, Mampong, Eastern Region. At University of Ghana's Special Needs Department, the focus group involved 5 Deaf students, 1 Special Needs Assistant and the Head of the department, and the main insights were that Deaf students depend on mobile applications, are encouraged to sit in front-rows during lectures, and use of manual methods. Also, at Church of Christ we interacted with 79 congregants where we noted that the Deaf rely entirely on sign language in communication and are not conversant with Speech-to-Text applications, and they feel safe and accepted in the church community due to measures instituted to accommodate them and their special needs. Finally, at School of the Blind, Mampong, we interacted with 20 Deaf students where we noted that brilliant students in Maths but struggle with English courses, and students engage in informal jobs to earn a living.

1) Data Sampling: Abreakdown of the total sample size involved in this research is as follows: The online questionnaire had 21 Responses. Many Deaf students depend on Mobile applications since it is easier and more convenient to use. Most of them use other technologies such as speech-to-text applications during classes and are highly encouraged to sit in the front rows of the class. The participants rely entirely on sign language in communication and it was also noted that many Deaf in Ghana are not given a chance to pursue science- related courses at the university level and are regularly pushed to social science courses.

First, on the first home page, the user logs in and gains the opportunity to utilise all the functionalities of the system. The user lands on the second home page and can navigate the about page, the dictionary, the translator, the e-resource, the e-forum and the e-payment system functionalities. After which, the user can log out of the system.

Fig. 2. Interactions with the AVTS



The insights derived from the primary research informed the design of the system to support the educational needs of the D/HH in a Ghanaian tertiary institution (refer to Figure 2). Some of the suggested features given by the participants of the focus group session and online survey include:

- The AVTS should have a speech-to-text application to help the Deaf students read the transcripts of the lectures and comments or questions from colleagues (i.e., Deaf and Non-Deaf),
- The text should be magnified to 18 pts,
- The system should be laptop and mobile compatible because most D/HH students mostly use mobile applications.

Based on the features mentioned, the proposed system is an Intelligent and E-learning web application that allows a D/HH:

- Enroll in a course
- Access course materials
- Attend an in-person class, or view course recordings with the help of a speech to text transcriber that takes the lecturer's audio or audio from a video and translates it to text.
- Then, the transcribed text is displayed on the student screen, which can be saved in any known document extension such as .pdf, and .doc format. On the other end of the system, the lecturer can login as an Administrator to monitor the student's login activities and upload course materials.

Based on both the system and user requirements provided above, the IILS composed of the signWithMe subsystem and AVTS is designed as a web application system (and to be implemented using HTML, CSS, Javascript and Bootstrap) to ensure user-friendliness. The IILS has been designed with clear and bold writing, warm colours, and features that ensure the signWithMe system is highly interactive and accessible.
