## A. signWithMe System Design Architecture

The signWithMe system is built as a web system with an efficient backend architecture that interacts with the database and updates the frontend of the system.

- 1) Web Application Architecture: The MVC approach will be used in implementing the signWithMe system. The system will be structured into three logical components, Model, View and Controller. When users query the signWithMe system for videos on the alphabet, the controller connects with the model-the model also connects with the videos' database. The database has the videos in the alphabet. Then, the view displays the video on the alphabet for the user to learn and interact with the system.
- 2) Database schema: The database has been designed to contain the entities and attributes of the data. The database schema contains the relationships between tables in the database and their data types.

## V. AVTS FEATURES

On the student part of the website, the Speech-to-text feature is the core functionality to support Deaf/Hard of Hearing students in a live class and this was implemented using two approaches. The first approach was developed using Google cloud speech API, and the transcriber function built in Python. The second approach was developed using Web Speech API in JavaScript, which interfaces easily with Google Chrome browser.

The transcription code developed is written in Python using several modules and libraries from Google Cloud API and native Python packages imported into a Python script. It takes streams of inputs by accessing the microphone of the user and stores the audio streams temporarily in a buffer. The audio stream input captured is sent to Google Cloud Speech API, where it is converted from speech to text in real time. To counter-check this translation, the camera module of a laptop is interfaced with a lip-reading module based on Long Short- Term Memory (LSTM) algorithm (see Figure 5). LSTM is an artificial recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture.

Fig. 5. Lip-Reading LSTM Architecture



After transcription is done, it displays the transcribed text on the terminal of the users' machine. The transcribed text is displayed on a web page using Python's FastAPI which supports web applications. The user is able to view the transcribed text through a specific route which in this application is the '/speak' route

## VI. DISCUSSION OF RESULTS

## A. Audio Visual Translation System

The translation functionality of the system was tested and measured over three criteria which are: accuracy, performance, and usability. Additionally, other features of the system for both the lecturer and the student were tested and evaluated using human computer interaction (HCI) system design principles such as efficiency, consistency, and error free.

## B. Word Error Rate

The word error rate is is a common metric used to compare the accuracy of the transcripts produced by speech recognition and transcription service. The AVTS system built used two transcription services to measure the Word Error Rate of translating audio recordings. After series of tests with various audio recordings, an average percentage value was derived relative to their word-error-rate (WER) as shown in the Table I below:

TABLE I WER OF SPEECH TRANSLATION SYSTEMS

| Speech Models α         |   WER (%) β |   WER with Accent (%) γ |
|-------------------------|-------------|-------------------------|
|                         |             |                      76 |
| Web Speech API          |          65 |                         |
| Google Cloud speech API |          25 |                      45 |

During a demo session, the Web Speech API and Google Cloud speech API transcription functionality were tested using several 100-words scripts read out for transcription. The accuracy of the transcribed text differed between the two speechto-text API's. The accuracy was measured by comparing the text from the original script with the words captured by each of the API's. After each transcription, the following were recorded: the number of correct words, the number of incorrect words captured, and the time spent in a transcription. In each of the 100-words scripts used, both APIs performed well in transcription accuracy. However, the Google Cloud speech API had the highest rate of accurate words because it supported wider range of languages such as EN-GH (Ghanaian-English) and vocabularies than the Web Speech API. Next, the performance of both APIs was extremely high and effective during translation in real time. However, both transcription services depend on strong internet connectivity and there are lags in transcription when there is unstable network.

## C. User Testing of the AVTS

The testing activity of the E-learning system was carried at in the School of the Blind Deaf Mampong. The school for testing was selected because it had a larger population of D/HH students in the upper classes of their high school journey which is also pre-university levels. During testing, the time given to interact with the 20 students was limited because the students had classes in session. The D/HH students had a positive experience with the system's features and suggested that the audio from the recorded videos on the system should not be too fast so that they can follow while the transcription is ongoing.

However, ten D/HH students were selected at random to interact with the student part of the learning system and one teacher was also selected to interact with Lecturer section of the system.Each student interacted with the different functionalities of the system for 10 minutes and after which provided their feedback. The primary language used for communication in the School of the Deaf and Blind is sign language. Thus, through the help of a sign language interpreter, the system was described to the selected students, and they were encouraged to explore the features of the system and provide feedback on their experience.

## D. Testing of signWithMe System

For the signWithMe subsystem, there are two tests implemented, the unit testing of all relevant methods and functions of the system and the user testing, which was conducted in the Mampong School for the Deaf. Through this process, the signWithMe subsystem has a sign language dictionary, translator, e-forum, e-resources and e-payment subsystems. The application system also meets the non-functional requirements.

Thus,

- the log-in/sign-up system ensures security by ensuring users log-in to access the functionalities and features of the application system. The system verifies the user's email address before he/ she can access the application's content.
- the Graphic User Interface (GUI) of the application system has been designed to ensure user-friendliness and interactivity. The navigation of the site is manageable and comprehensible, and
- the database and the hosting site have been secured such that the application system would always be available for users.

The signWithMe application system was evaluated by ten Deaf students, two teachers at the Mampong School for the Deaf, and some students at Ashesi University. They gave important feedback that the application is easy to use and navigate. One Deaf student, shared that because the videos are short and demonstrate a particular sign, it makes it comprehensible. Another Deaf student, shared that the system had bold and clear writings, making reading easier. The students were pleased with the explanation given on each of the signed words as it made learning more accessible. Also, the Deaf students looked through the signWithMe sign language dictionary and gave feedback on how some words should be signed. They also shared that the system can be a mobile application to be accessed on the phone.

## VII. CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS

This research explored what accessibility technologies and inclusion concepts will improve the classroom engagement for a D/HH student in Ghanaian schools. Through literature review and stakeholder engagements in the disability sector, specific system features were highlighted. As a result, the IILS was developed to provide a web platform where people can learn and practise sign language, and D/HH students to benefit from audio-visual transcription in their classrooms. Additionally, the IILS developed supports both students and lecturer. It can be concluded that since objectives 1-5 were achieved, the IILS reasonably improve classroom engagement for D/HH students in Ghanaian educational institutions. This research also focused on the Sustainable Development Goals 10 (Reduced Inequality) and 4 (Quality Education).

The IILS can be improved especially with the AudioVisual Transcription System (AVTS). During transcription, there were instances where the speech-to-text APIs displayed wrong words due to a noisy environment, an inaudible voice or the teacher speaking fast. The Google Speech API could not accurately identify words pronounced with African accents (45% WER). Here, more machine learning optimisation approaches like language and hyper-parameter models can be explored to improve the efficiency of the Google speech-totext transcription. Also, it must be trained using data sets with audio recordings from Ghanaians to help in producing better results for the speech-to-text transcription.

## Intelligent System for the Learning of Sign Language Based on Arti fi cial Neural Networks



```
, and R. Granizo 1 Universidad de las Fuerzas Armadas ESPE, Sangolqu í , Ecuador {drrivas,rmalvarez,jfguanoluisa1,mbzapata,japerez9, ragranizo}@espe.edu.ec 2 Ponti fi cia Universidad Cat ó lica del Ecuador sede Ambato, Ambato, Ecuador {egarces,jbalseca}@pucesa.edu.ec
```

Abstract. Sign language has become a form of communication for people who have some type of hearing impairment, in order to relate to the world around him and perform daily activities including education, work performance and personal development. In the knowledge society, the development of new Technologies for Information and Communication (TIC), they constitute a teaching tool that changes the conditions for learning and communication as the world is digitized. Therefore, the development of an Ecuadorian sign language learning system based on the use of a gesture sensor and an arti fi cial neural network multilayer feed-forward, implementing the Backpropagation algorithm, which takes advantage of the parallel property of decreasing the time required by a processor to distinguish the existing relationship between given patterns, represents a solution for improving the teaching-learning process.

The system consists of three main layers: The fi rst is responsible for the acquisition of data through a gestural device; the second uses the library of the gesture sensor to perform the acquisition and storage of information of the hand and the position of the fi ngers. Finally, the output layer, once the training of the neuron is analyzed, generates the real-time recognition of sign language.

Keywords: CSCL  Arti fi cial neural networks  Pattern recognition  Leap Motion

## 1 Introduction

The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that more than 5% of the world population suffers from some type of hearing disability, among them, 466 million are adults and 34 million are children [1]. In Latin America, the presence of hearing problems is 1.6% in children under 14 years of age; in people older than 15 years it is 8%; and 38.62% corresponds to people over 65 years of age. In Ecuador, according to the National Council for Disability Equality (CONADIS) there are 437,268 people with some degree of disability; Of these, 14.17% have hearing impairment, subdividing this percentage of the population as follows: 8.13% are children under 12 years, 13.13%

people between 13 and 65 years, and 19.05% people over 65 years. Of a total of 58,161 people with occupationally active disabilities, 16.03% are people with hearing disabilities, of this percentage 16.24% are people whose age is between 18 to 29 years, 78.49% people between 30 to 64 years and 5.28% they are people over 65 years [2].

Traditional education is mostly focused on people without any type of disability, which makes it dif fi cult for people with disabilities to have access to a quality education that has the improvements and technological advances developed throughout the world [3]. Therefore, promoting the inclusion of people with disabilities and developing new teaching tools is considered an appropriate option in the fi eld of education, new methodologies such as Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) are presented as an emerging area of the learning sciences regarding how people can interact together with the help of computers [4].

There is an interest in projects dealing with arti fi cial neural networks, or gesture sensors, focused on the teaching of sign language, as can be indicated in the following works; for example, in the article developed by [5], consists of the use of Leap Motion, a computerized pattern classi fi cation module and a graphical user interface for the teaching of Ecuadorian sign language.

The proposal made by [6], consists of a Sign Language Teaching Model (SLTM) designed to develop different Communication Skills (CS) in deaf children within a Collaborative Learning Environment with Mixed-Reality (CLEMR). In the work developed in [7], he proposes the use of a new information technology to model sign language based on the human computer interaction model. In addition, in [8] the recognition of patterns through arti fi cial neural networks is proposed.

Based on the above, a learning system is presented that uses as input device a gesture sensor, which acquires the complete data of the hand such as: size of the fi ngers, center of the palm, orientation with respect to the axes; performs the recognition and classi fi cation of the signs through the development of a neural network [9], on the other hand, it contains three environments created especially to improve the learning experience of sign language, to contribute in the process of educational and professional training of people with some degree of hearing disability.

This work is divided into six sections, including the introduction. The second section deals with the training of the arti fi cial neural network, in Sect. 3 the development of the system interface is exposed; Sect. 4 contemplates the tests performed on the system on users with and without disabilities, the presentation of the results analysis is found in Sect. 5 and fi nally the conclusions are located in Sect. 6.

## 2 Neural Network Classi fi er

In the recognition phase, a multilayer feed-forward Neural Network is used, with the Backpropagation algorithm; which takes advantage of the property of reduction of time required by a computer processing unit; to distinguish the existing relationship between given patterns [10]. The neural network has three layers: input, hidden and output; the fi rst is constituted by m entries, the hidden layer is composed of n neurons and a logarithmic sigmoid activation function f 1 , the output layer is composed of six neurons with a logarithmic sigmoid activation function f 2 ; this structure can be seen in the Fig. 1.

Fig. 1. Architecture of a three-layer arti fi cial neural network feed-forward.



The output given by the supervisor is responsible for establishing the response that forms the network from a speci fi c input, in this context we have the binary combination 000001 which is equal to 1, up to 100111 equivalents to 39; the same that represents the letters A to Z and to the numbers from 1 to 9 respectively.

The vector Y of the Neural Network, for an input vector P = (P1; … ; Pm), is given by the following expression:



When the output Y, express a probability that P belongs to a letter of the alphabet, W1 and W2; they express the matrices of the weights of the fi rst and second layers respectively, b1 and b2 determine the level of threshold or activation of the neuron of the input and hidden layer.

The activation function used in the Arti fi cial Neural Network is a logarithmic sigmoid function because the output vector has values of 0 and 1, f1 = f2 = 1 = (1 + e ( -z) ).

To perform the training of the neuron, a database was created in Amazon Web Server (AWS) with values of the angle between the normal vector and the direction of the palm of the hand, angles of the palm with respect to the x, y, z; the angles generated by the direction vector of the following phalanx, except the distal phalanx in the thumb. If the vector of entries belongs to a letter, the output will give us an approximate vector, for example, if letter is A, the output gives us a vector equal to [0 0 0 0 0 1], from number 9 the output is [100111].

## 3 Development of the Neural Network

The implemented network is a multilayer perceptron, structured by an input layer that has a vector with 21 features, a hidden layer with 25 neurons and an output layer with 6 neurons. Weights and tracks were initialized with randomic values between -0.5 and 0.5. The output layer and the hidden layer have a logarithmic sigmoidal activation function that limits the value of the output between 0 and 1, adopting values very close to 0 when the input is small, but as the value increases on the abscissa axis the function happens to be growing.

The weights and the values of the roads were calculated by the method of back propagation, which starts from the last layer to the fi rst, which causes the increase in error; to fi nd the gradient of the error totalized in each neuron, the new weights and paths are recalculated to the inverse direction together with the value of Alpha, which for this network has a value of 0.5, which represents the normal learning rate avoiding jumps in said learning, Fig. 2.

Fig. 2. Graphic description of the developed neuronal network



## 4 Structure of the System

The architecture of the system consists of three main layers: Inputs, Script and Outputs Fig. 3. The input layer is responsible for the acquisition of data by means of a gestural device; the script layer uses the library of Leap Motion, to perform the acquisition of the position of the fi ngers when forming a signal, the storage of the information of the hand is done in MySQL, for the effect the Amazon Web Server platform also communicates the Matlab and MySQL programing interfaces for data processing and neuron training. Finally, the output layer generates the recognition in real time of Sign Language, by creating a teaching-learning system made in Unity 3D.

## 5.2 Learning Tests

The tests of the learning system are carried out with a total of 10 users, of which 4 are children who have hearing impairment and 6 children without hearing impairment.

The learning tests starts with a stage of recognition of the system by the user, then the three learning modes must be completed: Sorted letters mode, disordered letters mode and learning mode or letters leakage; in the fi rst, the whole alphabet of the sign language is ordered in an orderly manner AZ, the second mode shows 10 letters of the alphabet interchangeably, and the third consists in making the greatest number of letters of a word in a time of 30 s at the end, the time is analyzed and the score obtained is indicated.

The learning curve on the part of the users who have auditory disability is appreciated, it can be observed that the performance and the level of learning increases in the 4th and 5th tests. The performance and level of learning of users who do not present any type of hearing impairment where it is observed that the learning curve increases exponentially.

Figure 7, shows the average learning curve obtained in children with hearing impairment versus children without hearing impairment, graphically you can see the similarity of the curves, which show an exponential growth, which allows to deduce that the system ful fi lled the teaching objective.

Fig. 7. Average learning curve of users with and without hearing impairment



## 6 System Usability

The SUS questionnaire allows evaluating the usability of the system once the learning is analyzed, a test is performed, collecting the data for analysis and study; The results obtained by the users are presented to each question posed [11].

For the system to be acceptable in terms of usability, the global average must exceed 68% according to the SUS questionnaire standard.

The results obtained in the questionnaire exceed the standard value by 80.25%. Therefore, it can be considered that the learning system developed is comfortable in its use, it does not present complexity in the manipulation and, above all, the results indicate that It is useful for learning sign language.

## 7 Analysis of Results

The system based on arti fi cial neural network presented a better response in comparison to the statistical classi fi er, since it was obtained more than 97% of correct answers compared to 87%, derived by the use of the statistical classi fi er.

The multifaceted neural network was adapted correctly to the data entered by the user, allowing to maintain an interaction between the student and the system, which is evidenced by an improvement in learning.

The use of assistance systems for teaching in cases of people with special abilities, allows the student to progress in their learning as it does not depend on the presence of an instructor to practice the different signs.

The teacher can integrate computer tools in their teaching process, including people with disabilities, allowing them to contribute to the development of their daily activities.

## 8 Conclusions

The development of the Ecuadorian sign language learning system through neural networks is a tool that has allowed the inclusion of new technologies in the learning of basic sign language for children with and without deterioration of the auditory system.

The responses of the average learning curves performed in the 10 users with and without auditory disability show an exponential growth, which indicates that the higher the number of training sessions the learning level increases.

## Paper Source: Interactive System Based on Artificial Intelligence and Robotic Arm to Enhance Arabic Sign Language in Deaf Children

## Interactive system based on artificial intelligence and robotic arm to enhance arabic sign language learning in deaf children



Imane Nedjar 1,2 · Mohammed M'hamedi 2

Received: 1 February 2024 / Accepted: 28 May 2024 / Published online: 13 June 2024 ©TheAuthor(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024

## Abstract

Tailored support is crucial for deaf and hearing-impaired children to overcome learning difficulties, particularly during primary education. The absence of listening profoundly hinders the progression of the learning journey, as it plays a pivotal role in language acquisition. Employing assistive technology is one approach to address this issue in the field of education. This paper introduces RSA, an interactive system designed for the recognition and simulation of letters in Arabic Sign Language. Our system's objective is to enrich language learning in an engaging manner. RSA utilizes artificial intelligence to identify and recognize the gestures corresponding to Arabic letters in real-time. Additionally, the system has the capability to replicate these letters through the utilization of a robotic arm. Thanks to its simplicity, the system holds promise in enhancing the acquisition of Arabic sign language skills for deaf children.

Keywords Deaf children · Learning difficulties · Arabic sign language · Artificial intelligence · Robotics

## 1 Introduction

The World Health Organization reports that 34 million children worldwide suffer from deafness (WHO, 2024). Hearing loss not only affects children's speech, but it can also impact their cognition, leading to social repercussions like seclusion, reduced self-esteem, and educational difficulties (WHO, 2024; Welsh et al., 2001).

B Imane Nedjar imane.nedjar@univ-tlemcen.dz Mohammed M'hamedi mohamed.mhamedi@univ-tlemcen.dz

1 Biomedical Engineering Laboratory, Tlemcen University, Tlemcen, Tlemcen 13000, Algeria

2 First Cycle Department, Ecole Supérieure en Sciences Appliquées de Tlemcen, ESSA-Tlemcen, BP 165 RP Bel Horizon, Tlemcen 13000, Algeria





The causes and severity of deafness vary from one child to another. It can be linked to prenatal factors like genetic predisposition or intrauterine infections. Alternatively, it may occur during the perinatal period due to oxygen deprivation during birth or severe jaundice in the neonatal stage. Other contributing factors include infections, injuries to the ear or head, medications with ototoxic effects, and deficiencies in nutrition (WHO, 2024). Furthermore, syndromic causes of deafness, such as peripheral auditory impairment or central nervous system dysfunction, may lead to the coexistence of additional disabilities, including behavioral disorders, developmental delays, deafblindness, and specific learning disabilities (Antia et al., 2009; Laughton, 1989).

Deaf children, like their hearing peers, can face educational challenges that encompass two primary obstacles. The first is the impairment of learning attributed to intellectual disability, emotional distress, environmental adversities, and economic factors (Edwards, 2010). The second challenge pertains to specific learning disabilities, including auditory processing disorder, dyslexia, and dyspraxia. According to the US Interagency Committee on Learning Disabilities (ICLD, 1987), these disabilities encompass a broad spectrum of disorders marked by significant difficulties in listening comprehension, speaking fluency, reading performance, writing, reasoning, and mathematical abilities.

Unlike their hearing peers, who acquire spoken language in school, deaf children learn sign language as their primary means of communication.

Typically, sign language relies on the movements of the hands, their shapes, palm orientations, and the positioning of the arms or body (Rastgoo et al., 2021). Additionally, certain sign languages incorporate lip-patterns and facial expressions to convey nuanced word meanings (Ahdal &amp; Nooritawati, 2012).

Sign languages vary by country, with examples including A merican S ign L anguage ( ASL ) in the United States, Spanish Sign Language in Spain ( L engua de S ignos E spañola, LSE ), and Ar abic S ign L anguage in the Arab world ( ArSL ). Moreover, there exists an international sign language known as I nternational S ign ( IS ), utilized during international gatherings.

As cochlear implants and middle ear implants technology have transformed the lives of numerous children, facilitating their integration into society, the use of other technologies is on the rise to further enhance the lives of deaf and hard of hearing individuals.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of computer-based sign language systems employing artificial intelligence by enabling the hearing-impaired to express themselves through sign language, while also facilitating comprehension for hearing individuals. Such advanced systems are designed to recognize sign language (Wadhawan &amp; Kumar, 2020; Wei et al., 2019; Cheok et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021; Sharma &amp; Singh, 2021; Sreemathy et al., 2023), interpret sign language (Dabre &amp; Dholay, 2014; Debevc et al., 2011), translate sign language (Abiyev et al., 2020; Estrada Jiménez et al., 2016; Yin &amp; Read, 2020; Kumar et al., 2018), and present sign language (Elliott et al., 2008; Vilhjálmsson et al., 2011; Lu &amp; Huenerfauth, 2014; McDonald et al., 2016; Ebling &amp; Glauert, 2016).

Onthe other hand, several researchers have leveraged the advantages of technology to enhance the learning of sign language. This includes the development of humanoid robot-assisted systems tailored for sign language tutoring (Kose &amp; Yorganci, 2011;



Köse et al., 2015; Kose et al., 2014; Luccio &amp; Gaspari, 2020; Kose et al., 2012; Uluer et al., 2015) as well as educational tools dedicated to supporting the instruction of children with hearing impairments (Imashev et al., 2024). For example, (Basiri et al., 2021) introduce the utilization of a social robot for adaptively teaching Iranian Sign Language to users. They achieve this by initially adjusting the robot's logic to align with the teaching content using a fuzzy logic mechanism during training sessions. Subsequently, the robot's teaching methods are intelligently adapted based on the user's past and present performance. Kose et al. (2014) introduced the utilization of interactive humanoid robot-based approaches for learning sign language. The primary goal of these interactive methods is to offer guidance to children with hearing impairments, aiding them in acquiring vocabulary from the Turkish sign language. The chosen set encompasses 10 signs: Spring, Throw, I/Me, Big, Mountain, Table, Black, Come, Baby, and Mother. Jemni and Elghoul (2008) have developed a web-based tool for creating multimedia courses aimed at teaching and learning sign language. This tool employs avatars to animate words extracted from the sign language dictionary. Another application, built upon educational games, was created by Kurniawan et al. (2022) to facilitate English learning for students with hearing and speech impairments.

Nawshin et al. (2020) introduced a model designed to assist children with hearing disabilities on their journey of independent reading and writing. This model employs Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to convert PDFs of paper books into sequences of Bangla sign language. Knoors and Marschark (2014) state that early hearing loss and limited communication can have a negative impact on cognitive and social-emotional development, potentially hindering learning. Nevertheless, interactive learning plays a significant role in enhancing a child's cognitive skills. Moreover, enjoyable and playful activities are known to be important for child development (Kose et al., 2014).

For this reason, in this work, we propose an interactive educational system that utilizes artificial intelligence and robotics to recognize and simulate letters of the Arabic sign language. We have named this system RSA , representing R ecognition and S imulation of A rabic sign language. The primary objective of RSA is to enhance the learning experience of Arabic sign language, making it more accessible and enjoyable through the incorporation of interactive and entertaining elements.

The article is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the Material and Method used. The evaluation results are presented in Section 3 and discussed in Section 4, Section 5 concludes the article.

## 2 Material and method

## 2.1 Proposed system

Children often have a short attention span and can be easily overwhelmed when exposed to a subject as complex as language signs. To sustain their attention and motivation for a longer period, we introduce the interactive system RSA for learning the letters of Arabic sign language.

RSA encompasses two key functionalities:



Gesture Recognition: this functionality leverages artificial intelligence to recognize and identify the gestures associated with Arabic letters in sign language.

Letter Simulation: the second feature involves the simulation of these letters using a robotic arm.

In RAS, there are two modules: the Recognition Module and the Simulation Module, as illustrated in Fig. 1. In the following sections, we will explain each module separately.

## 2.2 Recognition module

RSAisaninteractive system that enables real-time recognition of letters in Arabic sign language, empowering deaf children to correlate signs with their respective letters. In essence, the children perform a sign, which is then captured by a camera. The resulting image undergoes processing by the recognition module and subsequently displays the detected letter on a display device.

To achieve the identification and recognition of letters in Arabic sign language, we used Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). CNNs have been widely applied in computer vision tasks and have proven to be highly effective (Bhatt et al., 2021; Nedjar et al., 2022; Schaffter et al., 2020).

We have installed the proposed system on Raspberry Pi to ensure real-time detection and classification. Raspberry Pi is a small-sized nano-computer, that functions similarly to a standard computer but is reduced to its simplest form in terms of composition.

## 2.2.1 Recognition model

Out of the numerous CNN architectures available, we have selected MobileNet (see Fig. 2) as basic recognition model, primarily because of its lightweight nature (Sandler et al., 2018). This specific feature makes it highly suitable for embedded systems with limited resources.

We have employed transfer learning (Iman et al., 2023) by initializing MobileNet with pre-trained ImageNet weights. In addition, we have applied fine-tuning (Peng &amp; Wang, 2020) by adding the following layers:

## 2.2.2 Model configuration

Loss function we have utilized the cross-entropy loss function ( F ) for both training and testing stages.

Optimizer we employed the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) (Zinkevich et al., 2010) optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and a momentum of 0.9.

Epochs we trained the model for a total of 20 epochs.

## 2.2.3 Dataset

The recognition model was developed to classify 13 letters of ArSL, as depicted in Fig. 3. These same letters are also the ones that our robotic arm is capable of simulating.

We have utilized the RGB Arabic Alphabets Sign Language Dataset, proposed by Al-Barham et al. (2023) to train and test the recognition model. This dataset consists of fully labeled images that represent the letters of Arabic sign language. A total of 3,510 images were utilized, with 80% of them allocated for training the model, while the remaining 20% were reserved for testing. Figures 4 and 5 illustrates the distribution images for each class.

## 2.2.4 Data augmentation

Data augmentation techniques are used to improve the performance of CNNs by increasing the size of the original training dataset with artificially data (Taylor &amp; Nitschke, 2018).

In this study, we have incorporated a horizontal flip transformation, which horizontally reflects images. Furthermore, we have applied zoom transformations to magnify the images. Lastly, shearing transformations were also employed.



Fig. 5 The set of training and testing images for each class



## 2.3 Simulation module

The RSA simulation module operates by taking an Arabic language letter as input and producing the corresponding gesture in Arabic sign language. This simulation is carried out through the utilization of a robotic arm.

In the process of creating the robotic arm, we made use of the open-source 3D printed life-size robot known as InMoov (Langevin, 2024). Controlling the finger and wrist movements was achieved through the application of servomotors (specifically Metal Gears RG996R). Furthermore, for executing simultaneous movements of various fingers during the simulation, we implemented thread-based programming. In computer programming, threads serve to handle multiple concurrent actions. The electronic circuitry of RSA is illustrated in Fig. 6.

## 3.2 Analysis of the results

Figure 7 illustrates the learning process throughout epochs with the presentation of loss and accuracy curves. It is evident that precision steadily improves as the epochs progress. After 20 epochs, the model achieved an impressive training accuracy of 99.28%, with a corresponding loss value of 0.0508. On the test dataset, the model exhibits remarkable performance, achieving an accuracy of 98.56%, precision of 98.54%, recall of 98.46%, and an F1 score of 98.47%.

The utilization of the confusion matrix depicted in Fig. 8 offers a comprehensive perspective on the performance of our sign language recognition model. It effectively outlines the classification outcomes for the various letters in Arabic sign language. Upon analyzing the values within the confusion matrix, it becomes apparent that the recall ranges from 89% to 100%. Notably, the letters 'Beh', 'Dad', 'Jeem', 'Lam', 'Sad', 'Sheen', 'Theh', and 'Yeh' all achieved a perfect recall value of 100%. However, the letter 'Reh' exhibited the lowest recall at 89%, with 2% of its images misclassified as 'Yeh' and 9% as 'Dal'. This can be attributed to the significant resemblance between the letter 'Reh' and the letter 'Dal' (see Fig. 3), which likely contributed to the misclassifications.

Table 1 displays the Precision, Recall, and F1-score values for each letter, calculated from the confusion matrix. Notably, the results reveal that the letters 'Beh', 'Dad', 'Jeem', 'Lam', and 'Sheen' achieved an outstanding classification accuracy of 100%.

## 4 Discussion

Deaf and hearing-impaired children often face diverse learning challenges, which can result in lower academic achievement compared to their hearing peers (Marschark &amp; Knoors, 2012). Providing early educational support for deaf children is crucial to address these obstacles and ensure effective guidance for academic success.

In this study, we introduce an interactive RSA system aimed at aiding deaf children in learning Arabic sign language letters during primary education. RSA is intended to assist children in overcoming the prevalent challenges associated with learning disabilities. Indeed, learning disabilities have frequently been linked to memory issues, visual perception difficulties, and executive functioning challenges (Elliott et al., 1988). These can lead to specific learning disabilities such as language deficits, like dyslexia, which involve difficulties in reading and writing (Edwards, 2010).



Short-term memory (working memory) and long-term memory (semantic memory) both play crucial roles in language learning (Afraimovich et al., 2015). According to Marschark and Knoors (2012), deaf children encounter challenges in solving sequential tasks that require remembering information in a specific order. This difficulty is often attributed to what is known as sequential memory. It is suggested that this arises because deaf children fail to link information stored in short-term memory with the knowledge stored in long-term memory. In our interactive RSA system, deaf children are able to repeat the process of recognizing Arabic letters, which are subsequently simulated by a robotic arm. This serves to engage their long-term memory in memorizing these letters, while also providing practice in sequential tasks, given that the simulation follows the recognition phase.

On the other hand, deaf individuals are at a higher risk of experiencing vision impairment compared to their hearing counterparts. This is attributed to the fact that the causes of deafness can also impact the eyes (Wiley, 2012). Additionally, deaf children have a heightened sensitivity to peripheral vision, as their brains develop to allocate more attention to the visual environment. While this may seem advantageous, according to Dye et al. (2008), it can have a negative effect on the concentration of deaf children in a noisy classroom environment. To address these issues, our system incorporates a robotic arm for letter simulation, enabling deaf children to use both the tactile and visual senses.

Language is linked to individual cognition, with exclusive functions like thoughts and behaviors representing one aspect of cognitive processing. An important consideration in the learning process of deaf children is their struggle to determine whether they have acquired information, sometimes leading to overestimation of their understanding (Borgna et al., 2011; Marschark &amp; Knoors, 2012). So, it is beneficial for them to receive adequate assistance and be provided with the best practices for self-assessment. In RSA, as the deaf children enter the letter to be simulated by the robotic arm, they can verify if the result matches their expectations, thereby reinforcing self-evaluation.

The role of parents and the environment is crucial in the learning of sign language. However, communication between deaf children and hearing parents may not always be as effective as with deaf parents, and hearing parents often struggle to teach sign languagetotheir children, as highlighted by Razalli et al. (2019). Our primary objective in developing this system is to facilitate the learning of sign language for deaf children during their primary education, making it accessible not only in schools but also to parents. Considering that 80% of people with hearing disabilities reside in low and middle-income countries (WHO, 2024), we have taken into account the costeffectiveness of this system, which is significantly lower than utilizing a complete robot.

In the context of Arabic Sign Language, there have been efforts directed towards the creation and organization of Arabic sign language dictionaries, along with the incorporation of technology (Al-Fityani &amp; Padden, 2008; Balaha et al., 2023). Furthermore, a substantial portion of research and applications has been centered around ArSL recognition (Ibrahim et al., 2018; Tharwat et al., 2015; Alzohairi et al., 2018;



Kamruzzaman, 2020; Elatawy et al., 2020) and ArSL translation (Halawani, 2008; Luqman &amp; Mahmoud, 2019; El-Bendary et al., 2010). However, there are only a few works related to enhancing Arabic sign-language learning for children with hearing impairments. As an example, Mohammad et al. (2022) introduced a mobile application specifically designed to teach Arabic sign language, catering particularly to children under 12 years old. Another mobile application developed by Al-Nafjan et al. (2015), named Tawasol, aims to facilitate the acquisition of Arabic sign language. This application includes features such as a sign dictionary and fingerspelling. Compared to the aforementioned approaches, the proposed interactive RSA system integrates artificial intelligence and robotics to enhance the learning of Arabic sign language. In fact, the system can recognize ArSL letters in real time. Furthermore, it can simulate the signs using a robotic arm. This process is more engaging, as children can physically interact with the robotic arm, treating it as a toy.

## 4.1 Current limitations and future prospects

The RSA system, as it stands, is tailored to offer early support for deaf children in acquiring ArSL. However, there are certain constraints that could be refined in future endeavors, such as incorporating phonological knowledge. Phonological skills are pivotal for both hearing and deaf children in fostering proficient reading abilities (Trezek &amp; Malmgren, 2005). Furthermore, we aspire to augment the system's functionalities to encompass a wider spectrum of letters, words, and phrases. This enhancement is especially crucial given the typically less extensive vocabularies and conceptual knowledge observed in deaf children compared to their hearing peers (Marschark &amp; Knoors, 2012).

## 5 Conclusion

Language acquisition poses unique challenges for children, especially those who are deaf or hard of hearing. In this study, we introduce an interactive system RSA designed to recognize and simulate letters in Arabic sign language. The aim of this system is to assist deaf children in acquiring sign language during their primary education. Specifically, RSA addresses prevalent issues in learning disabilities, including memory recall, visual perception difficulties, and executive functioning.

The system comprises two modules: one for recognition and another for simulation. In the recognition module, we employed convolutional neural networks, specifically MobileNet,todetectthesignsassociated with Arabic letters. This enables deaf children to correlate the signs with the letters. We have evaluated the performance of this module using the RGB Arabic Alphabets Sign Language Dataset, achieving an accuracy of 98.56%, precision of 98.54%, recall of 98.46%, and an F1 score of 98.47%.

In the simulation module, there is a robotic arm capable of replicating the letters of Arabic sign language. This arm's movements are controlled by servo motors (Metal Gears RG996R), and we implemented thread-based programming to achieve simultaneous movement of different fingers. The RSA can be adapted to learn other sign languages by adjusting the two modules.



With robust technological support and moral encouragement, deaf children can excel in their academics and personal lives.

## Paper Source: Interactive, Visual-Learning based Tool for Hearing Impaired Children to Improve Language and Cognitive Skills

## Interactive, Visual-Learning based Tool for Hearing Impaired Children to Improve Language and Cognitive Skills

Saluka Udbhasa Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka udbhasa@gmail.com Parami Lelkada Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka lelkadaparami@gmail.com

Samitha Vidhanaarachchi Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka samithapva@gmail.com Modeesha Priyanka Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka modeesha.k@gmail.com Jagath Wickramarathne Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka jagath.w@sliit.lk

Abstract -Hearing impairment is a common condition that affects  millions  of  people  worldwide, with  approximately  1  in 1000 newborns experiencing some degree of hearing loss. This condition  can  significantly  impact  a  person's  quality  of  life, causing  communication  difficulties  and  social  isolation.  Early childhood hearing impairment can present significant challenges to a child's cognitive development, making it difficult for them to learn in a traditional educational setting. Consequently, there is an urge for effective learning tools that can  assist  hearing-impaired  children  in  learning  their  first language.  This  paper  introduces  visual-based  and  interactive learning  tools  as  a  promising  approach  to  enhancing  the learning experience and engagement of hearing-impaired children.  The  proposed  system  utilizes  machine  learning  to assess a child's initial status and subsequently generates adaptive content while continuously monitoring progress. Moreover, the system incorporates an object exploration feature that enables children to learn from their surroundings. Additionally, it employs natural language learning processes to present contextually similar content, supported by audio and lip movement analysis features that guide correct pronunciation. In response  to  the  ML  models  utilized,  object  detection  was accomplished  through  YOLO5,  while  lip  movements  were analyzed  using  LipNet.  Regression  models  were  deployed  for assessing a child's initial status and subsequent progress. The data  collection  process  involved  comprehensive  sources  that covered a wide array of visual, auditory, and linguistic elements, with  the  dataset  being  rigorously  tested  and  verified.  Testing implementations were conducted in various real-world settings, encompassing diverse environmental factors and learning conditions.  The  YOLO  model  demonstrated  an  accuracy  of 90.3%,  LipNet  achieved  92.2%  accuracy  in  lip  movement analysis,  and  the  multivariate  regression  models  showed  a prediction accuracy of 92.8% in evaluating child progress.

Keywords-Hearing impaired children, Learning tool, Language  development,  Cognitive  development.  NPL,  Object detection, Lip movement analysis, Regression models

## I. INTRODUCTION

Hearing impairment is one of the most common conditions that  affect  millions  of  people  worldwide.  According  to  the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 1 in 1,000 newborns have hearing loss ranging from mild to profound [1][2]. This condition significantly impacts a person's quality Esala Senarathna Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka esalasenarathne98@gmail. com Janaka L. Wijekoon Military Technological College, Muscat, Oman janaka.wijekoon@gmail.com of life because it causes communication difficulties, potentially leading to social isolation [3]. Hearing impairment refers  to  a  range  of  hearing  loss,  varying  from  mild  to profound.  This condition significantly impacts a child's auditory  abilities,  posing  challenges  for  their  learning  in traditional educational settings.

The learning journey of a child begins from the moment they are born. Cognitive development during early childhood lays the foundation for future academic success and lifelong learning [4]. The early acquisition of a first language plays a crucial  role  in  a  child's  overall  development.  Research  has shown that children should ideally learn their first language by the age of five [5]. Linguistic abilities have a profound impact on  memory  development,  attention,  and  problem-solving skills, all of which are directly linked to academic success [5]. In  the  case  of  hearing-impaired  children,  delayed  language development  can  lead  to  lower  academic  achievement  and social isolation [3].

With the significant advancement in medical technology of  the  past  decades,  there  are  many  advanced  treatment options  available  for  hearing-impaired  people  [25].  Even though  hearing-impaired  children  are  fortunate  to  get  the ability to hear with these advanced treatments, the 'Poverty of the  stimulus  argument'  by  Noam  Chomsky  explains  the condition where a lack of auditory stimulation makes mastering  a  language  difficult  for  a  hearing-impaired  child [24]. However, as incurred by the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN-SDG), the use of ICT can fill this gap effectively [23]. To this end, this paper presents a visualbased and interactive learning tool as an effective method for enhancing the learning experience and engagement of hearing-impaired children [23][25]. Compared to traditional learning tools, visual learning tools can be used for providing a more  dynamic  and  interactive  learning experience  to hearing-impaired children [26].

In  contrast,  this  study  uses  YOLO5  for  object  detection features, word embedding, and k-means clustering for similar word generation, LipNet for video-based lip detection, and the random Forest algorithm for level determination and progress evaluation.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Language  development  is  critical  to  a  child's  cognitive growth and communication [18]. However, hearing-impaired children struggle for learning language due to their difficulty in learning sounds and gestures, which can impact their ability to express themselves, understand others, and develop cognitive abilities like memory, reasoning, and visualization [19][20]. Hearing-impaired children's cognitive development can be adversely affected in areas like language and audible memory [23]. Therefore, alternative methods and techniques are necessary to improve their linguistic skills [11]. Language acquisition  during  the  first  4.5  years,  supported  by  brain plasticity, is crucial [12] and limited vocabulary exposure also impacts these children's education [13].

Language development comprises five stages as presented in [21] ranging from pre-production to advanced fluency, but hearing-impaired children may need to learn new words and improve their vocabulary to fully develop cognitive abilities. To enhance the cognitive abilities of hearing-impaired children, innovative methods like gamified language learning can be employed by allowing them to learn at their own pace, providing engaging content, and a customized learning experience  [22][23][7].  Online  learning  tools  which  apply gamification techniques have proven effective in improving teaching methods, suggesting suitable materials, and enhancing learners' growth [8][9]. Gamification encouraged specific behaviors, engaged hearing-impaired children effectively,  and  helped  them  to  track  their  progress.  Such studies also articulate that these tools are particularly beneficial  for  hearing-impaired  children  who  might  face challenges  in  accessing  audiology  centers.  With  the  rise  of online  education,  these  tools  offer  a  convenient  and  costeffective  solution  [21].  Consequently,  A  web-based  game application  in  Portugal  used  gesture  detection  to  teach  sign language [15], and an application in India focused on teaching Indian Sign Language (ISL) [16].

A study by the Community Child Health, Royal Children's Hospital, Australia, found a link between the age of detection of  hearing  impairment  and  education  outcomes  [14].  The study involved 132 students aged 7-8 years who underwent a three-hour assessment to measure educational outcomes under the  supervision  of  a  speech  pathologist  and  a  psychologist. The authors found that early detection of hearing impairment is crucial for better linguistic abilities. Additionally, the study done in [12] shows brain plasticity plays a significant role in rapid  language  acquisition [12],  whereas [13]  confirms  that hearing-impaired children have limited vocabulary exposure, affecting their education.

Referring  to  the  same  papers[12][13],  it  is  evident  that special education and early intervention can assist in developing language skills and cognitive abilities in hearingimpaired children. A  student-centric learning system is suggested that provides an interactive environment for children to learn from their surroundings. Furthermore, some computer games have been used to aid the development of sign language skills. In the identified applications, computer games have been strategically utilized to enhance children's attention  span  and  stimulate  their  cognitive  development. Similarly, this paper presents a study based on the Sri Lankan education  system  to  support  and  improve  the cognitive  and speech abilities of hearing-impaired children based on a real case study.

## III. METHODOLOGY

This  study  divides  into  four  sub-components  as  Object exploration, Similar Word Generation, Lip Movement Analysis,  and  Linguistic  Level  Determination.  High-level relationships between the components are illustrated in Fig. 1.

In  the  process  of  dataset  collection  for  the  system,  a combination of public datasets and locally sourced datasets from various institutes are used. Incorporating both types of datasets contribute to a more comprehensive and diverse data pool, which is instrumental in enhancing the system's effectiveness and adaptability. This approach also facilitates a robust  foundation  for  the  system's  processes,  enabling  it  to perform optimally across different tasks and settings.

Object detection uses a combination of the COCO dataset and 100 custom images from domestic environments to train the One-shot learning model and detections. In contextually similar  word generation, text data was extracted from over 300  children's  storybooks  and  40  children's  encyclopedias. This results in a corpus of 83 million tokens. The lip reading and  speech  therapy,  relied  on  the  GRID  corpus  dataset, comprising  audio  and  visual  recordings  of  34  speakers producing  1,000  sentences  each,  resulting  in  a  dataset  of 34,000  sentences  with  a  duration  of  28  hours.  The  level determination  utilizes  800  images  and  1000  audio  data collected from Twinkle Stars Pre School Rathnapura. These diverse data collection approaches provided a robust foundation for the research and its respective components.

## A. Object Exploration

Object exploration, aimed at teaching the child using their surrounding environment, is the primary teaching mode for a hearing-impaired  child.  The  process  comprises  two  main stages, identifying the object, followed by understanding its key features. It was achieved using several machine learning models to understand the surroundings. Initially, You Only Look  Once  (YOLO)  v3,  YOLOv4,  and  MobileNet  were evaluated for object detection through a video feed. Similar to research [31], the YOLO models were trained. The number of detections and accuracy of bounding boxes varied among the tested models. YOLOv5 outperformed the others in terms of  accuracy,  speed  of  detection  (766ms),  and  its  ability  to detect  small-sized  objects.  These  models  were  specifically trained for indoor, and domestic environments. Childfriendly class labels were used.

The  output frames of the detection model  have a complicated image of multiple detections and need to be reprocessed, to avoid multiple overlapping and repetition. For the child's better understandability, the number of bounding boxes needs to be reduced, hence the number of same-class objects, IOU (Intersection Over Union), and the total number of objects within a frame are considered input parameters for classification.  For  the  base  threshold,  IOU  0.6  is  used  to eliminate the overlapping bounding boxes.

Adding new labels to the pre-trained model was a major requirement of the system. This process was limited by the requirement of high-volume data and extensive training time. A Siamese network-based one-shot classification [27] is used to add new labels to the model. It was used to fulfill the need of training a classification model with less data. The Siamese model creates  a  similarity  score  between  0  and  1  for  each image and the comparison of the base images with the given images  determines  the  class  of  the  image.  The  model  was trained for certain threshold values and the best results were obtained with 38951745 trainable parameters and the input tensor  was  set  to  105px  ×  105px.  The  Siamese  model performs best in uniform backgrounds and results in overfitting on complex backgrounds.

Training models will be incorporated into an interactive, game-based environment to enhance the learning experience. The mobile device's camera will capture the environment in real time, with the YOLO object detection model identifying objects. The instance segmentation model will then segment these identified objects, amplifying the child's user experience.  The  game  displays  the  name  of  the  detected object in a scrambled form, accompanied by its pronunciation of it. The child's reaction time and spelling accuracy will be collected  while  the  child  is  interacting  with  the  gamified environment in the app.

## B. Contextually Similar Word Generation

This  study  aims  to  generate  contextually  similar  words using  the  gained  vocabulary  with  object  exploration.  Word generation utilizes explored words from object exploration as input and produces contextually similar words. Fig. 2 depicts the process of contextually similar word generation.

Given  the  nature  of  the  target  audience,  employing  a customized dataset for model training is essential to ensure a child-friendly language model. A language model, supporting the  word  generation  sub-process,  is  developed  using  the training corpus. Words in the corpus undergo encoding into fixed-length  vectors  through  a  positional  encoding  process, which conveys information about the tokens' order within a sequence. Positional encoding enables distinguishing between different token permutations. Dense, low-dimensional vector representations  are  resulted  from  this  process,  capturing semantic relationships between words.

Clustering  the  resulting  embeddings  into  'n'  groups  is accomplished  using  the  k-means  clustering  technique.  The goal  of  word  embedding  clustering  is  to  identify  groups  of similar words based on their contextual meanings. Adapting the  k-means  clustering  algorithm  involves  calculating  the distance  between  word  embeddings  as  a  similarity  metric. This approach assigns a word to a cluster where the sum of squared  distances  between  each  word  embedding,  and  its assigned cluster centroid is minimized.

Figure 2. The flow of similar word generation

The  acquired  vocabulary  serves  as  input  for  the  wordgeneration process. It first extracts the word embedding of the input word and subsequently determines the context class by measuring its distance against a pre-defined set of centroids. The  context  class  containing  the  centroid  with  the  least distance to the input word is considered the context class of the  input  word.  To  compute  the  distance,  the  Euclidean distance is used, which can be represented as follows.



The most contextually similar word is extracted from the input  word's  context  class  by  computing  the  Euclidean distance against words in the same context class. In addition to the similarity for a given word, word complexity from the Level  Determination  component  is  also  considered.  The chosen contextually similar word is displayed in a gamified environment as the final step of the Contextual Similar Word Generation.

## C. Speech therapy using voice and lip-reading-based feedback mechanism

The  speech  therapy  component  involves  a  feedback mechanism that captures the child's pronunciation using audio and  video.  A  composite  error  rate  is  calculated  for  the pronunciation correctness of the displayed word.

## 1) Speech detection using audio

A deep learning architecture called 'Deep Speech'[29] is used for on-device word classification using audio input. First, the raw audio signal is pre-processed to extract the spectrogram  features,  which  are  then  fed  into  the  model similar  to  the  literature  [30].  The  model  then  uses  multiple layers  of  LSTM  units  to  learn  representations  of  the  input features,  with  each  layer  adding  additional  complexity  and abstraction.

To further improve the accuracy of the model, Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) loss is used[29].  The  loss  function  of  this  algorithm  allows  it  to handle variable-length inputs and outputs, which is crucial for accurate speech transcribing.

The RNN model exhibits a simpler structure compared to similar  models  in  the  literature  [29].  This  simplicity  stems from limiting the design to a single recurrent layer, which is challenging  to  parallelize,  and  excluding  the  use  of  LongShort-Term-Memory (LSTM) circuits. Employing a homogeneous model optimizes the computation of recurrent activations for maximum efficiency. This optimization involves executing only a few highly optimized BLAS(Basic Linear  Algebra  Subprograms)  operations  on  the  GPU  and applying  a  single  point-wise  nonlinearity  to  compute  the ReLU outputs.

## 2) Video-based lip-reading

Lip-reading is the main mode of speech validation when audio noise is present. The input from the camera captures the facial  landmarks  and  the  lip  movements.  Fig.  3  depicts  the image-processing pipeline.

BlazeFace  model[28]  employs  an  enhanced  network architecture  derived  from  MobileNet.  The  original  authors observe  that  the  computation  time  for  a  3 × 3  depth-wise convolution  of  a  56 × 56 × 128  tensor  is  only  0.07ms  on  the iPhone X CPU, while the subsequent 1 × 1 convolution from 128 to 128 channels takes 4.3 times longer at 0.3ms. Based on this, 3 × 3 depth-wise convolution is used, which reduces the model's depth and improves processing speed.

Figure 3. Image processing pipeline

For  training  the  lip  movements  for  pronunciation,  the GRID  corpus  dataset  [17],  which  includes  both  audio  and video recordings of 34 speakers is used.

The proposed model is based on a 3D convolutional neural network that takes in video frames as input and outputs text at the  sentence  level.  The  fine-tuned  model  achieves  good results(89.2 %) in lip-reading accuracy.

The audio component's score and the LipNet's score are individually calculated and later aggregated using a weighted average. The results were then forwarded to level determination and other modules for their use.



## D. Initial Status Determination and Progress Monitoring

Consists of two sub-components, which aim to determine the initial status of the user and monitor their progress. The initial status of the user is determined using a dynamic quiz river.  The  quiz  river  illustrated  in  Fig.  4  contains  simple words that are divided into five levels. The accuracy of the response, response time, and the calculated difficulty score are inserted into the Random Forest algorithm to determine the user's initial status.

The  progress  monitoring  process  includes  a  feedback mechanism that motivates users to interact with the application.  Learning  materials  were  obtained  from  the CEHIC (Centre for Education of Hearing-Impaired Children) The  level of difficulty is determined  by  the  semantic difficulty and number of letters. Furthermore, this evaluates the  knowledge  of  basic  words  such  as  three-letter  words, four-letter words, five-letter words, and complex words that has  more  than  five  letters  or  a  combination  of  two  words. Each question is displayed along with a pronouncing voice clip of the word playing in the background.

The  component  uses  a  model  implemented  with  the regression algorithm to determine the level of the user based on  the  response  accuracy,  response  time,  and  final  quiz difficulty.  The  personalized  data  of  the  user  does  not  have linear  relationships  with  each  other,  so  this  method  can  be used to evaluate the progress level of the user.

The gamified solution has a quiz that has fifteen questions in  total  on  five  different  levels.  Three  questions  will  be randomly selected from each level for the quiz and those will be displayed. The child must select the accurate image and then drag and drop that into the basket. Fifteen seconds  are  given  to  answer  one  question.  The  audio  clip pronouncing  the  word  can  be  played  any  number  of  times within those fifteen seconds. If the child answers the question incorrectly, they can still try again until the fifteen seconds are over. The next question will be displayed as soon as the timer  reaches  zero.  There  is  an  option  available  to  skip  a question and navigate to the next question.

Figure 4. UI of Quiz River



The  dataset  used  for  the  training  of  the  random  forest algorithm consisted of the accuracy of answers given by the child for each question in the quiz. To acquire the difficulty of the question different points were given for each level of question. The points allocated to each question are equal to the difficulty level of that question. Those points are allocated if the answer was right and zero is allocated if the answer is incorrect.

The variables which are impacting heavily on the level of the  child  are  taken  according  to  this  and  then  data  is preprocessed and split as train and test data. In the developed solution 20% of data are taken for testing. Then the model is trained along with the hyperparameters which are n\_estimator, max depth, and min\_samples\_leaf. N\_estimator specifies  the  number  of  trees,  max\_depth  specifies  the number  of  splits  that  each  tree  is  allowed  to  make  and min\_samples\_leaf specifies the minimal number of samples required at the leaf. After the training of data, the results that give maximum accuracy for detecting the level of the user are taken and passed to get the maximum accuracy level of the child.

Parameter  tuning  in  the  random  forest  algorithm  was cruicial in optimizing the performance and accuracy of the predictions.  The  key  hyperparameters  in  random  forest algorithm are number of estimators (n\_estimator), maximum depth(max\_depth) and minimum samples per leaf (min\_leaf). Those parameters were tuned in the model under three ranges and hyperparameter values were tuned as 20, 20 and 1 for n\_estimator, max\_depth and min\_samples\_leaf respectively to finalize a model with highest accuracy.

## V RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The  model  for  Object  Exploration  primarily utilizes YOLO  v5  architecture  trained  with  the  publicly  available COCO dataset and 100 captured images from the domestic environment. 766ms of on-device inference time is achieved with model compression and fine-tuning. During optimizations, an ideal input size of 1280 × 1280 was identified.  Siamese network-based one-shot classification is used for updating pre-trained model weights to classify new labels. It demonstrated accuracies of over 89% under different environments/backgrounds. The limitations of this technique were  complex  backgrounds make  the  model  overfit  for  the images.  Using  the  trial-and-error  method,  parameters  were adjusted, and the best results were obtained with 38951745 trainable parameters and the input tensor was set to 105px × 105px.

The similar word generation mechanism  was developed that  generates  words  based  on  the  acquired  words  from  an object detection process. Word embeddings facilitate capturing of the contextual and semantic properties of words. These embeddings offer a lower-dimensional semantic space for high-dimensional word vectors, enabling accurate calculation  of  semantic  distances  between  words.  K-means clustering partitions this semantic space into distinct clusters based  on  the  semantic  relatedness  of  words.  This  process paves the way for computing the closest word to a given word based  on  the  distance  between  the  word  embedding  of  the given word and the pre-classified word classes using k-means.

Despite the promise, potential limitations of the approach include the assumptions made by k-means clustering and the possible inadequacy of word embeddings in handling words with  multiple  meanings  or  varied  contextual  usage.  Future exploration could delve into advanced clustering techniques and different word  embedding types to mitigate these limitations.  The  research  presents  a  significant  stride  in linking image processing and natural language processing.

The initial Status Determination component uses a model based on the random forest algorithm which is trained using a dynamic  dataset  collected  with  the  usage  of  Quiz  River. Datapoints  include  18  different  features  and  thousands  of records. The random forest algorithm tunes the most important hyperparameters which are n\_estimator, max\_depth, and min\_sample\_leaf and comes up with a level with 91.8% of accuracy. The usability of model and the has been validated at CEHIC to check whether the model predicts the  accurate  level  for  the  student  based  on  the  child's performance  at  the  quiz  river.  During  the  validation,  a correlation  matrix  is  used  to  analyze  the  correlation  of variables as illustrated in Fig. 5.

The  proposed  system  for  personalized  speech  therapy employs  multiple  models,  'Deep  Search'  for  audio-based phoneme  classification  which  was  optimized  for  on-device classifications. The accuracy of the model was limited by the variable length inputs, later it was improved to an accuracy of 93.4%  on  a  custom-made  test  dataset,  using  the  CTC  loss function.

For  the  lip-analyzing  vision  pipeline,  Blzaeface  model with  pre-trained  weights  is  used  for  near-real-time  face detection.  During  the  testing  on  a  mobile  GPU,  &lt;1ms detection time is achieved using 3 × 3 depth-wise convolution. The cropped frame is then fed to lip analyzer network which uses the 'LipNet' architecture. The fine-tuned model achieves an accuracy of 89.2% for inferencing the pronunciation using the  spatial  movement  of  lips.  It  was  observed  that  better performance can be achieved with sentence-level prediction.

The system's adaptability caters to diverse user needs and learning styles, with the gamified approach potentially enhancing learning outcomes. However, acknowledging limitations,  future  research  should  focus  on  validating  the system's effectiveness, incorporating user feedback, and exploring emerging technologies, such as augmented reality and haptic feedback. In conclusion, the proposed system presents a promising alternative to traditional speech therapy methods, contributing to a personalized and engaging learning experience. Further validation and user feedback integration could significantly impact speech therapy and improve hearing-impaired children's lives.

Figure 5. Coefficient Correlation Matrix



## VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Using a mobile app with gamified tasks and explorative learning  this  paper  proposes  a  method  that  can  improve language and cognitive abilities of a hearing-impaired child. It was observed that all the models perform with performance with better than 84% accuracy. The application should be used in  the  field  for  many  years  to  gather  its  real  impact  on  the students.  The  above  research  work  is  done  based  on  the English  language  and  further  extension  can  be  taken  to  do enhanced  visual  learning  in  other  languages.  Currently,  the models  are  compatible  with  mobile  versions  and  further enhancement related to increasing the compatibility of mobile phones can be done. The learning process is currently done with  the  supervision  of  a  teacher  on  premises  but  further improvements can be made to accommodate remote learning.

## LLM-Powered AI Tutors with Personas for d/Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Online Learners

HAOCONG CHENG, School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA SI CHEN, University of Notre Dame, USA and School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA CHRISTOPHER PERDRIAU, Computer Science, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA SHRIYA MOKKAPATI, School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA YUN HUANG, School of Information Sciences, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA

Intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) using artificial intelligence (AI) technology have shown promise in supporting learners with diverse abilities. Large language models (LLMs) provide new opportunities to incorporate personas to AI-based tutors and support dynamic interactive dialogue. This paper explores how DHH learners interact with LLM-powered AI tutors with different experiences in DHH education as personas to identify their accessibility preferences. A user study with 16 DHH participants showed that they asked DHH-related questions based on background information and evaluated the AI tutors' cultural knowledge of the DHH communities in their responses. Participants suggested providing more transparency in each AI tutor's position within the DHH community. Participants also pointed out the lack of support in the multimodality of sign language in current LLMs. We discuss design implications to support the diverse needs in interaction between DHH users and the LLMs, such as offering supports in tuning language styles of LLMs.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

In the United States, about two per 1,000 children have some level of hearing loss in one or both ears [26], and one out of 8 people (13%) aged 12 or above has hearing loss in both ears [44]. As one of the diverse ability populations, there are educational technologies designed to support d/Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) learners to address their accessibility
