An additional barrier to the widespread adoption of SL is the alphabetical disparity that exists from one country to another (Sutton-Spence and Woll 2004; Duarte et al. 2021).

In the realm of sign language recognition, extensive research has been conducted for various sign languages, including American English Sign Language (ESL) (Naglot and Kulkarni 2016; Rahman et al. 2019; Bird et al. 2020) Chinese Sign Language (CLS) (Jiang et al. 2020a, b), French Sign Language (FLS) (Fleurion et al. 2021; Belissen et al. 2020) among others. Pertaining specifically to the recognition of Arabic sign language (ArSL), investigations into ALS have been underway since 2005 (Mohandes and Deriche 2005).

Various techniques and algorithms have been designed to identify and recognize SLA using private databases (Mohandes and Deriche 2005; El-Bendary et al. 2010; Almasre and Al-Nuaim 2016). It is worth noting that despite these efforts, some studies in this field report recognition rates that do not exceed 70%. These results highlight the ongoing challenges in accurately recognizing SLA. In light of these limitations, researchers have increasingly turned to the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques (Alsaadi et al. 2022; Mustafa 2021) to enhance recognition capabilities.

The key contribution of our work is to accomplish a comprehensive evaluation of 12 pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures on the publicly available ArASL2018 dataset for Arabic alphabet sign recognition. This is an important contribution as previous studies have mainly relied on private datasets, limiting the generalizability of the research. The specific objectives of this study are:

- (a) Evaluate the performance of 12 pre-trained CNN models (including EfficientNet B7) on the 32-class ArASL2018 dataset, which contains the 28 standard Arabic alphabet signs as well as 4 additional signs (Latif et al. 2019).
- (b) Identify the best-performing pre-trained model for recognizing Arabic alphabet signs, with the goal of integrating it into a real-time application to assist users in learning the Arabic alphabet through sign language.

Our document is organized into distinct sections. In Sect. 1, we provide an overview of the topic and outline our objectives. Section 2 offers a comprehensive summary of existing work on Arabic alphabet sign recognition, exploring various proposals. The details of our methodology, including elements such as the dataset used and pretrained convolutional neural network models, are elucidated in Sect. 3. Section 4 is dedicated to presenting the results of our experiment, wherein we scrutinize performance metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and outline the steps to achieve the real-time application of Arabic sign recognition. Section 5 highlights the limitations of real-time sign identification and the so far proposed solutions. Finally, Sect. 6 serves as the conclusion to our article, summarizing the main findings and suggesting avenues for future research.

## 2 Related works

This section provides a concise overview of the key advancements in Arabic alphabet sign recognition. It will discuss the databases utilized and explore the various approaches employed in the research. Our goal is to offer a comprehensive review of the field, spotlighting significant methodologies and outcomes achieved during the investigations.

Several strategies have been proposed in the existing literature to address this problem. The initial research in this area began in 2005 (Mohandes and Deriche 2005), where the researchers proposed an approach to recognize the alphabets of Arabic Sign Language (ArSL), achieving a recognition rate of 63.5%. The methodology employed in this technique is based on an in-depth examination of various descriptors. The research results highlight the superiority of the Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) descriptor over others.

A system for the automatic translation of gestures into Arabic Sign Language alphabets (ArSL) was presented by El-Bendary et al. (2010). ArSL recognizes gestures using images of bare hands. The system includes five phases: preprocessing, best image detection, category detection, feature extraction, and classification. The extracted features are translation, scale, and rotation invariant. An accuracy of 91.3% using a minimum distance classifier was achieved, and 83.7% using a multi-layer perceptron.

Almasre and Al-Nuaim (2016) introduced a real-time letter recognition model for Arabic Sign Language (ArSL) using Microsoft's Kinect and Leap Motion Controller (LMC). The study aims to facilitate communication for Arabic hearing-impaired individuals by developing a system that recognizes ArSL letters in real-time. Participants were asked to gesture with the Arabic alphabet, and the model employs supervised machine learning to predict hand poses and dynamically convert these gestures into corresponding letters of the alphabet.

In 2019 (Deriche et al. 2019), an approach to recognize Arabic Sign Language was proposed. It began with acquisition for data collection, followed by a feature extraction step, including translation probability, finger length, and average tip position left. Deriche et al. classified these features using the Gauss Muscatine GMM model and Simple Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). They achieved an accuracy of 92%.

In 2020, two works were published in this field. The first (Elatawy et al. 2020) aims to develop a system for recognizing the alphabet of Arabic sign language using a combination of the neutrosophic technique and the fuzzy average method. The system achieves a 91% accuracy rate in classifying the Arabic Sign Language alphabet. The second (Mustafa 2021), conducted by Mustafa et al., involves a study examining different categorization techniques used by sign language recognition systems. Many classifiers have been implemented in this context, including convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), multilayer perceptron (MLP), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), Hidden Markov Models (HMM), artificial neural networks (ANN), support vector machines (SVM), and k-nearest neighbors (KNN).

Rawf et al. (2022) investigate Arabic, Persian, and Kurdish sign languages. In this study, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transfer learning methods are employed to categorize sign languages written in the Arabic alphabet. The goal is to establish a common standard for alphabetic sign language in these languages (Rawf et al. 2022). Additionally, a real-time Arabic Sign Language alphabet (ArSL) recognition model was presented by the authors of paper (Alsaadi et al. 2022), utilizing the AlexNet architecture. The results demonstrate that the AlexNet architecture achieved an accuracy rate of 94.81%.

Following a comprehensive analysis of the current state of research on Arabic alphabet sign recognition, it is noteworthy that a significant number of studies have primarily focused on the utilization of private databases (Mohandes and Deriche 2005; El-Bendary et al. 2010; Deriche et al. 2019). Notably, only one researcher (Alsaadi et al. 2022) has employed a complex database named ArASL2018 (Latif et al. 2019) created in 2018, encompassing 32 classes of Arabic alphabet signs.

Table 1 summarizes the related work, offering a concise overview and comparison of different approaches to Arabic alphabet sign recognition. In each row, the dataset used and the classifier employed by a different reference are detailed. The last row corresponds to our approach.

Table 1 Comparison of Arabic alphabet sign recognition approaches

Our study makes an important contribution to the field of Arabic alphabet sign recognition by providing a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of 12 state-of-the-art pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures on the publicly available ArASL2018 dataset. This is a significant advancement over previous research, which has primarily relied on private or limited datasets (Mohandes and Deriche 2005; El-Bendary et al. 2010; Almasre and Al-Nuaim 2016; Deriche et al. 2019; Elatawy et al. 2020). The use of the ArASL2018 dataset, which includes 32 classes of Arabic alphabet signs, allows for a more thorough and generalizable assessment of model performance compared to studies confined to smaller private datasets.

Moreover, the systematic comparison of 12 CNN models, including the powerful EfficientNet B7 architecture, represents a more extensive evaluation than prior works that have typically focused on a narrower set of classifiers (Mustafa 2021; Rawf et al. 2022). This breadth of models assessed provides a more robust understanding of the relative merits and limitations of different deep learning approaches for Arabic alphabet sign recognition.

Importantly, the goal of identifying the best-performing pre-trained model for integration into a real-time sign language learning application is a crucial step towards developing practical, user-friendly systems to assist Arabic-speaking deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals.

## 3 Our methodology

This section presents an in-depth analysis of the operational framework of neural networks VGG16 and VGG19, MobileNet V1 and V2, and EfficientNet from B0 to B7, in the context of Arabic alphabet sign classification. It covers distinct categories from the ArASL2018 image data. The objective is to select the optimal architecture that demonstrates efficient performance in this domain. To this end, variations in image size have been applied according to the architectures considered. The final objective is the use of the optimal model for the implementation of a real-time mobile application, thus facilitating the learning of Arabic alphabet signs and communication with deaf people.

## 3.1 Arabic alphabets sign language dataset

The Arabic alphabet sign language (ArASL2018) dataset (Latif et al. 2019) was created at Prince Mohammed Bin Fahd University in Saudi Arabia. It comprises 54,049 images capturing hand movements corresponding to the Arabic alphabet. The dataset is categorized into 32 classes as shown in Fig. 1, with varying numbers of photos per class. This resource is readily available for deep learning and machine learning research. The images have a pixel resolution of 64 9 64 and are in grayscale, with pixel values ranging from 0 to 255.

## 3.2 Pre-trained model

A pre-trained convolutional neural network is a model that has undergone training on an extensive dataset to recognize and comprehend a diverse set of visual patterns and features (Qiu et al. 2020; Han et al. 2021). The advantage of utilizing pre-trained CNNs lies in their capacity to capture general visual knowledge, which can be transferred to new tasks even when the available data is limited (Zhuang et al. 2020). This proves particularly advantageous for the classification of images containing Arabic alphabet signs (Kamruzzaman 2020; Chen et al. 2020).

In our study, we evaluated various pre-trained CNN architectures, including VGG, MobileNet, and EfficientNet. These models were initially trained on large-scale image datasets such as ImageNet (Barbu et al. 2019), enabling them to comprehend a broad spectrum of objects and scenes.

## 3.2.1 VGG16 and 19

VGG16 and VGG19 are convolutional neural networks (CNNs) characterized by their architecture, which is based on repeated blocks of 3 9 3 convolutional layers followed by 2 9 2 max-pooling layers. The architecture includes l such blocks, and the final output is obtained through fully connected layers. The softmax function is applied to produce class probabilities (Simonyan and Zisserman 2014; Qassim et al. 2018; Theckedath and Sedamkar 2020).

The VGG16 model consists of 16 weight layers (Guan et al. 2019) (13 convolutional and 3 fully connected), as in Fig. 2, while VGG19 extends this to 19 layers, enhancing the representational capacity at the cost of increased computational complexity (Simonyan and Zisserman 2014; Lincy and Gayathri 2020).

## 3.2.2 MobileNet V1 and V2

MobileNet V1 is a convolutional neural network architecture designed for mobile and edge devices. It employs depthwise separable convolutions to reduce computational complexity while maintaining expressive power. ## 3.2.3 EfficientNet B (0 to 7)

EfficientNet EfficientNet is a family of convolutional neural network architectures that aim to achieve better accuracy and efficiency by scaling the model's depth, width, and resolution. Let w l i ; j represent the weight parameters of the i   th fi lter at the j   th layer l (Tan and Le 2019).

The architecture introduces a compound scaling method that uniformly scales the network width, depth, and resolution. The depth scaling is denoted by a , width scaling by b , and resolution scaling by c (Tan and Le 2019; Marques et al. 2020; Kallipolitis et al. 2021).

Comparison between B0 to B7 EfficientNet comes in different scales from B0 to B7, each representing a different trade-off between model size and accuracy (Kallipolitis et al. 2021). As the scale increases from B0 to B7, the depth, width, and resolution of the network increase accordingly (Tan and Le 2019; Marques et al. 2020; Kallipolitis et al. 2021; Hoang and Jo 2021; Ali et al. 2022).

- (a) B0 has the smallest model size and computational complexity (Mulim et al. 2021) as shown in Fig. 4.
- (b) B7 has the largest model size and computational complexity, providing higher accuracy but requiring more resources (Ali et al. 2022).





The choice between B0 to B7 depends on the specific requirements of the application, considering factors such as available resources and desired model performance (Cenggoro 2020; Koonce and Koonce 2021).

## 3.3 Metrics

To determine the optimal architecture for classifying Arabic alphabet signs, we relied on metrics commonly employed by prior researchers in this field (Alsaadi et al. 2022; Rawf et al. 2022) These metrics include test accuracy as represent in Eq. 10, Macro Avg Precision as shown in Eq. 11, Macro Avg Recall as in Equation, and Macro Avg F1-score, in Eq. 12. Additionally, we computed Weighted Avg Precision, Weighted Avg Recall, and Weighted Avg F1-score, as in Eqs. 13, 14, 15, respectively, to ensure a comprehensive assessment of performance (Chicco et al. 2021; Chicco and Jurman 2020; Yi et al. 2021; Flach and Kull. 2015; Chen et al. 2018; Han and Jeong 2020). ## 4 Results

This section provides a detailed explanation of the operational framework of the pre-processing method employed to augment the number of images per class and elaborates on the classification of Arabic alphabet signs. It encompasses distinct classes from the (ArASL2018) image database, utilizing twelve pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). This approach allows for the selection of the most effective architecture for our specific problem, thereby facilitating the choice of the most performant model for the creation of a more robust real-time application.

## 4.1 Pre-processing

The ArASL2018 dataset used in this study had varying numbers of images for each of the 32 Arabic alphabet classes. This imbalance in the dataset could negatively impact the learning process of the classification models. To address this issue, we implemented data augmentation techniques (Khalifa et al. 2022; Rhee et al. 2008; Ng et al. 2004) to equalize the number of training images per class.

Specifically, we divided the dataset into 80% for training, 10% for validation, and 10% for testing. We then applied the following data augmentation techniques to the training set:

- Horizontal flip: Flipping the images horizontally to create new samples.
- Rotation: Rotating the images by up to 20 degrees in either direction.
- Horizontal shift: Shifting the images horizontally by up to 20% of the image width.
- Vertical shift: Shifting the images vertically by up to 20% of the image height.
- Zoom: Zooming in on the images by up to 20%.

These augmentation techniques, as shown in Fig. 5, helped to create additional training samples and homogenize the distribution of images across the 32 alphabet classes, as illustrated in Table 2. By balancing the number of images per class, we aimed to minimize the impact of the initial data imbalance on the learning process of the classification models.

In total, 11,161 images have been generated as augmented images. Figure 6 shows some examples of the Arabic alphabet signs after augmentation.

## 4.2 Classification results

After pre-processing and balancing the number of images per class, the training set now contains 1700 images for each of the 32 Arabic alphabet classes. We then evaluated the performance of twelve pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures on this dataset, as shown in Fig. 7, to identify the most effective model for Arabic alphabet sign classification.

where x represents the input tensor subjected to Batch Normalization. The momentum is set to 0.99, and the epsilon value is 0.001, which are common settings used to stabilize the Batch Normalization process.

Table 4 presents a comprehensive comparison of the twelve pre-trained models, highlighting their performance on the ArASL2018 dataset. Key metrics such as training accuracy, validation accuracy, best performance epoch, and execution time are evaluated. The results demonstrate that the EfficientNet B7 model stands out as the best-performing architecture, achieving an exceptional training accuracy of 99.89% and a validation accuracy of 99.45%. Notably, EfficientNet B7 reached this high level of performance as early as the 17th training epoch, indicating its efficiency and suitability for real-time applications.

Although the execution time of 147 min for EfficientNet B7 is slightly longer than some other models, this factor can be overlooked given the superior classification performance. These findings underscore the importance of carefully selecting the most appropriate pre-trained model for the specific task of Arabic alphabet sign recognition, with EfficientNet B7 emerging as the optimal choice.

## 4.3 Select the best Pre-trained model

The comparative analysis of model performance in the context of Arabic alphabet sign classification, using the ArASL2018 dataset, was carried out based on key evaluation metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and test accuracy. These metrics are crucial in the field of classification, as they enable us to assess a model's ability to effectively discriminate between different classes.

Table 5 summarizes the results obtained from the experiments, highlighting the performance of different models, including VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet V1, MobileNet V2, and the various EfficientNet variants (B0 to B7). The metrics examined include test accuracy, Macro Average Precision, Macro Average Recall, and Macro Average F1-Score.

The results show that the EfficientNet B7 stands out as the model offering the best overall performance among all the evaluated architectures. Specifically, the EfficientNet B7 achieved the highest test accuracy rate at 99.24%, outperforming the other models. Additionally, the Macro Average Precision (99.27%), Macro Average Recall (99.25%), and Macro Average F1-Score (99.26%) for the EfficientNet B7 are also the highest across all the examined models.

These results demonstrate the superiority of the EfficientNet B7 model in the specific context of classifying Arabic alphabet signs from the ArASL2018 dataset. The model's exceptional performance across multiple evaluation metrics, including the highest test accuracy and Macro Average scores, highlights its suitability and effectiveness for this task.

The implications of these findings are significant, as the choice of the right pre-trained model is crucial for developing robust and efficient real-time applications for Arabic alphabet sign recognition. The EfficientNet B7 architecture, with its exceptional classification capabilities, can serve as a strong foundation for future research and the deployment of practical solutions in this domain.

Table 6 presents the top 10 classification errors in a model designed to recognize 32 classes in the ArASL2018 dataset. These classification errors can be attributed mainly to the incorrect formation of hand gestures rather than the model's performance. Even though these errors exist, they are relatively few (the highest being 6 errors for a specific misclassification), indicating that the model is well-trained overall. The EfficientNet B7 performs accurately across the majority of the 32 classes.

Table 7 provides a detailed analysis of the classification performance. Each row of the table represents an Arabic alphabet class, with the following metrics evaluated for each class: precision, recall, F1 score, and support, which represents the number of occurrences of that class in the dataset.

Looking at these results, it is clear that EfficientNet B7 performs exceptionally well across all classes, with high values for precision, recall, and F1 score. In particular, some classes such as 'ain', 'khaa', 'waw', 'ya', and 'yaa' show perfect results with 100% precision, recall, and F1 score.

Table 8 represents the overall test accuracy of the model as 99.24%, underlining its excellent ability to classify Arabic alphabet signs correctly. The Weighted Avg (weighted average by the number of occurrences of each class) values further reinforce the overall excellence of the model, with high scores of 99.27%, 99.25%, and 99.26% respectively. This high level of performance underlines the relevance of the EfficientNet B7 and its usefulness in reallife image recognition applications.

Figure 9 represents the misclassification errors observed in the test set for each specific class. In particular, the 'dha' class stands out with seven misclassified images, closely followed by the 'kaaf' class with four misclassified images. The 'thal', 'tha', and 'gaaf' classes each have three misclassified images. It is essential to stress that these misclassifications can be attributed to a variety of factors, such as annotation errors in the database or variations in the way the signs were formed by different volunteers.

It should be noted that a significant source of error comes from the presence of incorrectly categorized images in the database. For example, images representing the alphabet sign 'tha' were found in the class 'gaaf'. In addition, errors can also arise from the diversity of sign formation styles used by volunteers, introducing significant variations into the data.

## 4.4.1 Model conversion and adaptation

The foundation of our application lies in the conversion of the EfficientNet B7 model from TensorFlow to TensorFlow Lite. This crucial step, depicted in Fig. 10, serves the purpose of optimizing the model for mobile deployment on the Android platform (Fadlilah and Handaga 2021; Ahmed and Bons 2020; Pratama and Pratama 2021). The model, now saved as a '.h5 file,' undergoes this transformation to ensure its efficiency and seamless integration within the Android environment.

The conversion to TensorFlow Lite is essential for achieving optimal performance, enabling a smooth user experience and real-time functionality on mobile devices. This adaptation aligns with the stringent requirements for deploying applications on the Android platform, ensuring that our Arabic alphabet sign recognition model is both effective and user-friendly. Additional steps include:

- Quantization: Reducing the model size and improving latency by converting the weights from floating-point to a more efficient data type, such as 8-bit integers.

## 4.4.2 Integration into android studio application

Figure 11 provides a visual representation of the subsequent steps in our application's development. We seamlessly integrated the TensorFlow Lite model into the Android Studio application, leveraging the OpenCV library for enhanced functionality. The resulting system is designed to simplify the process of learning Arabic alphabet signs through an interactive and visually engaging experience. Steps include:



- Android Studio Setup: Configuring the development environment, including installing necessary SDKs and setting up the project structure.
- TensorFlow Lite Interpreter Integration: Adding the TensorFlow Lite dependency and writing code to load and run the model using the TensorFlow Lite Interpreter.
- OpenCV Integration: Incorporating OpenCV for image processing tasks, such as hand detection and preprocessing the input images for the model.
- User Interface Design: Creating an intuitive user interface that allows users to interact with the application easily.

## 4.4.3 User interaction and learning process

As illustrated in Fig. 11, our system offers a user-friendly interface for learning Arabic alphabet signs. Users select the ' 'Arabic Alphabet Sign Recognition'' option and use their device's camera to position their hand and form an Arabic sign. The system, powered by the TensorFlow Lite model, detects the hand gesture, frames it in red, and displays the corresponding Arabic character at the top of the screen. This interactive approach facilitates an immersive learning experience.

## 5 Limitations and challenges

Despite the satisfactory performance of our system, as demonstrated in Fig. 14, there are inherent limitations and challenges that affect real-time sign identification. These issues stem from variations in brightness and changes in the background, which can hinder the system's ability to detect signs promptly. It is essential to note that the EfficientNet B7 model, trained on greyscale images with simple backgrounds from the ArASL2018 database, exhibits detection errors when confronted with background alterations. In instances where the background remains simple, the system operates optimally, but it may fail to detect signs in more dynamic environments.

Figure 13 shows examples of Arabic signs that were not successfully detected and recognized by our system. Notably, these failures occurred under changing background conditions, highlighting the vulnerability of the system in such scenarios. Among the causes were the printed background and the level of brightness. Sometimes our hand was not even framed, i.e., detected, and other times the frame existed but did not detect the region of interest (the hand), resulting in poor recognition.

While our results are promising, addressing these challenges is crucial for enhancing the real-time recognition rate of our system. In light of these limitations, we have outlined plans for further research to overcome these obstacles. Ongoing efforts focus on refining the model to adapt to varying backgrounds and brightness levels, ensuring robust performance in diverse settings. While our results are promising, addressing these challenges is crucial for enhancing the real-time recognition rate of our system. In light of these limitations, we have outlined plans for further research to overcome these obstacles. Ongoing efforts focus on refining the model to adapt to varying backgrounds and brightness levels, ensuring robust performance in diverse settings.

We introduce a new comprehensive database, ArASL ? , encompassing 28 classes of Arabic letter signs. This database consists of 90 color photos per class, each measuring 64 9 64 pixels, as shown in Fig. 14. The images are captured from various angles, under different brightness levels, and against complex backgrounds.

## 6 Conclusion

In conclusion, our work centers on the development of an educational application tailored for acquiring proficiency in the Arabic sign alphabet, addressing the unique requirements of deaf individuals within the Arab community. This endeavor leverages the ArASL2018 dataset, to provide a resource that aligns with the specific linguistic and cultural nuances of Arabic sign language.

Our investigation encompassed the thorough presentation, evaluation, and analysis of twelve Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classification models, all implemented on a computer processor. The overarching objective was to discern the optimal model for the intended application. Through meticulous experimentation, the results unequivocally endorsed the EfficientNet B7 model-a pre-trained CNN architecture-as the standout performer. This model showcased remarkable prowess, achieving an impressive accuracy of 99.24% on test data.

Furthermore, the application's real-time capabilities stand as a noteworthy advantage, facilitating instantaneous feedback and interaction for users. The EfficientNet B7 model's robust performance ensures swift and accurate recognition of Arabic sign alphabet gestures, enhancing the learning experience. This real-time functionality not only expedites the learning process but also fosters a dynamic and engaging educational environment, crucial for effective language acquisition.

## Real-time sign language recognition using parallel multi-scale CNN to enhance inclusive education for deaf and hard of hearing students

Naoufal El-Marzouki 1 · Imane Lasri 1 · Anouar Riadsolh 1 · Mourad Elbelkacemi 1

Received: 22 November 2023 / Revised: 16 January 2025 / Accepted: 7 February 2025 / Published online: 11 March 2025

©The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

## Abstract

Inclusive education, a fundamental right for all individuals, presents unique challenges in higher education, particularly when it comes to students with disabilities. Our research focuses on rectifying the gaps in catering to the needs of deaf university students by introducing real-time sign language recognition through a parallel multi-scale CNN. We conducted model testing with five different optimizers, including Adam, Nadam, Adadelta, RMSprop, and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). Notably, the best test accuracy of 99.70% was achieved using SGD on the Sign MNIST dataset, which comprises 7200 images categorized into 24 alphabet classes (excluding 'J' and 'Z'). The parallel multi-scale CNN outperformed the conventional CNN model, which achieved an accuracy of 96%. Our approach outperformed other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating superior performance based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The model was tested in real-time scenarios with Moroccan deaf students pursuing degrees in electronics, computer science, and robotics at Mohammed V University in Rabat. This testing underscores the model's adaptability and its potential to improve inclusivity in higher education.

Keywords Inclusive education · Deaf students · Sign language recognition · Parallel multi-scale CNN · Deep learning

Naoufal El-Marzouki, Imane Lasri, Anouar Riadsolh, and Mourad Elbelkacemi contributed equally to this work.

## 1 Introduction

In today's educational landscape, the call for inclusive education has gained substantial momentum, largely driven by the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) Article 24 and its General Comment Number Four [36]. This influential declaration urges nations to swiftly establish fully inclusive education systems, grounded in the belief that segregating children with disabilities results in an education of subpar quality.

Within the realm of inclusive education, a diverse spectrum of individuals exists, each with its unique learning requirements and abilities. This encompasses students with a wide range of challenges, including students facing language barriers, visual impairments, cognitive difficulties, and physical disabilities, as well as students with hearing impairments who rely on sign language and various other conditions. In this environment, the goal is to create a setting where every learner, regardless of their abilities or disabilities, can thrive and access the same educational opportunities.

Inclusion is more than just the physical presence of students in general education classrooms, it prioritizes active engagement in a meaningful and challenging instructional program. Managing a classroom in inclusive education can present several significant challenges for teachers. One of the major challenges lies in the diversity of students' needs, which can vary significantly based on their abilities and specific requirements. Teachers must develop flexible and tailored lesson plans to address these diversified needs, which can be a complex and demanding task. Additionally, class size can be an issue as there may be a substantial number of students with special needs requiring individualized attention. This can lead to time and resource constraints as teachers strive to balance the needs of the entire class [24].

Communication is another major challenge. In an inclusive classroom, there can be a wide variety of communication modes, including sign language, communication aids, or augmented and alternative communication needs. Teachers must be prepared to use these different communication modes to ensure that each student has the opportunity to express themselves and understand the information presented in class. While some teachers excel in managing such diverse classrooms, the majority may face difficulties, often due to inadequate training and support [22]. Numerous traditional studies have employed information and communication technology (ICT) within the framework of inclusive education. Otta and Pozzi [28] emphasize the pivotal role of ICT in fostering e-inclusion and underscore the need for accessible tools and teacher competencies to achieve genuine inclusive education. Huang et al. [13] study on ICT education in rural Taiwan highlights the critical importance of adaptable teaching materials and localized methods in enabling successful information application learning in underserved communities. Drigas and Ioannidou [10] emphasize the transformative role of ICTs in special education, highlighting their capacity for more comprehensive assessment and effective interventions, ultimately enhancing the learning experiences of students with special educational needs.

Recent studies have explored inclusive education by harnessing the advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning to better support students with disabilities. Srivastava [32] underscores the role of AI-driven Smart Learning Assistance tools in promoting inclusive education, ensuring equitable access, and effective communication for students with disabilities within the classroom. Won et al. [15] show the value of deep learning algorithms in predicting school absenteeism among autistic students, potentially enhancing their access to essential educational and therapeutic support while minimizing the risk of dropout. Ketcham [18] highlights the promising potential of the intelligent glove in aiding individuals with visual impairments by detecting obstacles and providing real-time location data, setting the stage for future enhancements in improving its functionality and user experience. Lasri et al. [23] show the potential of deep learning and transfer learning in facial expression recognition to evaluate engagement levels of deaf and hard-of-hearing students, offering a promising approach for enhancing classroom experiences and assessing student engagement more effectively.

In a related context, recent studies in sign language recognition have made significant advancements, particularly in enhancing communication for deaf and hard-of-hearing students. Utilizing machine learning and deep learning techniques, researchers have developed systems that can translate sign language gestures into text or spoken language, bridging the communication gap between sign language users and those unfamiliar with sign language. These developments hold great promise for promoting inclusivity and breaking down communication barriers, ultimately enriching the educational experience for individuals with hearing and speech impairments. Notably, Bin Munir [2] underscores the importance of improved communication between deaf-mute and non-mute individuals through an intelligent sign language interpretation system. Additionally, Kothadiya [20] presents a deep learning-based algorithm employing long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent units (GRU) networks, offering a promising solution to enhance communication for those with impaired speech or hearing by accurately detecting and recognizing sign language gestures. Furthermore, Pigou's [29] research leverages technology, including Microsoft Kinect and convolutional neural network (CNN), to automate sign language recognition, offering a promising solution to improve communication between the deaf community and the hearing majority. According to these studies, it is evident that there are numerous obstacles in the field of inclusive education, especially concerning the integration of sign language to ensure effective communication.

In response to these challenges, we have developed a model based on parallel multi-scale CNN to comprehensively address these obstacles. Notably, our approach stands out as a unique contribution, as there is currently no existing work that employs our specific model in this context, and we are pioneers in applying this innovative model in the context of inclusive higher education. The motivation behind this research stems from the urgent need to enhance inclusive education, particularly for deaf and hard-of-hearing students. Despite technological advancements, significant barriers to communication and learning access persist in inclusive classrooms. Teachers often face challenges in meaningfully engaging all students, resulting in disparities in educational access and outcomes. This research aims to bridge this gap by leveraging innovative technologies, specifically a parallel multi-scale convolutional neural network model, to improve real-time sign language recognition. We aspire to empower educators and create an inclusive learning environment where all students can thrive.

Furthermore, we conducted rigorous testing using five different optimization techniques, including Adam, Nadam, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Adadelta, and Rmsprop. We applied the model to deaf and hard-of-hearing students pursuing inclusive bachelor's degrees in electronics, computer science, and robotics at the Faculty of Sciences, Mohammed V University in Rabat, Morocco, to ensure its effectiveness and adaptability. Our model aims to revolutionize the education system by introducing a cutting-edge solution for seamless communication between teachers and students through sign language. We recognize the importance of inclusive education, and our innovative approach leverages technology to bridge the communication gap. This model will empower teachers to learn and effectively use sign language, breaking down barriers and ensuring that students who rely on sign language have equal access to quality education. By incorporating this solution into classrooms, we strive to create an inclusive learning environment where all students, regardless of their communication abilities, can fully engage.

## 2 Related work

Sign language recognition systems have been developed using diverse approaches, including artificial neural networks (ANNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), each aiming to address the challenges posed by variable backgrounds, lighting conditions, and computational complexity. Various feature extraction techniques have been explored to enhance recognition accuracy across different sign languages and alphabets. Yasir et al. [37] adopted support vector machines for Bengali sign language recognition, leveraging shift-invariant feature transform (SIFT) and k-means clustering. Similarly, Jin et al. [7] employed SVMs for American Sign Language (ASL) recognition, using Canny edge detection and seeded region growing for hand gesture segmentation. Hartanto et al. [12] and Huong et al. [13] experimented with HSV color space segmentation, achieving varying degrees of success in Indonesian and Vietnamese sign language recognition. Notably, Jimoh et al. [16] designed an Android-based system using OpenCV template matching for English vocabulary recognition, emphasizing potential improvements through different feature extraction techniques. Kulkarni and Lokhande [21] utilized artificial neural networks and Otsu's segmentation, coupled with Canny edge detection for feature extraction. While achieving decent accuracy, they struggled with computational demands and sensitivity to background variations.

In efforts to enhance accuracy and address the challenges, advanced techniques like Histogram of Oriented Gradient (HOG) and CNNs have been applied. Tabassum et al. [33] used Canny edge and HOG for ASL alphabet recognition, while Masood et al. [25] used very deep convolutional networks (VGG16) to achieve impressive results with the Massey dataset [4]. Tolentino et al. [35] focused on beginners' ASL learning using a CNN and skincolor technique, attaining notable accuracy rates. Dudhal et al. [11] introduced a CNN-based Indian sign language recognition system, employing hybridized adaptive thresholding and SIFT techniques. Wadhawan and Kumar [26] extended this approach with grayscale and color images, achieving high training accuracy. Das et al. [9] and Jain et al. [14] utilized CNNs to recognize American Sign Language and highlighted the significance of filter size, demonstrating the potential for improvements.

Mittal et al. [26] designed a sign language recognition system using LSTM and Leap Motion. They applied a four-gated LSTM cell with a 2D CNN for sentence recognition, achieving 72.3% accuracy. Individual word recognition attained an accuracy of 89.50% with this system. Aparna and Geetha [3] propose a pioneering sign language recognition method, blending CNNs and LSTM networks. They use pre-trained CNNs for feature extraction, followed by LSTM layers, achieving a notable 94% accuracy on the Indian Sign Language (ISL) dataset, demonstrating its significance in deep learning-based sign language recognition.



Despite these advances, significant challenges persist, particularly regarding background interference, illumination variations, and computational complexity. Existing methods often struggle to accurately recognize signs in diverse real-world environments, where background clutter can obscure hand movements and lighting changes can lead to misinterpretations. Additionally, many models face high computational demands, hindering their deployment in real-time applications. Our study addresses these issues by utilizing a robust architecture designed to effectively manage background variability and illumination fluctuations. We also incorporate optimized feature extraction techniques that enhance accuracy while reducing computational requirements. By employing a standardized dataset, we aim to fill gaps in the literature and enable clearer comparisons across different sign languages, ultimately improving the reliability and effectiveness of recognition systems.

## 3 Proposed methodology

In this section, we will address key elements, including the proposed system architecture for real-time sign language recognition using a parallel multi-scale CNN, model optimization strategies, and the evaluation of the model's performance through various metrics.

## 3.1 Proposed system architecture for real-time sign language recognition using parallel multi-scale CNN

Figure1 presents the flowchart for the proposed model, outlining the overall process of the multi-scale convolutional neural network. Following this, Fig.2 details the architecture of the multi-scale convolutional neural network, which is designed with parallel branches. Within the convolutional block, three branches utilize 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7 convolution kernels, respectively. Each branch applies a rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function to introduce nonlinearity, as shown in (1). This multi-branch architecture enables the model to effectively capture diverse spatial patterns across multiple scales.

Afterward, a max-pooling layer with a 2x2 kernel size and a stride of 2 is employed for down-sampling. The flattened layers play an important role in converting multidimensional feature representations extracted from each frequency band into one-dimensional feature vectors.

Theresults obtained from the various convolution kernel branches are combined, capturing the spatial-temporal connectivity characteristics of the four frequency bands. This fusion result is then fed into fully connected layers. The first layer consists of 1000 neurons, while the second layer has 512 neurons. The output layer comprises 24 neurons, aligned with the number of classes being predicted, facilitating the computation of predicted probabilities for each letter class. A Softmax function is applied to the output layer, as described in (2).

Where θ represents the model parameters that we aim to optimize, while η denotes the learning rate controlling the step size during parameter updates. The function J (θ, x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) serves as the cost function, measuring the model's error for a given training example ( x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) . Additionally, ∇ J (θ, x ( i ) , y ( i ) ) corresponds to the gradient of the cost function concerning the parameters θ for that specific training example.

- Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) [19]: is a commonly used method. The moment the update is converted into an exponential moving average. The equation of the ADAM optimization algorithm is represented as follows:





θ represents the model parameters we want to optimize. α is the learning rate, which controls the step size when updating the parameters. m and v are the first and second moments (moving averages) of the gradients. t is the current iteration step. β 1 and β 2 are the exponential decay rates for the first and second moments, typically close to 1. /epsilon1 is a small constant to prevent division by zero.

- Nesterov Adam (Nadam) [27]: combines the techniques of Nesterov Accelerated Gradient (NAG) and Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) into a single optimization algorithm.
- Adadelta [38]: is a variant of SGD that introduces adaptability in learning rates for each dimension. It aims to mitigate two primary issues encountered in traditional gradient descent: the gradual reduction of learning rates during training and the necessity for manual selection of a global learning rate. Adadelta represents a more resilient advancement over Adagrad, as it dynamically adjusts learning rates by considering a moving window of gradient updates instead of accumulating all past gradients. This unique approach allows Adadelta to maintain effective learning, even in scenarios where numerous updates have already taken place.
- RMSprop [34]: maintains a decaying average of squared gradients and normalizes the current gradient by the square root of this average. The centered variant further calculates the average of gradients to estimate variance.

## 3.3 Model evaluation

In the domain of classification studies, the assessment of deep learning models frequently involves the utilization of performance metrics derived from the confusion matrix. This matrix serves as a visual representation that illustrates the correspondence between the predicted class labels generated by the model and the actual labels assigned to input images.

True Positive (TP) instances occur when the deep learning classifier accurately identifies an image as displaying the intended sign, correctly predicting a sign language gesture when the image is labeled as such. Conversely, False Positive (FP) cases arise when the classifier incorrectly identifies an image as depicting a different sign. On the other hand, False Negative (FN) situations happen when the deep learning model of the classifier wrongly predicts an image as representing a different sign. Lastly, True Negative (TN) scenarios occur when an image is correctly predicted as not representing a particular sign by the classifier's deep learning model.

We utilize a set of four performance metrics, denoted as (6), (7), (8), and (9), which encompass:

- Accuracy: these metrics gauge the proportion of correct predictions (TP and TN) relative to the total number of predictions made.



- Precision: evaluates the model's ability to make accurate positive predictions and is calculated as TP divided by the sum of TP and FP.





- Recall: measures the model's capacity to identify all relevant instances and is computed as TP divided by the sum of TP and FN.



- F1 Score: is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, offering a balanced measure of a model's performance



## 4 Experimental results and discussion

In the upcoming subsections, we will begin with the experimental setup, providing insights into the configuration and parameters employed. Following that, we will delve by explaining the dataset used in our study. Afterward, we will thoroughly examine and present the outcomes obtained through the application of the proposed model. Finally, we will discuss the results of real-time sign language recognition for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, emphasizing the practical implications of our research.

## 4.1 Experimental setup

We employed the Python-based Keras library [8] to facilitate the integration of models with different layer counts into the training workflow. The input images were resized to dimensions of 224 × 224 pixels before being fed into the models. We used the parallel multi-scale CNN model. The entire execution took place within the Google Colab environment, utilizing GPUs to ensure consistent conditions for all four models. Throughout the training phases, we monitored model weights to capture the highest validation accuracy.

In the process of training our deep learning model, we applied several data augmentation techniques designed to enhance the diversity and robustness of our training dataset. Firstly, we rescaled the pixel values of our images to a range of [0, 1] to ensure consistency in data representation. We then introduced randomness through various transformations. While we didn't apply image rotation, justifying this decision by the fact that it doesn't significantly affect the interpretation of alphabet characters in a meaningful way, we did employ other transformations. We allowed for random shifts in the height and width dimensions of the images, with a maximum shift of 20%. Furthermore, we applied zooming to our images, randomly zooming in by up to 20%, providing the model with different scales of the same objects. Additionally, horizontal flipping was enabled, which mirrors images horizontally, adding further diversity. Lastly, in the case of any new pixels created during these transformations, we used the 'nearest' pixel to fill them, ensuring the integrity of the image. Table 1 provides a summary of the optimal hyperparameters utilized during the training process. Following training, various performance metrics were assessed to evaluate the effectiveness of the models.

## 4.3 Experimental results

In this study, we have compared the performance of our proposed model parallel multi-scale CNN with CNN. Using four evaluation metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, and f1-score, as shown in Table 2 and Fig.5, parallel multi-scale CNN stands out as the top performer with an outstanding accuracy rate of 99.7%. While the CNN model reaches 96%.

The performance comparison of different optimizers, as displayed in Table 3, reveals insightful findings based on test accuracy. Notably, the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer outperforms the others with a remarkable test accuracy of 99.70%. The Adam optimizer also delivers a competitive performance with a test accuracy of 95.63%, Furthermore, the Nadam optimizer achieves a test accuracy of 82.50%, followed by the Adadelta optimizer at 76.50%, and the RMSprop optimizer with a test accuracy of 72.40%. These results provide valuable insights into the impact of different optimization algorithms on the model's performance, with SGD emerging as the most effective choice in this particular context. This performance difference can be attributed to the fact that SGD is particularly effective for image-based tasks, such as sign language recognition, where spatial patterns are important. In comparison, optimizers like Adam, Nadam, Adadelta, and RMSprop, which perform better in tasks with sparse gradients, such as text classification, struggle to capture the necessary details in image recognition tasks.

In contrast, our proposed parallel multi-scale CNN model stands out with an exceptional accuracy rate of 99.70% on the Sign MNIST dataset, alongside a precision of 100%, recall of 99%, and an F1-score of 100%. This remarkable accuracy can be attributed to the use of three different convolution kernels (3x3, 5x5, and 7x7) in parallel within the convolutional block, enabling the model to capture diverse spatial patterns across multiple scales and providing a richer feature extraction process. The 3x3 kernel captures fine details, while the 5x5 and 7x7 kernels detect larger, more global patterns. Furthermore, the ReLU activation function applied after each convolution introduces non-linearity, allowing the model to learn complex and varied feature representations. This combination of multi-scale feature extraction and non-linear activation enables the model to generalize effectively, achieving high accuracy by adapting to both small and large variations in sign language gestures. Unlike some more complex architectures, our method leverages the power of multi-scale feature extraction while maintaining simplicity. Our approach, compared to single-kernel CNN models or more intricate designs, enhances performance without overcomplicating the model, demonstrating that simpler models can yield superior results in this specific context.

## 4.4 Results of sign language real-time recognition for deaf and hard-of-hearing students

We conducted a real-time sign language recognition experiment at the Faculty of Sciences in Rabat Mohammed V University, Morocco, to assess our model's performance for deaf and hard-of-hearing students pursuing degrees in licence of electronics, computer science, and robotics. This experiment occurred in the Ibn Al-Baytar amphitheater and involved four participants, one male and three females, with two of them using hearing aids. We obtained their consent after providing a detailed explanation of the study's objectives, the methodology, and the use of their hand gestures for research purposes. Figure8 illustrates that the parallel multi-scale CNN model effectively detected and accurately identified the hand signs executed by the participants, facilitating clear communication between the participants and the system. The hand signs were precisely delineated by black outlines, highlighting the model's capability to isolate the regions of interest (the hand gestures) from the surrounding image, an important aspect for precise recognition. Our model provides invaluable support to educators by enhancing real-time sign language recognition in the classroom, which significantly improves the quality of interaction between teachers and deaf or hardof-hearing students. By facilitating seamless communication, the system eliminates the traditional barriers that often hinder full participation in classroom discussions, lectures, or activities.

The integration of this technology not only ensures effective communication but also promotes active student engagement, empowering deaf students to take part in the learning process on equal footing with their peers. From a pedagogical perspective, this model helps educators adapt their teaching strategies to be more inclusive and responsive to the needs of students with hearing impairments. Teachers can now deliver lessons without relying solely on interpreters, allowing for more spontaneous and dynamic exchanges between them and their students. Additionally, the system can support the implementation of differentiated instruction, where educators can tailor their teaching methods to accommodate different learning styles and abilities, thereby fostering a more personalized and effective educational experience.

## 5 Conclusion

Our research underscores the paramount significance of inclusive education. In this context, we have developed a model based on a parallel multi-scale CNN to overcome the challenges hindering the effective integration of sign language. The multi-scale convolutional neural network in our study employs a parallel architecture with three branches that utilize 3x3, 5x5, and7x7convolutionkernelsrespectively and ReLUactivation functions. A max-pooling layer reduces the dimensions of feature maps, while a Flatten layer transforms multi-dimensional features into one-dimensional vectors. The outcomes from these branches are combined to capture spatial-temporal connectivity across four frequency bands. The fully connected layers encompass a 1000-neuron layer, a 512-neuron layer, and a 24-neuron output layer with Softmax activation for class prediction, with each class representing an alphabet letter (excluding 'J' and 'Z'). Additional ReLU activation, batch normalization, and dropout layers with a 0.1 probability enhance learning and mitigate overfitting. We conducted rigorous testing with five different optimization techniques, including Adam, Nadam, SGD, Adadelta, and Rmsprop, to determine the optimal optimizer.



Our findings affirm the effectiveness of our parallel multi-scale CNN model, which achieved an outstanding accuracy rate of 99.70% on the MNIST dataset using SGD with a learning rate of 0.1, a momentum of 0.9, decay of 1e-4, a batch size of 200, and 100 training epochs. Our proposed model surpassed state-of-the-art methods. We applied our model to both typically hearing students and those who are deaf or hard of hearing, pursuing an inclusive bachelor's degree in electronics, computer science, and robotics at the Faculty of Sciences of Mohammed V University in Rabat, Morocco, ensuring its efficacy and adaptability. Our model stands as a unique contribution, with no comparable work in this field. We are pioneers in the application of this innovative model within the realm of inclusive higher education. By introducing this model into classrooms, our aim is to foster an inclusive learning environment that enables all students, regardless of their means of communication, to actively engage in the educational process.

While our model successfully addresses many challenges, it is important to note the absence of the letters 'J' and 'Z' from the dataset, as these require dynamic motion for accurate representation. We plan to address this limitation in future work by developing solutions that employ sensors to capture and enhance the dynamic movements associated with these letters. Furthermore, we are committed to expanding our research to Moroccan Sign Language, which will broaden the scope and impact of our work in creating inclusive educational environments tailored to diverse sign language communities.

## Sign to Text: Automated Sign Language Interpretation using LSTM and Computer Vision

Mr Sankara Mahalingam M

Assistant Professor

Department of Computer Science and Engineering

Kalasalingam Academy of

Research and Education,

AbstractSign language serves as a crucial communication tool  for  individuals  with  speech  or  hearing  impairments. Recent advancements in computer vision and deep learning offer opportunities to develop efficient, real-time sign language  recognition  systems  that  bridge  communication gaps. This study proposes a sign language recognition model utilizing the Mediapipe model and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)  networks  to  detect  and  interpret  American  Sign Language (ASL) gestures in real time. The proposed system extracts and analyzes key landmarks across the body, hands, and  face,  leveraging  CNN-LSTM  architecture  to  capture both  spatial  and  temporal  features  essential  for  accurate gesture recognition. Evaluated on a diverse ASL dataset, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 92%, demonstrating robustness  and  adaptability  in  varied  environments.  The proposed approach holds promise for applications in assistive technologies  and  educational  tools,  providing  an  accessible solution for sign language interpretation.

Chintapudi Harika

Department of Computer Science and Engineering Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education, Virudhnagar,Tamilnadu,India 99210041167@klu.ac.in

Dasari Pavan Kalyan

Department of Computer Science and Engineering Kalasalingam Academy of Research and Education, Virudhnagar,Tamilnadu,India
