## SIGNSPEAK: Integrating Computer Vision and Speech Synthesis for Alphabet Filipino Sign Language (FSL)

Jayvee N. Mapote Mapú a Institute of Technology at Laguna Mapú a Malayan Colleges Laguna, Cabuyao City, Laguna, Philippines jmapote@live.mcl.edu.ph

Abstract -In our interconnected world, effective communication  is  a  fundamental  human  right  fostering  social interaction, education, and personal growth. However, individuals with sensory impairments,  such as hearing loss, encounter significant barriers in communication, hindering their participation  in  society.  This  challenge  is  pronounced  in  the Philippines, where Filipino Sign Language (FSL) is vital for the Deaf community. The "SignSpeak" study addresses these challenges  by  integrating  computer  vision  and  speech  synthesis technologies.  Utilizing  platforms  like  Raspberry  Pi  and  Jetson Nano, SignSpeak interprets hand gestures in real-time, converting them into audible speech, and translates spoken language into text, enabling bidirectional communication. This approach empowers individuals with varying sensory abilities, fostering inclusivity and enhancing educational opportunities. SignSpeak promotes social equity  and  empowers  the  Deaf  community  in  the  Philippines through  rigorous  software  and  hardware  development  and  a commitment to linguistic inclusivity. Beyond technical innovations, SignSpeak envisions a future where individuals of all abilities can communicate freely and participate in society. The study results were highly successful, demonstrating 95%  accuracy,  96% precision,  94%  recall,  and  a  95%  F1  score.  Additionally,  the prototype received positive feedback, with an overall mean score of 4.845. These outcomes highlight SignSpeak's effectiveness and potential impact in improving communication accessibility for the Deaf community in the Philippines.

Keywords -Filipino Sign Language, Deaf Community, Communication Accessibility, Computer Vision, Speech, Synthesis, Real-time Interpretation, Inclusivity, SignSpeak study, Technology Integration, Social Equity

## I. INTRODUCTION

In  the  rapidly  evolving  digital  era,  the  importance  of inclusive communication cannot be overstated. For individuals with sensory impairments, such as hearing loss, communication barriers  persist  due  to  the  limited  availability  of  accessible communication tools. The ability to communicate effectively is not just a fundamental human right but also a cornerstone of social  interaction,  education,  and  personal  development  [1]. However,  for  a  significant  portion  of  the  global  population, communication  barriers  persist  due  to  sensory  impairments, such as hearing loss, and the limited availability of accessible communication tools [2].

In  the  Philippines,  a  nation  known  for  its  rich  cultural diversity, there exists a vibrant Deaf community. According to the 2000 Philippine census, an estimated 121,000 Deaf Filipinos were identified. Despite this sizable population, the Maribelle Dequilla-Nicerio [formerly Maribelle Dequilla-Pabiania] Mapú a Institute of Technology at Laguna Mapú a Malayan Colleges Laguna, City of Cabuyao, Laguna, Philippines mdnicerio@mcl.edu.ph ; mdpabiania@mcl.edu.ph

prevalence  of  sign  language  users  in  the  country  remains relatively low. This disconnect between the Deaf community and  mainstream  society  underscores  the  pressing  need  for innovative  solutions  to  bridge  the  communication  gap  and promote  inclusiveness.  Although  there  is  a  significant  Deaf population, a noticeable gap remains in effective communication  support.  Even  with  the  importance  of  sign language, many  Deaf  Filipinos still face  communication barriers  in  school,  at  work,  and  in  other  areas  of  their  lives. There is a shortage of FSL interpreters, and FSL is not as widely known or utilized in the Philippines as it should be. However, there is a growing awareness of the significance of FSL in the Philippines,  and  many organizations  are  working  to  promote FSL and provide services to the Deaf community.

The "SignSpeak" study addresses this issue by integrating computer  vision and  speech  synthesis technologies. This innovative approach aims to facilitate real-time interpretation of  hand  gestures  into  audible  speech  and  convert  spoken language  into text,  enabling  bidirectional  communication. SignSpeak has the potential to revolutionize how individuals with sensory impairments interact with the world, promoting greater accessibility and inclusivity in various aspects of daily life. The general objective of the study is to design and develop an  integrated  communication  device  for  seamless  interaction between individuals with auditory and visual impairments. This device aims to provide real-time translation of hand gestures into  audible  speech  and  convert  spoken  language  into  text. Specific objectives include developing a hardware microcomputer for the SignSpeak system, integrating computer vision  algorithms  for  hand  gesture  recognition  and  speech synthesis  for  real-time  interpretation;  creating  software  to provide an inclusive tool for effective communication for deaf individuals in diverse environments; and innovating the system to support bidirectional communication, allowing users to input signs and voice for translation and receive real-time synthesized speech. The scope includes hardware and software development within a limited timeframe, focusing on inclusivity  and  accessibility.  The  system's  design  considers public health and safety, cultural adaptation, societal benefits, and environmental considerations. Utilizing the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model, the study outlines clear inputs -voice  and  visual  sign  language  gestures  captured  via microphone  and  camera,  respectively.  These  inputs  undergo processing:  computer  vision  interprets  gestures,  while  speech recognition  converts  voice  to  text.  Integrated  outputs  include synthesized  speech,  facilitating  seamless  communication  by transforming diverse inputs into coherent speech output, enhancing accessibility across user needs

## II. METHODOLOGY

The  study  employed  a  Rapid  Application  Development (RAD)  software  development  lifecycle  for  the  planning  and implementation of the device. Rapid Application Development (RAD). RAD places a high emphasis on swift prototyping, realtime  feedback,  and  ongoing  adaptation,  favoring  these  over prolonged  planning  and  development  phases.  This  approach offers the advantage of flexibility and adaptability during the creative process, enabling continuous input and evolution as the project unfolds. By reducing the planning stage and maximizing prototype development, the study aims to effectively  tackle  time  constraints  and  maintain  a  consistent pace of progress [6]. Fig. 2 shows the hardware representation of the system.

Fig. 2. Hardware Representation of the System



As illustrated in Fig. 2, the hardware connections demonstrate how these components are integrated to achieve the desired functionalities. The first step in hardware development was to identify and select the appropriate components that would support the functionalities required by the  system.  Complementing  this  setup,  the  NVIDIA  Jetson Nano  managed  intensive  computational  tasks  with  its  USB connectivity  for  input  devices,  HDMI/DisplayPort  for  screen output, CSI port for camera integration, and power via barrel jack or USB-C. The configured settings across both platforms enabled seamless communication and data transfer critical for real-time gesture recognition and interpretation.

The  software  development  began  with  data  gathering, where  detailed  requirements  were  collected  to  ensure  the system  met  the  needs  of  Deaf  individuals,  sign  language interpreters,  and  other  stakeholders.  This  phase  included  a comprehensive  review  of  existing  technologies  in  computer vision,  speech  synthesis,  and  sign  language  interpretation  to identify gaps and opportunities. Engaging with members of the Deaf  community,  sign  language  interpreters,  and  educators helped understand their specific needs, challenges, and preferences, which were documented along with the functional and non-functional requirements, emphasizing real-time processing,  high  accuracy  in  gesture  recognition,  and  userfriendly  interfaces.  A  dataset  of  FSL  alphabet  gestures  and corresponding  voice  samples  was  prepared  for  training  and testing the system.

Based  on  these  requirements,  the  system  design  phase involved  creating  seamless  system  architecture  and  selecting components such as the Raspberry Pi for processing, NVIDIA Jetson  Nano  for  enhanced  GPU  capabilities,  and  appropriate cameras and microphones. Suitable computer vision algorithms like Mediapipe and TensorFlow were chosen for hand gesture recognition,  alongside  text-to-speech  algorithms  for  speech synthesis. The system architecture developed included modules for gesture recognition, speech synthesis, and the user interface.

The software development covers the following: (a) Computer  Vision  Module  for  the  implementation  of  gesture recognition using  Python  libraries  such  as  OpenCV  and Mediapipe,  ensuring  accurate  detection  and  interpretation  of FSL gestures; (b) Speech Synthesis Module for the development of the speech synthesis component using text-tospeech  libraries,  converting  recognized  gestures  into  audible speech;  (c)  Integration  for  the  computer  vision  and  speech synthesis  modules  to  work  cohesively,  allowing  seamless translation  of  gestures  to  speech  and  vice  versa;  (d)  User Interface was designed a user-friendly interface using Tkinter for  ease  of  interaction,  enabling  users  to  input  and  receive translations.

The  software  development  process  for  the  'SignSpeak' project involved several key steps to ensure the system could accurately  interpret  Filipino  Sign  Language  (FSL)  and  hand gestures. This includes collecting data, creating datasets, training  machine  learning  models,  and  developing  a  userfriendly interface. The integration of the SignSpeak system involves connecting  hardware  components  such  as  Raspberry  Pi  and Jetson Nano  to ensure seamless operation and effective communication between devices, as shown in Figs. 6 and 7. Fig. 7. Jetson Nano Setup



The formula for Accuracy Metrics is as follows:

Accuracy . The proportion of correctly classified samples to the total number of samples.



Precision. The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to the total predicted positive observations.



Recall. The ratio of correctly predicted positive observations to all observations in the actual class.



F1 Score. The weighted average of precision and recall.

## IV. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the 'SignSpeak' study represents a significant advancement  in  overcoming  communication  barriers  for  the deaf  and  hard-of-hearing  community  in  the  Philippines. ## II. ENHANCING ACCESSIBILITY AND EDUCATION THROUGH SMART COMPUTING IN COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS

- A. Transformative Role of AI and NLP in Inclusive Education for the Deaf Community
- a) Enhancing Accessibility through Multimodal Communication Systems Using AI : Communication serves as a cornerstone of education, particularly for children with

hearing impairments. Multimodal communication systems, which integrate various modes such as speech, text, images, and gestures, are essential in bridging communication gaps within the deaf community. These systems leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, including Computer Vision (CV) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) , to process and translate spoken language into sign language and vice versa. By combining sign language recognition, real-time text captions, and gesture-based interfaces, these systems provide an interactive learning experience that enables deaf children to engage with educational content alongside their peers. The integration of AI-powered translation models further enhances the adaptability of these platforms, accommodating different dialects and sign language variations across diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

- b) Scalable Smart Communication Platforms for Special Education Using Cloud Computing and NLP : The scalability and flexibility of communication systems in special education can be significantly enhanced through the adoption of cloud-based platforms . Cloud computing enables centralized storage and access to educational resources, making learning materials readily available to students regardless of location or time. The integration of NLP technologies allows these platforms to deliver personalized learning experiences by analyzing student performance and dynamically adjusting educational content. Such platforms can assess individual learning patterns, adapt instructional materials in real-time, and provide immediate feedback. Moreover, cloud-based communication tools facilitate remote monitoring by educators, enabling them to track student progress and provide targeted support. The inclusion of sign language recognition and speech-to-text functionalities further enhances accessibility, making the platform suitable for diverse learning needs.
- c) Real-Time Emotion Recognition and Context-Aware Learning for Inclusive Education : Real-time emotion recognition technologies offer significant potential for creating adaptive and inclusive educational environments. These systems analyze facial expressions, body language, and other behavioral cues to infer the emotional state of the learner. For children with hearing impairments, understanding emotional context can improve the delivery of educational content and foster a more supportive learning environment. By integrating emotion recognition with context-aware learning systems , smart communication platforms can dynamically adjust content delivery to suit the emotional and cognitive needs of each learner. For instance, if a student exhibits frustration during a lesson, the system can provide additional sign language-based explanations or switch to more engaging content formats. This personalized approach enhances the overall learning experience by addressing both the educational and emotional needs of the learner.

## B. System architecture

The system architecture for the proposed web-based application is designed to integrate Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and sign language recognition into an accessible platform. The architecture is divided into four primary layers, each handling specific functionalities.

Fig. 3. System Architecture



a) User Interface Layer: The User Interface (UI) Layer acts as the bridge between the user and the system, emphasizing accessibility and ease of use. Its key components include:

- Interactive dashboard providing sign language tutorials, safety education, and emergency communication tools.
- Responsive design supporting various devices, including desktops, tablets, and smartphones, to enhance inclusivity.
- Multimedia content integration combining videos, images, and real-time subtitles to create an interactive learning environment.

b) Application Logic Layer: The Application Logic Layer manages the core functionalities and user input processing. It consists of:

- Sign language recognition module that utilizes computer vision techniques to interpret gestures into text or speech.
- NLP module for processing textual data and generating subtitles to improve content accessibility.
- Safety module offering interactive simulations and guidelines on emergency protocols.

c) AI and Processing Layer: This layer enhances the application's intelligence by leveraging AI technologies. Its key components include:

- NLP algorithms for real-time subtitle generation and adaptive content delivery.
- Machine learning models trained to accurately recognize and interpret sign language gestures.
- Data analytics engine that monitors user interactions and optimizes learning outcomes based on feedback.

d) Data Management Layer: The Data Management Layer ensures secure and efficient data storage. It includes:

- Cloud-based storage solutions for multimedia content and user profiles.
- Database management system (DBMS) to maintain organized datasets of gestures and educational materials.
- Security measures such as encryption and access controls to protect user privacy.
- e) Future Enhancements: The system architecture is designed with scalability in mind, enabling future developments such as:
- Integration of advanced NLP libraries like NLTK and spaCy for improved linguistic analysis.
- Multilingual support to cater to diverse user communities.
- Real-time gesture recognition with enhanced hardware and software capabilities.

## C. Units

- Primary Units : In this paper, SI (MKS) units are used as the primary measurement system for all technical specifications. For example, distances related to sensor placement are measured in meters (m), response times in seconds (s), and data sizes for processing sign language videos are measured in bytes (B). English units are provided only as secondary references within parentheses, where relevant.
- To maintain consistency and accuracy in measurements, SI units are used exclusively within the same context. For instance, if the latency of a sign language recognition system is measured in milliseconds, all related time measurements within that section are also expressed in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms). No combination of SI and CGS units is used, ensuring dimensional consistency.
- he paper maintains consistency in the usage of unit abbreviations and full spellings. For example, sign recognition accuracy is reported as a percentage (%), and processing durations are given in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms).

Units are fully spelled out in running text, such as '...the system processed the sign in 1.5 seconds.

- Decimal Points : All decimal values are written with a leading zero to prevent confusion. For example, the latency of the real-time sign language interpreter is reported as 0.45 seconds instead of .45 seconds.

## D. Equations

The system's key performance metrics are represented by the following equations:

Translation accuracy evaluates the correctness of sign language translation compared to the ground truth.



Processing time measures the system's efficiency in translating input videos into sign language gestures.



Recognition score assesses the system's performance using the exponential function to reduce the impact of higher error rates.



Latency represents the total time delay during sign recognition and translation.



where α and β are constants derived based on the model parameters.

Sign duration represents the average length of each sign gesture in the input video.



## E. Motivation of the Proposed Methodology

The motivation behind the proposed methodology arises from the critical need to address the accessibility and communication challenges faced by hard-of-hearing children, particularly in educational and safety contexts. Conventional approaches often overlook the specific requirements of this demographic, creating barriers to equitable learning and personal safety. The key factors driving this initiative include:

## 1) Addressing Educational Gaps:

Hard-of-hearing children often encounter limited access to traditional educational resources due to their dependence on visual and sign language-based communication. The lack of tailored solutions leaves them at a disadvantage in gaining foundational knowledge. This methodology seeks to fill this gap by offering interactive and accessible educational content that caters to their unique needs.

## 2) Promoting Safety Awareness:

Personal safety is a fundamental aspect of every child's development. However, safety education programs rarely accommodate hard-of-hearing children, leaving them vulnerable in emergency situations. The proposed system integrates safety modules specifically designed for hard-of-hearing children, providing them with critical tools to recognize and respond to potential risks.

## 3) Advancing Inclusivity:

Inclusivity in education and safety programs is essential to ensure equal opportunities for all children, regardless of their abilities. By leveraging technologies such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) and sign language recognition, the methodology aims to create a platform that bridges communication gaps and fosters a more inclusive learning environment.

## 4) Harnessing Emerging Technologies:

The rise of smart computing technologies offers innovative solutions to longstanding accessibility challenges. By incorporating NLP and advanced computing frameworks, the proposed system ensures the delivery of personalized and effective content, empowering hard-ofhearing children to engage with educational and safety materials independently.

## 5) Fostering Long-Term Impact:

The scalability and adaptability of the proposed system ensure its potential to address global accessibility challenges. By focusing on universally applicable solutions, this methodology aims to create a lasting impact, fostering inclusivity and safety for hard-of-hearing children worldwide.

## V. Contribution of the Proposed Methodology

## I. INTRODUCTION

In an increasingly digital world, the inclusion of students with diverse needs remains a critical challenge in educational technology. Among these needs, ensuring effective learning tools  for  deaf  and  hard-of-hearing  students  is  of  paramount importance.  Traditional  educational  methods  and  resources often fall short in providing engaging and accessible content for  these  learners,  particularly  when  it  comes  to  interactive and  visually-driven  activities.  These  limitations  can  hinder their academic progress and limit their ability to engage with the curriculum on an equal footing with their peers.

Deaf and hard-of-hearing students face unique challenges in educational settings, relying heavily on visual and tactile information  to  facilitate  learning.  Classroom  environments Interactive  quizzes  are  a  crucial  element  of  modern education, aiding in the reinforcement  of  concepts  and providing  immediate  feedback  to  learners.  However,  most existing  quiz  systems  are  designed  with  an  audio-visual approach that may not be fully accessible to deaf and hardof-hearing  students.  There  is  a  pressing  need  for  a  system that  transcends  these  barriers  and  provides  an  inclusive, engaging, and effective learning environment. This necessitates the development of educational technologies that can cater to the  unique  needs  of these students  while enhancing their overall learning experience.

To  address  this  gap,  the  development  of  innovative systems  that  leverage  advanced  technologies  is  essential. This paper introduces SmartSignQuiz , a novel colour-based interactive  quiz  system  designed  specifically  for  deaf  and hard-of-hearing students. SmartSignQuiz integrates state-ofthe-art AI-driven facial and gesture recognition technologies to create an engaging and adaptive learning experience. By utilizing  these  technologies,  the  system  is  able  to  interpret users'  responses  through  gestures  and  facial  expressions, providing  a  natural  and  intuitive  mode  of  interaction  that aligns  with  the  communication  styles  of  deaf  and  hard-ofhearing individuals.

Associate Professor,  Department of Computer Science and Engineering

The  colour-based  interaction  model  not  only simplifies  the  interface,  making  it  more  intuitive,  but  also enhances visual engagement. This method  provides an alternative  to  text-heavy  interfaces,  allowing  students  to interact with content in a manner that is visually stimulating and easily comprehensible. Furthermore, colour-coded feedback  mechanisms  are  employed  to  indicate  correct  and incorrect responses, providing immediate and clear feedback that is essential for effective learning.

The implementation of SmartSignQuiz represents a significant advancement in the field of educational technology for special needs. Its unique combination of AIdriven  facial  and  gesture  recognition  with  a  colour-based interactive framework offers a holistic solution that not only addresses accessibility concerns but also enriches the learning process. By  enabling  deaf and  hard-of-hearing students  to  interact  with  quiz  content  in  a  manner  that resonates with their natural modes of communication, SmartSignQuiz  has  the  potential  to  significantly  enhance their educational outcomes.

This paper explores the design, development, and implementation  of  SmartSignQuiz,  detailing  the  technical aspects of its AI-driven features and the colour-based interaction model. We examine the potential of SmartSignQuiz to enhance the learning experience for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, highlighting both its innovative approach and its practical applications in educational settings.  The  system  is  evaluated  in  terms  of  usability, effectiveness, and impact on student engagement and learning outcomes.

Through  this  research,  we  aim  to  contribute  valuable insights  into  the  creation  of  effective,  inclusive  educational technologies and to set a precedent for future innovations in this field.

The proposed  method  demonstrates  potential  for  various  image processing tasks requiring precise colour identification.

## III. METHODOLOGY

In  the  SmartSignQuiz  system,  computer  vision  plays  a central  role,  utilizing  several  key  techniques  to  facilitate facial recognition and color detection. The complexity of the proposed model lies in its real-time processing capabilities, which involve facial recognition and color detection modules. The system uses OpenCV and the face\_recognition library, both of which are optimized for efficient video frame processing.  The  deep  learning  model  for  facial  recognition has a computational cost proportional to the number of faces in  the  database,  requiring  high  processing  power  for  larger datasets. However, the system maintains real-time performance with modest hardware by limiting image resolution and  optimizing  data storage with lightweight encoding files. The color detection module, using HSV color space analysis, has a minimal computational footprint, enabling quick recognition even in changing lighting conditions. This library uses a deep learning-based approach for face detection and recognition, providing a highly accurate method to identify students in real-time.

In the system, computer vision techniques are applied in two  main  areas:  face  recognition  and  color  detection.  For facial  recognition,  the  process  begins  with  capturing  video frames from a webcam using OpenCV. Each frame is resized and  converted  from BGR  (the  default color  format in OpenCV) to RGB to align with the input requirements of the face\_recognition library. The face\_recognition library simplifies the complex process of face detection and recognition using deep learning. Initially, it detects faces in an image using a deep neural network that has been trained on a large dataset of face images. This network identifies key facial features, such as the eyes, nose, and  mouth,  to determine the precise location of the face within the image. After detecting the face, the library extracts facial encodings by  mapping  the  detected  features  onto  a  128-dimensional space.  These  encodings  are  essentially  feature  vectors  that encapsulate  the  unique  characteristics  of  a  person's  face, making it possible to distinguish between different individuals.

When the system needs to identify a face, it computes the face  encoding  for  the  detected  face  in  the  real-time  video frame.  It  then  compares  this  encoding  to  the  set  of  known encodings stored during the initial data collection phase. The comparison  is  done  using  the  Euclidean  distance  metric, which measures how close the new encoding is to the known encodings. A lower distance indicates a higher likelihood of a match.  If the computed  distance  is below  a  certain threshold, the system recognizes the face as belonging to one of  the  known  students.  This  method  allows  for  highly accurate recognition even in varying lighting conditions and angles, making it ideal for real-world educational environments.

This section introduces the SmartSignQuiz system, outlining its purpose as an interactive quiz platform designed specifically for deaf and hard-of-hearing students. It highlights the integration of facial recognition, gesture recognition, and color detection technologies to facilitate an inclusive learning experience.

## A. Data Collection and Face Encoding

The system starts by gathering facial images of students, which are stored in a designated folder with filenames acting as unique student identifiers. Using OpenCV  and  the face\_recognition library, the system extracts facial encodings from  these  images.  This  involves  converting  images  to  the RGB  format  and  detecting  facial  landmarks  to  generate  a unique numerical representation for each face. These encodings  are  then  saved  in  a  file  ('EncodeFile.p')  using Python's  pickle  module,  serving  as  a  reference  for  student identification during quiz sessions. The evaluation of SmartSignQuiz utilized a  dataset  of  facial  images  collected from  participating  students,  which  is  stored  securely  for privacy reasons. These images were processed using OpenCV  and  face\_recognition  libraries  to  generate  unique facial encodings. The dataset references have been included to  ensure  transparency  and  enable  reproducibility  of  the research  findings.  Future  studies  will  expand  the  dataset  to include diverse demographic groups, enhancing the generalizability of the results.

## B. Real-Time Face Recognition and Identification

The  system  employs  a  webcam  to  capture  real-time video  frames.  OpenCV  is  used  to  initialize  video  capture, ensuring  that  the  resolution  is  adequate  for  precise  facial feature capture. The face\_recognition library detects faces in each video  frame,  computes  their  encodings,  and  compares them to the stored encodings to identify the student. Functions like compare faces and face distance are used to match  the  real-time  encodings  with  known  faces,  enabling accurate and swift student identification.

## C. Color-Based Interaction for Quiz Responses

The Color-Based Interaction for Quiz Responses module allows students to interact with the quiz system using colored cards.  Upon  recognizing  a  student,  the  system  identifies  a specific region of interest (ROI) in the video frame where the student is expected to hold a colored card, typically near their face or hands. The ROI is converted to the HSV color space, enhancing color detection accuracy by accounting for different  lighting  conditions.  Predefined  HSV  ranges  help identify specific colors like red, green, and blue, which serve as the students' method of answering quiz questions.

## D. Region of Interest (ROI)

After successfully identifying a student in the frame, the system dynamically defines a Region of Interest (ROI) where the color card is expected to be held. Typically, this ROI is positioned  near  the  student's  body,  such  as  the  area  to  the bottom right or left of the detected face. The location of the ROI can be adjusted based on practical usage, ensuring that the color card is within the camera's view while minimizing interference from the background.

## E. Color Detection Mechanism for Response Identification

The  system  extracts  the  Region  of  Interest  (ROI)  from the video frame based on predefined coordinates relative to the student's face to focus on the area where the color card is expected to be held. To detect colors accurately within this ROI,  the  system  converts  the  image  from  the  BGR  color space  (used  by  OpenCV)  to  the  HSV  (Hue,  Saturation, Value) color space. The HSV color space is more effective for  color  detection  as  it  separates  the  chromatic  content (color)  from  intensity,  making  it  more  resilient  to  lighting variations. The system then uses predefined HSV ranges for the target colors, such as red, green, and blue. For each color, it  applies  a  mask  to  the  ROI  using  these  HSV  ranges, isolating pixels that fall within the specified range. The color with  the  highest  number  of  matching  pixels  in  the  ROI  is identified as the detected color. For instance, if most pixels in  the  ROI  fall  within  the  HSV  range  for  blue,  the  system classifies the color as "Blue."

Fig 1 : Flowchart of the Proposed System



## F. Quiz Execution and Response Tracking

During the Quiz  Execution and Response  Tracking phase, the system manages  the quiz flow. It displays multiple-choice  questions,  each  linked  to  a  specific  color response.  As  students  hold  up  colored  cards,  the  system continuously  monitors  the  ROI  for  changes.  The  detected color  is  then  compared  against  the  correct  answer  for  the question. If there is a match, the student's score is incremented. The system also tracks the time taken for each student to respond, logging "No response" if a student does not  answer  within  the  specified  time  limit,  typically  10

seconds. The quiz advances to the next question either after receiving all responses or reaching the time limit, repeating this process until all questions are completed.

## G. Final Score Calculation and Output

After the quiz, the system enters the Final Score Calculation and Output phase, where it compiles scores for each student, providing a summary of correct answers. This final  scoring  gives  educators  a  clear  assessment  of  student performance.  Additionally,  the  system  can  store  responses and  scores  for  future  analysis,  helping  educators  identify areas where students may need additional support or adaptive teaching methods.

The  SmartSignQuiz  system  employs  facial  recognition and color detection to facilitate an interactive quiz experience  for  deaf  and  hard-of-hearing  students.  Initially, facial images are collected and encoded to create a database of student profiles. During the quiz, the system captures realtime video and uses facial recognition to identify students.

Fig 2: Sample Output of the Encoding File



Fig 3: Sample Output the System



It  then  defines  a  Region  of  Interest  (ROI)  near  the student's face to detect colored cards, which students use to answer quiz questions. The ROI is converted from BGR to HSV  color  space  for  accurate  color  detection,  leveraging HSV's  resilience  to  lighting  variations.  Predefined  HSV ranges help isolate  and  identify  the  colors  displayed  by  the students. The system matches these detected colors with the correct  answers  for  the  quiz  questions,  updating  scores  in real-time.  By  using  this  combination  of  facial  recognition and color detection, the methodology offers an inclusive and accessible way for students to interact with the quiz.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

To evaluate the effectiveness of SmartSignQuiz, usability testing was carried out with a target group of students facing communication  challenges.  Metrics  such  as  identification accuracy, response time, and user engagement were monitored. Additionally, the system's impact was compared against conventional quiz methods, highlighting improvements in participation and comprehension. The adaptive  color-coded  feedback  and  personalized  response tracking demonstrated significant benefits in retaining information, validating the model's effectiveness in fostering an inclusive and engaging learning environment.

The  results  indicated  that  the  SmartSignQuiz  interface was  perceived  as  highly  intuitive  by  all  participants.  The colour-based design was praised for its user-friendly nature, with participants appreciating the visual clarity provided by the color-coded feedback.

This  design  facilitated  quick  comprehension  of  correct and incorrect responses, aligning well with the visual learning  preferences  of  the  users.  The  real-time  feedback mechanism  was  particularly  well-received  for  its  role  in maintaining engagement and encouraging continued interaction with the quiz content.

In terms of learning outcomes, participants demonstrated a  noticeable  improvement  in  their  performance  on  quizzes after using SmartSignQuiz. The adaptive learning algorithms of the system adjusted question difficulty based on individual progress,  which  helped  reinforce  learning  objectives  and support better retention of material. This personalized feedback proved effective in enhancing students' understanding of the content.

However,  some  challenges  were  identified  during  the testing  phase.  A  few  participants  experienced  minor  issues with  the  facial  and  gesture  recognition  components  of  the system,  leading  to  occasional  inaccuracies  in  interpreting responses. These issues have been noted and will be addressed through further refinements to ensure more reliable performance.

Overall,  the  initial  results  from  the  one-week  testing period  suggest  that  SmartSignQuiz  is  a  promising  tool  for enhancing  the  educational  experience  of  deaf  and  hard-ofhearing  students.  Its  innovative  approach  to  colour-based interaction  and  adaptive  feedback  has  shown  potential  in improving engagement and learning outcomes. The feedback obtained from this small sample provides a solid foundation for  further  development  and  broader  testing  to  ensure  the system's reliability and effectiveness.

## V. CONCLUSION

While SmartSignQuiz has shown  promising results, several practical limitations need  to be addressed.  The system's effectiveness is influenced by environmental factors like  lighting  conditions,  which  can  impact  color  detection accuracy. Additionally, color differentiation may be challenging for students with color vision deficiencies, suggesting the need  for alternative interaction  methods. Hardware limitations, such as camera quality, can also affect facial  recognition  precision.  Future  iterations  will  focus  on mitigating these constraints through advanced image processing techniques and adaptable interface design.

The  one-week  usability  testing  with  a  small  group  of participants demonstrated that the system is highly effective in  enhancing  student  engagement  and  comprehension.  The color-coded feedback and adaptive learning algorithms contributed significantly to improved quiz performance and better  retention  of  material.  These  features  align  well  with the visual learning preferences of the target audience, providing a clear and immediate understanding of responses.

Despite  the  overall  positive  feedback,  the  testing  phase revealed some challenges, particularly concerning the accuracy  of  the  facial  and  gesture  recognition  components. These  issues  underscore  the  need  for  further  refinement  to ensure consistent and reliable performance. Nevertheless, the results indicate that SmartSignQuiz holds significant promise in advancing the field of educational technology for deaf and hard-of-hearing  students.  Future  development  and  broader testing will be crucial to address the identified challenges and to enhance the system's capabilities. Overall, SmartSignQuiz represents  a  substantial  step  forward  in  creating  inclusive educational  tools  that  support  diverse  learning  needs  and promote a more equitable learning environment.

## VI. FUTURE ENHANCEMENTS

While  the initial  deployment  of  SmartSignQuiz  has shown  considerable  promise,  there  are  several  areas  for future  enhancement  that  could  significantly  improve  the system's  effectiveness  and  reach.  A  key  focus  will  be  on refining  the  facial  and  gesture  recognition  technologies  to enhance  accuracy  and  reliability.  This  improvement  could involve integrating more advanced machine learning algorithms, broadening the range of recognized gestures, and conducting extensive  validation  across  diverse  user  groups. These  steps  are  essential  to  ensure  that  the  system  can consistently  interpret  user  interactions  and  provide  accurate feedback.

Additionally, expanding  SmartSignQuiz  to  include  a wider variety of educational content and interactive features could  further enhance  its  utility.  Integrating  multimedia elements such as videos and animations, as well as offering customizable quiz formats, would enrich the learning experience.  Moreover,  incorporating  accessibility  features for users with color vision deficiencies and actively seeking ongoing  feedback  from  educators  and  students  will  help tailor the system to meet diverse needs. Broader testing with larger  and  more  varied  populations  will  also  be  crucial  to validate the system's impact and ensure it effectively supports different educational settings and learning styles.

## Paper Source: SynapSign: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for American Sign Language Recognition  Utilizing a Novel Landmark-Based Dataset

## SynapSign: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for American Sign Language Recognition Utilizing a Novel Landmark-Based Dataset

Erdoğan UYSAL Department of Computer Engineering Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat University Antalya, Türkiye erdoganuysalbs@gmail.com İrem BALIKCI Department of Computer Engineering Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat Universtiy Antalya, Tükiye irembalikciii98@gmail.com Yılmaz Kemal YÜCE Department of Computer Engineering Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat University Antalya, Türkiye yilmaz.yuce@alanya.edu.tr

Abstract -Hearing  loss  is  a  common  condition  affecting  a significant proportion of the world's population, creating barriers to effective communication. Sign language, particularly American Sign Language (ASL), is an important tool for the social integration and personal growth of people with hearing loss.  The  need for effective tools to facilitate the learning and practice of ASL is increasingly recognized. Although there are many  studies  and  proposed  softwares  that  execute  based  on certain  approaches  such  as  recognition  of  signs  by  machine learning techniques with relatively high accuracy, it is apparent that  there  exists  a  need  for  higher  performance.  This  paper presents SynapSign, a desktop application designed to enhance ASL learning using  machine learning  algorithms.  To  develop the  application  using  the  machine  learning  model  having  the highest accuracy, the performances of Random Forest, XGBoost and Deep Neural Network (DNN) classifiers were investigated. To this purpose, an image dataset consisting of 2600 images was prepared. For each letter of 26 letters for ASL, 100 images of hands showing 21 hand landmarks was built for accurate hand gesture recognition using Google's MediaPipe  technology. Thereafter, the three classifiers were trained on this extensive dataset of ASL hand images. Acquired models were tested and their performances were compared based on accuracy, precision and recall metrics. The results reveal that the model of Random Forest classifier performs slightly higher for all three metrics with 99.6%, 99.3% and %99.7, respectively, than other models. Therefore, SynapSign was developed using this model with a user interface that allows user to input sign image from a video stream via a camera and labelled with 21 hand landmarks by  MediaPipe  Framework's  default  hand  detection  model. Compared  to  traditional  methods,  the  application  provides  a more  interactive  and  engaging  learning  experience,  allowing users  to  practice  and  improve  their  ASL  skills with  real-time feedback. Our findings suggest that SynapSign could serve as a valuable  tool  for  both  educational  and  accessibility  purposes, addressing the gap in resources available to ASL learners.

Keywords-Hearing  Impairment,  Interaction  System,  Sign Language,  Random  Forest,  XGBoost,  Deep  Neural  Network (DNN), Hand Gesture Recognition, Machine Learning

## I. INTRODUCTION

The  World  Health  Organization  (WHO)  estimates  that approximately 466 million individuals worldwide are affected by  hearing  impairment,  a  condition  that  poses  significant challenges to daily communication [1]. Hearing impairment, as defined by the WHO, is a condition that severely hinders the ability to understand speech, for which sign language has proven to be a highly effective solution [2]. Therefore, sign language is a vital communication tool for the deaf community, however, it serves not only as a communication tool for the hearing impaired but also as a crucial instrument for social integration and personal development. There exist types of sign language with respect to spoken languages, such as American Sign Language (ASL).

Numerous  studies  have  been  conducted  on  teaching, learning and practicing sign language. Learning sign language is  reported  to  enhance  cognitive  flexibility  and  language acquisition, while technology-supported learning tools further facilitate the process and increase motivation [3].  The cognitive and social benefits of learning ASL have garnered significant attention. As a result, the ASL alphabet is chosen as the  primary mode  of  communication,  with  research underscoring the importance of phonological features, such as hand shape, in sign production [4]. ASL is now recognized as the third most common language in the United States, gaining prominence due to its deep roots in Deaf culture [1].

The advent of mobile technology has spurred the development  of  numerous  language-learning  applications. However, a significant lack of means and resources exists for those wishing to learn sign language. To address this gap, our research group has undertaken the development of an automatic sign language recognition system. Developing an automatic sign language recognition system presents several challenges. Nonetheless, several models targeting recognition of ASL have been constructed using the MediaPipe Framework and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

Özge Öztimur KARADAĞ Department of Computer Engineering Alanya Alaaddin Keykubat University Antalya, Türkiye ozge.karadag@alanya.edu.tr algorithms, particularly  for  detecting  gesture-based  ASL expressions, as illustrated in 'Fig. 1' [1]. These efforts aim to facilitate communication within the deaf and hearingimpaired community [5].

Fig. 1. American sign language



The effectiveness of immersive learning environments for ASL learners has been demonstrated, with findings showing that such environments enhance both receptive and expressive skills [6]. The impact of mobile applications on ASL learners has also been examined, revealing that these tools significantly enhance vocabulary and signing accuracy [7].  The  use  of  virtual  reality  (VR)  technology  in  sign language education has been explored, with findings showing that  VR  increases  learner  interest  and  motivation,  thereby improving skill retention [8]. The impact of online courses has been  examined,  with  results indicating that online learners achieve similar or even superior progress compared to  traditional  classroom  learners  [9].  The  advantages  of community engagement for sign language learners have been demonstrated, with those engaging regularly showing increased  confidence  and  competence  [10].  A  2021  study examined  the  impact  of  sign  language  clubs  on  learner motivation and skill development, finding that participants in these  clubs  experienced  significant  improvements  in  both motivation  and  signing  abilities  [11].  However,  current methods  for  teaching  and  practicing  ASL  face  several limitations.  Firstly,  there  is  a  notable  lack  of  standardized assessment  tools  to  measure  ASL  abilities  among  deaf learners,  leading  practitioners  to  rely  on  modified  Englishbased assessments [12]. Secondly, the scarcity of large-scale datasets  related  to  ASL  comprehension  and  production hampers the advancement of deep learning research in sign languages. Moreover, the existing datasets are often inadequate  for  practical  application  [13].  Finally,  despite some progress in developing ASL training applications, the absence  of  real-time  sign  recognition  systems  significantly limits the effectiveness of these learning tools [14]. Therefore, there is a clear need for the development of more diverse  and  accurately  labeled  datasets  [15].  These  studies collectively demonstrate the effectiveness of various methodologies and technological innovations in sign language  teaching  and  practice,  providing  learners  with diverse options to achieve greater proficiency and confidence. The  objective of this study is  to  enhance opportunities for students to practice sign language learning. To  this  end,  we  developed  an  application  using  a  model trained on our own dataset.

## A. Literature Review

Research has shown that the use of virtual reality (VR) technology  in  sign  language  education  increases  learner interest and motivation, leading to better retention of skills [8].  In  the  literature,  MediaPipe's  real-time  hand  gesture recognition  capabilities  have  been  successfully  applied  to various  virtual  reality  applications  and  have  been  used efficiently in human-computer  interactions [26].  Taken together, these results highlight the effectiveness and versatility  of  MediaPipe  in  enhancing  gesture  recognition systems in various applications and scenarios. MediaPipe's high success rates in hand gesture recognition are highlighted throughout the literature, and similar results were obtained in this study. This study extends MediaPipe's success in recognising ASL hand gestures and improves its accuracy by combining  it  with  algorithms  such  as  Decision  Tree  and DNN.

## II. MATERIALS AND METHODS

The  objective  of  this  study  is  to  develop  a  software application with a machine learning model that is capable of identifying the letters of the American Sign Language (ASL) alphabet  with  high accuracy  using image data. The project employs sophisticated techniques, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Networks (DNN), to harness the capabilities of MediaPipe for precise hand landmark extraction and gesture recognition. The incorporation of these methodologies  into  the  SynapSign  application  represents  a novel approach to enhancing real-time sign language recognition, with a focus on accuracy, usability, and accessibility.

## A. Random Forest Classifier

The  decision  tree  is selected for its  simplicity  and interpretability, with the data space being partitioned iteratively  and  models  constructed  in  each  partition.  A random  forest  classifier  is  a  powerful  ensemble  learning method  that  consists  of  multiple  decision  trees  trained  on random  subsets  of  the  data.  It  addresses  issues  like  block under-utilization  and  data  over-read  in  training  algorithms [16]. Additionally, random forest classification proved to be highly  effective  in  healthcare,  specifically  in  predicting individual responses to transcranial direct current stimulation for tinnitus relief, outperforming traditional statistical approaches with high accuracy and identifying key predictors of treatment response [17].

## B. XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting)

XGBoost  is  a  powerful machine  learning algorithm commonly used for hand gesture classification tasks. Research studies have shown that XGBoost, along with other classifiers like  Random  Forest,  Support  Vector  Machine  (SVM),  and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), has been implemented  successfully  in  classifying  hand  gestures  with high  accuracy  [18].  XGBoost  has  demonstrated  impressive accuracy rates, with studies reporting values close to 97% in hand  gesture  recognition  tasks,  making  it  a  popular  choice among  researchers  for  its  efficiency  and  effectiveness  in classification tasks [19].

## C. Deep Neural Network (DNN)

Deep neural network (DNN) classifiers differentiate hand gestures by leveraging advanced techniques such as automatic feature extraction and deep learning models. Various studies have shown the effectiveness of DNNs, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs)  and  multistream fusion 1-D CNNs, in accurately classifying hand gestures [20] [21]  [22]  [23].  These  models  excel  in  capturing  intricate details  like  hand  shape,  motion  profiles,  and  positioning, crucial for accurate gesture identification [23].

## D. Modality And Articulations

A unimodal approach was used, as the system in question utilizes images captured by the camera as input and attempts to  comprehend  sign  language  by  processing  hand  gestures within  these  images. In  this  context,  the  user  is  required  to perform the following tasks:

- Hand Gestures and Signs: The user will be required to perform hand gestures in order to create certain signs.
- Finger Positions: The position of the fingers and the hand  as  a  whole  can  be  used  to  determine  the meaning of a sign.
- Hand Coordination: The coordination of hand movements  is  of  significant  importance  for  the accurate transmission of signs.

## E. Dataset

A machine learning model was developed specifically to identify the letters of the American Sign Language alphabet. A  dataset  of  2600  2D  images  was  built,  consisting  of  100 images  with  1280x720  resolution  and  16:9  aspect  ratio  for each letter of ASL alphabet (i.e., 26 letters). In addition, there are 21 landmarks for each hand image as shown in 'Fig. 2'. The  data  collection  process  was  carried  out  through  the camera  over  the  indices  allocated  for  each  class  and  this process  was  repeated  for  each  class.  Hand  gestures  were identified,  coordinates  extracted  and  normalized  from  hand images using the MediaPipe hands module. These data and labels were saved in a pickle file for use in training machine learning models.

Fig. 2. The analytical localization of 21 hand landmarks.



## F. Development Approach and Tools

American Sign Language (ASL) hand gestures are identified  using  MediaPipe  technology  with  Decision  Tree and Deep Neural Network (DNN) classifiers. Previous studies have shown that the MediaPipe technology achieves very high accuracy rates in recognising ASL hand gestures, and that the feature  extraction  process  performed  on  this  data  yields successful  results  [24][25].   Additionally,  in  the  context  of virtual  reality  technology,  Mediapipe,  in  conjunction  with OpenCV, is employed for real-time hand gesture recognition, enabling efficient human-computer  interaction  in virtual environments.  A  multilayer  network  is  trained  on  the  hand sign  data  using  the  DNN  method,  which  models  complex patterns through non-linear relationships, employing activation  functions  like  ReLU  to  capture  intricate  data patterns. ReLU enhances the expressivity of neural networks, allowing them to approximate any continuous function with high  precision  when  the  network  is  wide  enough  [27]. MediaPipe also  assists  in  the  identification  and  tracking  of hand  gestures,  extracting  key  landmarks  that  are  used  for training both classifiers. This dual-method approach utilizes the simplicity of decision trees and the  deep learning capabilities of DNNs, enhancing robustness in hand gesture recognition.

## G. System Design

System design is a process that defines how the components in an often-complex engineering project will fit together and how they will work together [28]. This includes the  process  of  specifying  the  functions  and  performance designed  to  meet  the  requirements  of  a  product,  system  or process [28].

The study is based on users initiating the process to detect sign  language  gestures  through  their  cameras.  The  images captured by the camera are subjected to direct analysis by a pre-trained model, which is then used to recognize specific sign language gestures. Based on the outcome of the analysis, the model determines whether the gesture has been correctly identified. Whenever  a  sign  is recognized, the  system displays  the  translation  result  to  the  user.  This  process  is performed using advanced object detection and classification algorithms as MediaPipe and deep learning models.

The  Sign  Language  Recognition  System  incorporates integration with the camera device, enabling users to log in and  manage  their  user  account  with  a  range  of  functions shown in Figure 3. This integrated system facilitates communication for individuals with hearing impairments by effectively performing sign language recognition and translation.

Fig. 3. Use case diagram



Fig. 4. System architecture



## H. Interface

The SynapSign application, which was developed as part of the project, was designed to facilitate the demonstration of letters in sign language. Upon initial use of the app, users are prompted to grant access to the camera. Once permission has been granted, the application login screen appears, as shown in Figure 5. The camera is then activated and users can point their  hands  at  the  camera  to  display  the  letters  in  sign language. The application will display the letter corresponding to the character shown, and these letters will continue to appear as text on the screen until the application is closed or the Clear button is pressed, as shown in Figure 6

## III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

## A. Results

The Random Forest model exhibited the highest performance, with a recall of 0.997, an accuracy of 0.996, a precision of 0.993. In contrast, the XGBoost model exhibited slightly lower values, achieving 0.993 recall, 0.992 accuracy, 0.985  precision.  In  contrast,  the  DNN  model  exhibited  a comparatively inferior performance, achieving a recall rate of 0.974, an accuracy rate of 0.984, a precision rate of 0.986. The results demonstrate that the Random Forest model is the most effective  model,  exhibiting  particularly  high  accuracy  and recall rates.

Fig. 7. Results graph



## B. Discussion

It is conceivable that the project could be further expanded by incorporating additional sign languages in the future. Furthermore, augmenting the dataset with images of individuals  representing  diverse  demographic  groups  will enhance  the  model's  precision.  In  subsequent  stages,  in addition to the letters presented in fixed images, the detection of letters formed as a result of movement (e.g., the letters "j" and "z") and phrases will also be incorporated, allowing the project  to  advance.  Subsequently,  the  desktop  application developed for the project can be enhanced to enhance its userfriendliness and compatibility with different platforms.

The study evaluated the performance of Random Forest, XGBoost  and  Deep  Neural  Network  (DNN)  models  using Precision, Recall and Accuracy metrics. The Random Forest model showed the highest performance with 99.3% Precision, 99.7% Recall and 99.6% Accuracy. These results show  that  Random  Forest  provides  high  accuracy  and reliability,  but  previous studies have  not  achieved  this performance with results such as 77.94% in [29], 87.1% in [30], and 96.3% in [31]. The XGBoost model provides 98.5% Precision, 99.3% Recall and 99.2% Accuracy, providing high Recall  and  high  Accuracy,  but  slightly  behind  Random Forest.

The  DNN  model  performed  the  lowest  with  97.4% Precision,  98.6%  Recall  and  98.4%  Accuracy.  This  result shows  that  although  DNN  has  high  Recall,  it  lags  behind Random  Forest  and  XGBoost  in  Precision.  Comparisons show that Random Forest is the most effective model in this context  and  XGBoost offers  a  competitive  alternative.  The lower Precision of DNN  may  be  limiting for certain applications.

|--------------------|-------------|----------|------------|
| Random Forest      | 99.3%       | 99.7%    | 99.6%      |
| XGBoost            | 98.5%       | 99.3%    | 99.2%      |

| Decision Tree [30] | 87.2%       | 87.1%    | 87.1%      |
| Random Forest [31] | 96%         | 96%      | 96.3%      |

In  this  study,  the  performance  of  different  machine learning models was evaluated with metrics including accuracy, precision and recall. Nevertheless, these performance  metrics  may  not  be  sufficient for a final prototype. Particularly in real-time applications, it is necessary to  consider  the  response  time  of  the  models  and decide  which  model  is  more  appropriate  to  implement. Therefore,  in  future  studies,  it  is  crucial  to  examine  the response  time  in  model  selection  and  include  it  in  the decision-making process.

## IV. CONCLUSION

To observe the development and effectiveness of SynapSign,  a  desktop  application  designed  to  aid  in  the learning and practice of American Sign Language (ASL). The application  employs  machine  learning  models,  including Random Forest, XGBoost, and DNN, to effectively recognize American Sign Language (ASL) hand gestures and provide users with an interactive and educational platform. In particular, the Random Forest model showed higher performance  in  terms  of  recall,  accuracy  and  precision.  In addition, it was also more accurate in practical use with the camera. Future enhancements to the application, including the incorporation of dynamic sign recognition and the expansion of the dataset, will enhance  its efficacy and usability. SynapSign has the potential to facilitate improved communication, reduce feelings of isolation, and enhance the quality of life of individuals with hearing impairments.

## Paper Source: Synergistic integration between internet of things and augmented reality technologies for deaf persons in e-learning platform
