## Synergistic integration between internet of things and augmented reality technologies for deaf persons in e-learning platform



Malek Alrashidi 1

Accepted: 11 November 2022 / Published online: 23 November 2022 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2022

## Abstract

The development of the Internet of Things (IoT) accentuates the interweaving of the digital  with  the  physical,  raising  multiple  issues,  including  for  learning  and  more specifically  for  the  learning  of  the  deaf.  While  emerging  technologies  may  have given rise to various methods and modes of learning, the implications of the IoT for deaf learning are not yet understood. This study aims to propose the possible integration of the IoT and augmented reality (AR) to support deaf learning from three dimensions of analysis: data, interfaces and pervasiveness. The axes of applications identified suggest that the IoT promotes learning characterized by experimentation, adaptation (to the context and to the learner), the manipulation of objects and exploration without the constraints of time or space. In order to achieve this integration, preliminary survey is collected from deaf learners. Based on the results, a deaf intelligent learning model is proposed and discussed.

Keywords Augmented reality · Communication · Deaf learners · E-learning · Emerging technology · Internet of things

## 1  Introduction

The availability of online learning resources has enabled deaf and hard of hearing (HH) students to access lectures  [1,  2].  E-learning  is  a  revolutionary  way  to  prevent disability discrimination, as previously most disabled people in the community were unable to follow their education. However, for several reasons, online learning is not the preferred option for many deaf and HH people. Indeed, a person who grew up having sign language as the main means of communication can have difficulty understanding the concepts described in an academic text, for example. Simply viewing this type of text on a computer screen is not of much interest unless a qualified interpreter is present to assist the student in the library, at home or remotely. Likewise, videos with automatic captions can facilitate communication. However, in reality, the captioning may be out of synchronization with the topic being discussed in the video. It is essential that tutors encourage feedback on the effectiveness of the material made available online. A deaf or HH person who faces countless obstacles in their personal progress may feel fundamentally discouraged. Deaf and HH learners may also prefer learning in interactive groups and having note-taking interpretation and assistance because they are able to use visual clues by observing the faces and expressions of other learners and tutors. Such holistic learning can be an integral part of the process of building meaning and understanding beyond words. Of course, online learning does not exclude the possibility of group meetings, face to face. It is also very important to avoid stereotypes about deaf and HH learners. Indeed, deaf learners  are  far  from  constituting  a  homogeneous  group  whose  members  all  have identical needs. On the contrary, any set of support measures made available to them must be tailored to individual needs and preferences.

* Malek Alrashidi mqalrashidi@ut.edu.sa

1 Department of Computer Science, Applied College, University of Tabuk, Tabuk, Saudi Arabia





Deaf learning concerns the process of teaching deaf people with deafness or hearing loss. The latter does not only require adapted educational techniques on the individual and group level, but also needs a specific material and environment allowing the deaf learners to independently assimilate the educational content to allow them to have the same learning level of non-deaf students.

For this, education systems for the deaf should involve IoT and AR technologies to  achieve  the  needs  and  services  necessary  for  deaf  students  and  their  educators without having to resort to voice interpreters, visual cues or note takers.

In addition to the functionalities offered by the IoT and AR equipment, the latter must also positively influence the degree of engagement of deaf students in the lectures by minimizing the auditory and visual distraction of the deaf students and also their agitation or movement in the room.

The needs of deaf students mainly concern their levels of engagement in school activities. This includes their participation in the discussions, their ability to follow the teacher's instructions, and their degree of concentration and accomplishment of school tasks.

The Internet has become an essential communication tool for deaf people. It has far greater importance than the telephone for hearing people. The webcam promotes an authentic exchange, linked to emotions. The expression of emotions is visually received by the interlocutor in the same way as the intonation of the voice informs about feelings. The use of webcams allows a rich exchange, since a real dialogue takes place through an interposed camera. The number of connected objects is growing, and its uses are multiplying, including smartphones, tablets, connected watches and bracelets, and tactile and interactive tables [3]. These connected objects are the main players in the Internet of Things (IoT). The development of the IoT tends to tie technology more deeply with the environment. Through everyday objects, technology supports individuals at every moment and in every action, especially regarding the learning of deaf persons.

Indeed,  the  IoT  can  be  an  excellent  medium  for  the  social  integration  of  deaf people. Easy access to information and communication are the two most important reasons for their use of the Internet. For them, the Internet represents accessibility, autonomy and personal development. This explains the appropriation of the Internet by  deaf  persons  as  a  tool  to  support  communication,  training  and  empowerment. Our study leads us to conclude that the 'deaf' uses of the IoT-in terms of access to information related to deaf identity, communication and training-allow deaf people to assert their identity as a group for better integration into society.



It  is  first  and  foremost  by  promoting  relations  with  the  hearing  world  that  the Internet and the IoT play a role in the social integration of deaf people. Indeed, the Internet  and  the  IoT  help  deaf  persons  to  understand  the  hearing  world.  As  mentioned earlier, the use of the Internet offers deaf people fertile ground for communication with hearing people. If we believe that social integration involves being able to  understand  and  be  understood  and  that  the  handicap  of  deafness  is  linked  to  a mode of communication different from the majority, we can conclude that Internet mediation promotes deaf users' social integration by allowing easier access to the hearing world and a better understanding of the hearing society.

Additionally, another technology seems to be very promising when used for deaf learning is augmented reality (AR). AR is the superimposition of reality and other media elements (sounds, 2D and 3D images, videos, etc.) [4,  5] calculated by a computer system in real time. It often refers to the different methods that allow the realistic  embedding  of  virtual  objects  in  a  sequence  of  images.  It  also  applies  to visual  perception (the superimposition of virtual images to real ones) and to proprioceptive perceptions, such as tactile or auditory perceptions. These applications are multiple and affect more and more numerous fields, such as video games, education, cinema, industries (conception, design, maintenance, assembly, piloting, robotics, etc.) and medical fields. AR is one of the emerging phenomena enabled by the development and democratization of information and communication technologies (ICT). It is involved in certain augmented forms of collaborative work and the collaborative economy. AR inserts synthetic images into real-world images using a cell phone camera or specific video glasses. Small cameras located in the middle and outside  each  lens  send  continuous  video  images  to  two  liquid  crystal  displays  on the inside of the glasses via a mobile processor. When connected to a smartphone or computer, the glasses combine computer data with live filmed reality, creating a unique stereoscopic field of view on the LCD screen, where synthetic images overlap with those of the real world. The use of AR in deaf learning will be discussed later in the paper.

A major question that our study tries to answer is: can IoT be used with AR to solve learning challenges?

Indeed,  AR  is  an  emerging  technique,  qualified  as  the  technology  allowing to better use the potential of the IoT. AR takes advantage of data issued from the IoT infrastructure to facilitate the visualization of the real context. Therefore, IoTAR deployment strategies  must  be  developed  by  companies  to  take  advantage  of both  technologies.  Moreover,  IoT  facilitates  connecting  virtual  and  physical  contexts. Indeed, data are gathered from IoT objects, transformed into information and instantly integrated into the AR application to augment the real context.

Another major question of this study is the interest of AR-IoT models in context of learning. In this regard, due to rapid social changes, education is a field that is rapidly evolving. IoT with AR enables revolutionary progress in education processes aligned with the new demands of society, teachers and learners.



Therefore, the IoT uses the physical objects in the educational environment to establish  a  more  efficient  learning  process.  This  allows  an  effective  synergy  between  the digital  and  physical  environment,  which  facilitates  the  understanding  of  educational situations  by  students  and  facilitates  group  learning.  Using  IoT,  students  can  collect information about homework completion time, feelings, and degree of satisfaction of students.  This  helps  teachers  to  measure  their  methodologies  and  personalize  their interventions to solve students' difficulties.

Another educational issue can be easily solved by IoT-AR synergy. It concerns the visualization  of  pedagogical  learning  situations  that  become  realizable  and  rapidly understandable using AR which brings life to IoT data. On the other side, the IoT feeds the AR augmented scenes in real time. This creates a visual and intelligent learning environment that allows an interactive learner participation.

The research questions considered in this study in relation to the use of the IoT and AR in deaf learning are as follows:

- What are the appropriation modes for promoting deaf people's communications and social integration?
- How do deaf people use the IoT and AR in practice?
- What role does deaf identity play in the social construction of the uses of the IoT and AR?
- What place does the use of the IoT and AR take in the daily communication practices of deaf users, and what are its consequences on their integration into society?

The objectives of the research are as follows:

- Draw up a portrait of the uses of the Internet and IoT devices by deaf people to understand their contribution to deaf learning.
- Analyze how the daily context of the use of the IoT and AR affects the construction and nature of the social connections of deaf persons.
- Understand  how  these  uses  transform  the  way  deaf  people  communicate  on  a daily basis and, more generally, the way they integrate into society.

The rest of the paper contains the following sections: Section. 2 presents a literature review. Section 3 illustrates the IoT methodology used for deaf learning. Section  4  presents  the  numerical  results,  and  Section  5  provides  a  discussion.  Then, Section. 3.3 describes the suggested deaf intelligent learning model. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper.

## 2    Literature review

Deafness represents the incapacity of an individual to  hear  and  recognize  voices. The vast majority of HH persons are additionally discourse-disabled, and they utilize gesture-based communication (sign language) as the primary method of interacting with others [5]. Communication through signing utilizes hand gestures, looks, lip examples and non-verbal communication rather than sound ones. Like communication with dialects, gesture-based communications differ among nations, which have their own jargon and sentence structures [6].



An advanced education for HH people is a main aspect in every country's schooling improvement. HH understudies in advanced education are a source of information about the boundaries these learners face in getting content from lectures. A deep exploration should be achieved about the adequacy of help administrations-such as deciphering, notes composing, examining and understanding courses-which affect their scholarly accomplishment [7]. E-learning is a valuable method used for educational reasons. It incorporates schooling for HH learners.

One  of  the  main  significant  effects  of  technological  advancement  has  been achieved in schooling and learning domains by the invention of e-learning, which is extremely advantageous for individuals in various demographical areas who cannot proceed with formal classic education [8]. E-learning frameworks help HH individuals to communicate with hearing individuals. However, the majority of existing e-learning platforms are not easily accessible and helpful for HH learners in light of their components and content, which are not adequate for HH learners. These learners frequently experience issues in getting access to the data and using it appropriately [9].

Actually,  e-learning  provides  new  possibilities  for  ICT  in  training  by  utilizing numerous multimedia types, such as images, video and sounds. E-learning can be achieved inside or outside lecture halls [10]. All categories of persons in the community may benefit from the e-learning advantages, including incapacitated individuals [11].

Indeed,  specialists  have  utilized  new  technologies  like  AR  to  help  HH  people in various fields, such as medical care and education. In [12] introduced a virtual reality (VR) homeroom called 'DAVEE.' It helps HH people to pose inquiries and receive answers in each virtual class. Likewise, they can communicate with other learners in this virtual class and record it for asynchronous learning. The outcome of the AR experience showed the impacts of utilizing AR to develop HH learners' correspondences in the class. In [13] fostered a framework for deciphering discourse, changing it to text and showing it as captions in an AR environment. This framework helps HH people go to live theaters and comprehend the exchanges. In light of their outcomes, more HH people want to take care of and appreciate live sessions by utilizing their framework. In [14] utilized AR to further develop enlistment abilities among HH children. They showed that AR can help HH children to better master school abilities. Additionally, this platform is useful for HH people's future relations and communications with society. Researchers have shown that haptic and wearable gadgets are exceptionally valuable for HH people, particularly in the field of sound awareness.

Researchers in [15, 16, 17, 18 and 19] showed that we can utilize clever earworn gadgets to move material data on the two ears. Likewise, in [18] and [19] planned  and  assessed  a  head-mounted  material  model  and  a  vibro-tactile  AR device to help situational and spatial awareness among persons. However, none of  these  specialists  tried  their  gadgets  on  deaf  or  HH  people.  In  [20]  assessed representations for spatially finding sound on AR devices and giving consciousness  of  natural  sound  on  visual  presentations  to  HH  people.  They  showed  that people with hearing issues utilize obvious signs to perceive and recognize sounds. In [21], an online review is led to examine inclination for versatile and wearable sound  mindfulness  frameworks  among  HH  members.  They  showed  that  practically all members needed both visual and haptic input gadgets. In [22], authors planned  a  cell  phone-based  acoustic  detecting  and  warning  framework  called 'UbiEar'  and  showed  that  this  framework  can  help  HH  learners  to  familiarize themselves with significant acoustic events in their everyday lives.



Some other analysts utilized a haptic input framework to instigate the sensation of tap moving to HH people [23]. They showed that HH people who utilized their framework had a totally different sensation of tap moving and delighted in it, regardless of whether they could hear the sound. In [24] created a framework for HH people called 'MuSS-Bits,' which helps them feel instruments of sounds on their skin utilizing haptic criticism. Another research designed an exceptional gauntlet  for  HH  people  that  can  decipher  gesture-based  communication  to  discourse.  It  further  develops  HH  people's  interchanges  and  collaborations  in  AR conditions [25]. There are numerous cases, for example, LIVEJACKET [26], that showed the impacts of utilizing haptic criticism gadgets for HH people.

The  study  in  [27]  provides  an  educational  environment  for  teaching  the  IoT security. The study presents a set of data in the form of an IoT security database. A  real  prototyping  is  achieved  on  an  online  educational  system  based  on  AR. However, during the prototyping, certain assumptions were not considered, such as taking into account the functional components of the used system. Moreover, there is no prototyping results.

The study in [28] focuses on the contribution of the IoT and AR in the construction of intelligent learning involving a set of complex communications using devices  such  as  smartphones,  watches  and  glasses.  However,  the  investigated studies were not criticized and discussed.

In  [29],  a  smart  augmented  reality  concept  is  introduced  in  mobile  phones to  enhance  the  learning  process  in  which  students  follow  augmented  3D  models  established  by  the  teacher.  It  is  shown  by  experiments  that  the  subjects  are explained  by  3D  AR  models  better  than  classical  teaching  methods.  Moreover, the proposed system is easily deployable in android devices and supports the recognition of multiple targets. On the other hand, this AR system must be combined by AI to obtain smarter automated applications.

Authors in [30] introduces an intelligent learning system based on game theory technique. This game model uses and integrates mobile IoT, AR and web techniques  in  the  context  of  e-learning.  By  interacting  in  the  intelligent  classroom, this system determines the interests, impressions and degree of motivation of the learners. To assess the knowledge of students, this system offers an IoT course on Moodle in the University of Belgrade. Unfortunately, the size of the sample of evaluation is limited. Moreover, this learning system does not offer a module that personalizes the learning process and does not integrate student participations in the configuration and development of the courses.



The study in [31] suggests a mobile AR system to learn telugu language. This system uses the smartphone's camera to identify external objects and then augments the real images with virtual information to facilitate the language learning. A set of sampling tests were achieved to assess the efficiency of the system in the learning of language. On the other hand, the efficiency of the proposed system must be verified with higher number of users.

Authors in [32] suggest an IoT-AR-based technologies prototyping to enhance the learning process of student having learning problems. Unfortunately, this prototype is not experimentally tested on a real classroom. Moreover, a questionnaire on a set of undergraduate students can be achieved as a quantitative analysis.

Another study in [33] proposes the integration of AR and IoT for the learning of students. A set of 90 learners divided in two groups were used in experiments of 120 min. The findings of the study illustrate the improvement of the knowledge about the air pollution. Moreover, by comparing the degree of satisfaction of two groups of students; a first group using VR and a second one using the IoT; it was noticed that there is no difference in the level of satisfaction of the two groups.

Recently, utilizing various sorts of wearable gadgets in AR has become exceptionally normal. Unfortunately, most of these gadgets are intended for people with no hearing issues. Moreover, there is no thorough examination of the convenience of these gadgets for HH people. The significant point in the majority of these cases is that HH people can utilize them; however, they cannot appreciate them like people without hearing issues.

AR  and  IoT  learning  Media  is  a  relevant  component  which  is  necessary  to enhance of the learning quality. In this context, numerous studies suggest to design and use AR learning media to address the students learning issues:

In [34], a AR learning media based on elementary mathematics is used as a learning medium to learn geometry in elementary schools. This study deduces that AR learning media helps teachers to increase the motivation and enthusiasm of students in  the  learning  process.  Moreover,  the  AR  media  allows  the  learning  outside  the school.

The study in [35] suggests an android platform for geometry learning using AR media.  The  proposed  system  was  designed  to  teach  three-dimensional  objects  for high school students. The aims of the study were to evaluate the efficiency of the way  the  student  uses  the  AR  media,  and  to  the  degree  of  comprehension  of  the geometry concepts. The findings of this study illustrates that the use of the proposed android-based AR learning media enhances the positive responses of the students and the learning of the three-dimensional geometrical concepts.

Another study in [36] introduces a development of an AR learning media for the learning of electricity related concepts. The study suggests the preliminarily results using a single pretest-posttest group of thirty learners from the first-year classes in a high school in Garut. The experimental process reveals that the proposed AR learning media improves the understanding of students.

In  [37],  the  authors  introduce  a  design  of  a  smartphone  and  AR-based  learning  media  to  increase  the  autonomy  of  the  students  during  the  learning  process. The  used  mobile  media  involves  android  smartphones,  tablets  and  cameras  features to run AR technology. To measure the efficiency of the used media, a set of questionnaires were proposed to learners and teachers. The results shows that the use of AR learning media rises the user's learning autonomy.

In most of these studies, a unique AR context or gadget should be intended for HH people. AR engineers should utilize captions, images, interpreters, features, and so forth in the AR environment to make it usable for HH people. In actual systems, HH people cannot utilize AR applications that are intended for people without hearing issues. Contrary to other studies investigated in this section, our study is based on experimental real data issued from a case of study and a survey. It also suggests a hybrid IoT and AR intelligent E-learning environment.

## 3    The internet of things and augmented reality methodology for deaf learning

## 3.1    The internet of things for deaf persons

The IoT represents a 'network of networks' of connected objects, identifiable in a unified way so that we can act on them or know their state [38, 39]. It designates various technical solutions (RFID, TCP/IP, mobile technologies, etc.) whose role is to identify objects, capture, store, process and transfer data in physical environments and between physical and virtual environments. The major challenge is not to invent new technologies but simply to adapt already existing ones in order to connect and integrate  them.  Connected objects are equipped with sensors to measure environmental parameters and exchange the data generated between objects. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this data ultimately travels to service platforms for storage and analysis. Figure 2 illustrates the proposed AIoT architecture.

The IoT can be easily used in different types of applications. For example, sensors in lamps can be used to make buildings smarter. Moreover, the IoT allows easier  control  of  the  mobility  of  objects.  Through  the  use  of  control  chips,  actuators and motors are integrated into the same design. As these IoT components are integrated into a common environment, there are some challenges regarding communication interfaces, noise levels and power consumption. We must therefore investigate the possible articulations of the IoT and connected objects to better support learning through the IoT. There are three dimensions of analysis: data, interfaces and pervasiveness.

Fig. 1 Illustration of the IoT concepts





Fig. 2 Proposed AIoT architecture



Data :  The  functions  of  connected  objects  are  based  on  data  corresponding  to environmental parameters collected through sensors.

Interfaces :  Human-machine  interfaces  tend  to  bring  together  the  methods  of controlling and entering information with its representation: interfaces define how humans interact with connected objects.

Pervasiveness : The growing entanglement of digital and physical environments tends  to  give  ICT  a  ubiquitous  character:  objects  exchange  with  each  other  and with humans having access to information and digital tools without time and space constraints.

## 3.2    Augmented reality and the internet of things for deaf persons

The hybrid IoT-AR model can be justified as follows: The advantages of using IoT in e-learning can be summarized as follows: it automates most of the teaching tasks and subsequently it reduces costs, it allows the improvement of learners' productivity. Besides, the IoT optimizes the use of educational resources and anticipates the needs of students by obtaining information from the educational context. This information allows the rapid identification of problems of students.

On the other hand, the use of AR in e-learning has several advantages which can be summarized as follows: AR promotes communication and student engagement for a more optimized experience. Moreover, in learning as in business, AR increases the responsiveness, visualization, and implementation of services by increasing the knowledge of users that should be often personalized. This enhances the user experience and subsequently makes learning easier and more comfortable.



AR is an innovation with huge promise. It is arising as the key that will open the maximum capacity of the IoT. AR applications are utilizing the numerous types of information created by IoT gadgets and segments to assist IoT workers to be more efficient.

Indeed, AR offers a helpful and natural way for clients to imagine and collaborate with IoT objects and their related information. Besides, AR services are made conceivable by utilizing and taking advantage of the more refined data context offered by IoT devices.

AR and the IoT have received huge consideration as a key to empowering innovations for making educational environments more intelligent and intuitive. AR is a kind of intuitive medium that gives a perspective to reality in an increased space by spatially enlisting valuable produced data to assist individuals in understanding the world and intensifying their insight for tackling issues. The IoT represents a set of connected gadgets and devices installed with minimum processing components for detecting and gathering data and communicating.

## 3.3    Proposed intelligent learning model

The intelligent learning model that we propose in this study is based on the IoT by treating the three dimensions of analysis (data, interfaces and pervasiveness). The interweaving of the digital with the physical environment operated by the IoT also promotes the  implementation  of  authentic  situations  where  the  object  of  learning is  contextualized.  Learning,  in  which  knowledge  is  constructed,  is  important  on the real and social levels. On the other hand, the use of IoT objects for educational objectives has been theorized in several studies agreeing on three points: the need to learn by experience, the need to be active, and the model of interactions between learning objects and people [40].

The IoT data help to better understand the learner. Connected objects and their tangible interfaces interact with the environment and provide the ability to control learners.  The  pervasiveness  of  the  IoT  reduces  the  constraints  of  time,  space  and support.

The reduction in component costs and their miniaturization combined with the concreteness of the data allow the use of connected objects to understand the learning  environment.  Using  the  sensors  of  connected  objects  (GSM,  tablet,  etc.)  and self-assembly component kits (Arduino, Raspberry, etc.), learners have accessible measurement tools to contextualize the learning.

The data generated by connected objects provides information about the activities and movements of the learner, allowing monitoring beyond digital training devices. This information is related to activities of informal learning: reading a book on an online library using the IoT, watching a documentary or attending a conference. The learning and training systems can refine their models and improve the monitoring process.



The design process of each phase in the proposed AIoT-based learning system is represented by Fig. 3.

To overcome the challenges that deaf students face (as discussed above), the deaf intelligent learning model is proposed. The aim of this model is to enrich deaf learners  with  meaningful  learning  that  is  extracted  from  learning  objects  and  achieve effective  communication between deaf learners and teachers. Meaningful learning is described as a means to increase students' knowledge regarding learning objects by using visual and auditory resources [41]. The suggested model, which is based on the IoT network, consists of the following phases, as shown in Fig. 4:

## · Phase 1: Speech recognition

The speech acquired from the teacher is recognized and converted to text using a speech recognition system to facilitate the next phase. The suggested speech recognition system relies on an intelligent algorithm that recognizes spoken vocabulary items. This algorithm uses the speech audio signal to identify the acoustic indices. Then, it computes the probability of the index string being caused by a particular hypothesized utterance element.

## · Phase 2: Text summarization

One of the aforementioned challenges is the difficulty of understanding long texts due to the low working memory limit of deaf students. This problem can be solved by applying the technique of text summarization, which helps in producing a summary of the input text that contains the main idea. This phase relies on a process that collects the relevant information from the text to construct a reduced version of the text. In this process, the words are not reformulated; they are selected and rearranged to build a new shorter structure of the text.



Fig. 3 Functionalities proposed in the suggested AIoT (AR + IoT) learning system



Fig. 4 Deaf intelligent learning model based on augmented reality and the internet of things



## · Phase 3: Augmented reality content creation

The AR content creation phase is responsible for creating virtual elements that are related to the summarized text from the cloud server. This phase relies on collecting multimedia elements from different sources (from the cloud) in relation to the summarized text. The text is analyzed, and relevant keywords are extracted to be used in the search.

## · Phase 4: Augmented reality scene

The AR scene phase is responsible for visualizing the created VR elements on the  wearable VR glasses. This phase is based on the use of AR hardware, which transforms the VR elements into an AR scene. Image classification algorithms can be incorporated into the phases of the suggested deaf intelligent learning model to enhance its accuracy and efficiency.

Indeed,  connected  objects  are  accompanied  by  new  human-machine  interfaces that can be used in learning to control activities promoting bodily engagement and interaction  with  the  environment.  Among  the  human-machine  interfaces  of  connected objects, we can distinguish tangible user interfaces (TUI) and surface user interfaces  (SUI).  With  TUIs,  information  takes  the  form  of  a  tangible  object  that the user can manipulate. A robot for learning programming without code and without screen is an example of a TUI. By ordering parts corresponding to instructions (forward, backward, etc.), it is possible to program and direct the robot. SUIs refer to the interfaces of interactive tablets and whiteboards: it is a screen or a projection, horizontal  or  vertical  [39].  The  use  of  sensors,  virtual  or  AR,  and  ambient  interfaces add an interactive layer to the environment and improve the learning process. LEDs indicating the ON / OFF position of electronic devices and the use of radio frequency identification (RFID) and near field communication (NFC) tags are examples  of  IoT  objects  [42].  Due  to  the  pervasiveness  of  connected  objects,  learning and control activities are part of mobility. The learning and control experience persists through the supports used by the learner, and the context is taken into account by training  systems.  Improving  the  performance  of  connected  objects  (computing power, bandwidth, battery, etc.) makes training devices and educational resources accessible and usable on mobile devices, since mobility is becoming an aspect of online learning.



These  conditions  encourage  new  practices,  such  as  micro-learning  and  'Bring Your Own Device.' Micro-learning refers to the distribution of a course on a mobile device in the form of several short units. For education, it is good practice to invite students to use their personal devices rather than those of the institution [43].

## 4    Results

## 4.1    Data collection

We envisioned the data collection in two stages. The first step involved the technique of logbooks that our participants had to fill out. The information collected in these logbooks was intended to provide an initial portrait of the Internet use by deaf people and to better define the questions proposed to the participants. The second stage of data collection involved semi-structured interviews with the same participants.

## 4.1.1    Survey

The  questionnaire  method  seems  to  be  more  judicious  in  obtaining  information about the use of the Internet by deaf persons. Considering that culturally deaf people are very direct, more precise answer choices involving fewer personal data seem more appropriate. The questionnaire (Appendix I) asks participants for information about their type of use and frequencies of use of IoT and AR devices. We decided not to ask for precise information about the visited sites, but rather we distinguished between different types of use that we presented in several categories. These types of use concern the search for information, viewing of videos, frequentation of social networks,  communication,  entertainment,  training,  viewing  news  sites,  viewing deafness sites, and viewing utility and commerce sites. For each of these categories, participants were asked to rate their frequency of use (daily, several times a week, once a week, rarely or never) and their average durations of use. We believe that this tool was more culturally appropriate for our participants than the logbook, for which we  only  had  one  feedback.  Of  course,  several  participants  did  not  complete  the questionnaire. We followed up twice with the participants but did not want to insist, as  their  participation  in  this  research  was  voluntary,  and  they  were  not  forced  to respond. It should also be noted that we received the questionnaires after conducting the interviews, whereas we would have liked to receive them before to be able to better identify the user profiles prior to the interviews. At the end, the questionnaires received provided us with valuable information that seems consistent with what was said in the interviews.



## 4.1.2    Selection of respondents

The participants in our research were recruited using the so-called snowball method [44]. This method consists of identifying a first person who meets our selection criteria and who agrees to participate in our research. This person is asked to recommend another close person who also meets these selection criteria and who is likely to contribute to our research. Ideally, this second participant will in turn recommend someone close to them and so on. One advantage of this recruitment technique is that  it  speeds  up  the  selection  process,  which  could  otherwise  be  quite  lengthy. Three criteria for selecting participants guided the recruitment. Firstly, the participants  had  to  have  a  sufficient  level  of  literacy  to  be  able  to  use  the  Internet  in  a general way and to express themselves in writing. The second criterion implied a certain mastery of the daily use of the Internet. Finally, all participants had to be over 18 for ethical reasons.

## 4.2    Data analysis

The objective  of  the  analysis  of  the  completed  questionnaires  was  to  identify  the user 'patterns' based on the frequencies and types of use of the participants. This descriptive  information  supplemented  the  information  gathered  during  the  interviews. The analysis of the interviews aimed to grasp the meanings of uses related to these patterns and to identify the place of the Internet in the daily communication practices of the participants.

The first step of analysis was the transcription of the data. This step allows us to appropriate the content in order to codify and analyze it. The transcription stage allowed  us  to  do  a  pre-analysis,  which  revealed  the  recurring  response  elements both  within  the  same  interview  and  between  interviews.  Following  the  transcription of the interviews, we proceeded to the second step, which consisted of an indepth read of the content, line by line. At the same time, we created summary sheets specific to each interview. The summary sheet allowed the researcher to summarize the addressed themes and identify the important elements and particularities of the participants.

The third step consisted of coding the transcripts to determine the main categories  of  learning  in  the  collected  data  and  highlight  those  that  were  recurrent.  The coding was conducted by analysis aid software, and then we analyzed each interview first individually, then using a cross-sectional analysis of all the interviews to identify the similarities and disparities among the participants.

The  results  of  the  application  of  the  survey  to  126  participants  are  shown  in Table 1 and the figures below.

The results (Figs. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) showed that the attentional capacities of deaf people  can  undoubtedly  be  redirected  by  visual  periphery  distractors  due  to  their hearing problems. Online modules through a reasonable course with interactive content could help deaf persons in the learning process. Besides, most deaf people give signs of a low working memory limit due to motion-based communications. Thus, learning  modules should not be incredibly long, and an effort should be made to isolate the learning content into short modules, which can be more easily followed by the learners. Deaf people seem to imagine that understanding texts is a challenging task due to partitions in their working memory and the absence of hear-capable information. The latter is the central driver of their veritable difficulties in text creation. Therefore, the presentation of the learning modules is a fundamental step for improving the educational outcomes for deaf persons.

The results have shown that course information and content should be presented in a visual way for nearly deaf and hearing weakened learners using pictures, chronicles with subtitles and, clearly, correspondence by means of signal accounts, as they can  deal  with  pictures  and  chronicles  more  significantly  than  words.  Hence,  it  is apparent that the informative material should similarly be given in correspondence through motions chronicles, as this is the best strategy to help deaf persons in the learning process.

Regarding evaluation strategies, HH persons had positive viewpoints toward the presence of exercises after an online course to complete their adjusting needs. Given this, an e-learning system should provide an electronic examination system, considering certain completion principles for self-appraisal.

In this section, we use regression to test the first two hypotheses H1 and H2 and study the relationship between pairs of the model. The value of α is set to 0.05. Table 5 summarizes the regression results.

Since the p -values are lower than α for the dependence DU-DS and DF-DS, then  the  dependence  is  confirmed  between  the  degree  of  understanding  and degree of satisfaction; and between difficulty of use and degree of satisfaction.

However, since the p-values are higher than α for the dependence DP-DS, then there is no dependence between of pleasure of use and degree of satisfaction.



## 4.7    Testing null-hypothesis

Let's    z 2 = ∑ n i -= 1 ( OBS i -EXP i ) 2 ∕ E i be  a  hypothesis  that  evaluates  the  behavior of the deaf students. It assesses the difference between observed values OBSi and expected EXPi ones. The following Null hypotheses are considered:

NH1 The degree of use of online services does not affect the relevance of IoT-AR system for deaf students.

NH2 The degree of use of devices does not affect the relevance of IoT-AR system for deaf students.

NH3 The method of communication of deaf learners with teachers does not affect the relevance of IoT-AR system for deaf students.

As an example, the result of evaluation of NH2 are described in Table 6.

The  null-hypothesis  NH2  is  rejected  with  a  considerable  significance  level. Hence, it can be confirmed that the frequency of use of smart devices by deaf students has an influence on the importance of a possible IoT-AR system for learning.

## 5    Discussion

The current study concerns an exploratory examination of deaf individuals regarding their interactions with e-learning systems. The study objectives were to grasp the deaf scholarly characteristics and points of view in order to identify the way in which they learn better and implement more appropriate e-learning systems for deaf persons.

Regarding ICT techniques, the assessment of deaf individuals seems to support PDA, tablets and new devices more than PCs. For the web, for example, deaf people communicate through interfaces, electronic media, email and getting news. They participate in e-learning, e-banking and entertainment activities less frequently.

These results demonstrate that there are no apparent differences among participants  regarding  their  gender  or  cultural  background.  Moreover,  the  results  demonstrate  that  there  are  no  differences  between  inborn  deaf  individuals  and  people who lost their hearing after birth. Nevertheless, age, social and educational status appeared  to  essentially  influence  the  e-learning  motivations  of  deaf  persons.  Furthermore, the use of new IoT and AR-based technologies and devices seems to be very attractive for deaf persons and contributes to enhancing the learning process for them. Moreover, these technologies seem to ameliorate the way deaf persons interact and communicate with society.

|        |   Smartphones (%) |   Tablets (%) |   Computers (%) |   Smart watches (%) |   IoT Con- nected devices (%) |

Table 6 Analysis of results of question 8 for the evaluation of NH2



Practical implications of learning media are as follows: IoT and AR offer benefits individually, collectively, virtually and physically. These technologies encourage  student  motivation,  interaction,  and  engagement  to  facilitate  the  achievement of their goals. Pedagogically, the design of the AR approach of learning influences the educational process which encompasses different but balanced facets of teaching techniques. On the other hand, the technical progress of the devices used in augmenting the real learning context allows the engagement of the student in the educational process. Likewise, teaching and learning practices influence the experience of learners.

## 6    Conclusion

This  paper  presents  the  use  of  new  technologies  such  as  the  IoT  and  AR  in  deaf learning.  The  IoT  refers  to  technological  advancements  in  computer  networking using real-world IoT objects that can be connected to communicate with each other over the Internet. The IoT and AR have greater potential to remove all barriers in deaf education. Therefore, this study suggests a model for deaf intelligent learning that may overcome the challenges in deaf education. Much remains to be done for the IoT and AR to make deaf learning even simpler and easier. We faced constraints of  several  kinds  during  the  realization  of  this  research.  The  most  important  constraint appeared at the stage of interpreting the results. Adaptability is also one of the central topics of this research. It has been one of our priorities throughout the data collection process. Of course, in order to interview deaf participants, we had to collaborate with sign language interpreters.

## SynthoTranslate: Multimodal Knowledge Assimilation Tool for Overcoming Auditory Barriers and Bridging Language Barriers

Priyadarshan Dhabe Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune priyadarshan.dhabe@vit.edu

Basun Kundu Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune basun.kundu21@vit.edu Ojas Joshi Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune ojas.joshi211@vit.edu Arman Nandeshwar Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune rajesh.arman21@vit.edu

Abstract -This  paper  introduces  an  automated  system to  improve  educational  accessibility  through  multilingual video  translation  and  dubbing.  It  uses  advanced  speech-totext (STT) technologies, natural language processing (NLP), and voice conversion models for accurate subtitles, translations,  and  dubbed  audio  in  Indian  languages.  Key components  include  Whisper  and Wav2vec  for subtitle generation,  GoogleTrans  for  translation,  and  Silero  models for  natural-sounding  voice  cloning.  Indian  Sign  Language (ISL) transcription is integrated to support hearing-impaired students, with Wav2Lip  ensuring  precise lip-syncing of dubbed audio. Evaluation shows a Word Error Rate (WER) of  1.9%  and  cosine  similarities  over  95%.  The  system  also offers content summarization and Q&amp;A to enhance engagement.  Future  work  will  focus  on  optimizing  speech recognition  and  improving  ISL  transcription  for  greater accessibility.

Jignesh Barhate Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune jignesh.barhate21@vit.edu

Manthan Gujar Information Technology Vishwakarma Institute of Technology Pune manthan.gujar21@vit.edu

India's  linguistic  diversity  highlights  the  vital  role  of translation  in  connecting  languages and preserving  cultural heritage. While English is widely used, translation is essential for intercultural communication, especially online, and promotes social harmony. The NLP translation market is projected to reach US$5.92 billion by 2024, growing at an annual  rate  of  12.40%,  and  hitting  US$11.94  billion  by 2030.  The  U.S.  will  dominate  with  US$2,122  million  by 2024[4].  These  stats  emphasize  translation's  importance  in global connectivity. Previous systems often lacked accuracy and contextual depth, particularly for Indian languages [5]. The talks about the projection of the Multilingual Language Translation market by 2030.This also states the dire need of translation  of  different  languages  as  a  way  of  providing inclusive educational platforms to all.

KeywordsMultilingual Translation, Voice Cloning, Indian Sign Language (ISL), Video Dubbing and Subtitling.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Discovery Digital Network saw a 7.32% view increase by adding subtitles, emphasizing their value in educational content  and  reviews.  Many  Facebook  videos  are  watched without sound,  and one-third of internet users  watch YouTube  daily, with subtitles increasing engagement. Closed  captioning  boosts  user  time  by  40%,  and  80%  of users prefer subtitles, aiding  accessibility for  the  360 million with hearing loss. However, challenges like speaker  identification  and  timing  persist.  Voice  dubbing retains  emotional  tone,  crucial  in  education,  but  systems like  DeepSpeech  face  memory  and  accuracy  issues  in longer videos.

Our  project  integrates  customizable  components  into  a single,  free  platform  for  diverse  educational  needs.  Using RVC-based voice cloning, it outperforms paid alternatives, offering  automatic  summarization  and  interactive  Q&amp;A. Additionally,  Indian  Sign  Language  (ISL)  is  incorporated alongside  subtitles,  enhancing  accessibility  for  hearingimpaired students. AI-driven algorithms personalize learning experiences, setting our approach apart.

## A. Subtitle Summarization and Question-Answer Generation

Subtitles  help  viewers  quickly  grasp  the  essence  of video content, making a summary strategy vital for saving time.  With  data  projected  to  exceed  180  zettabytes  by 2025, concise summaries are essential for condensing vast information into digestible formats. In education, questions and answers boost engagement, comprehension, and critical  thinking, offering  valuable  insights  for  instructors. However, challenges like accurately identifying verbs and matching  tokens  can  affect answer  precision.  Limited answer extraction domains may hinder broader applicability,  especially  when  using  specific  datasets  like medical  data,  which  can  lead  to  inaccuracies  in  complex sentences. Despite achieving 80% accuracy, further improvements  are  needed  to  handle  nuanced  questions requiring deeper semantic understanding. [6].

## B. Indian Sign Language(ISL) Translation

The Americans with Disabilities Act (2016) mandates auxiliary aids like closed captions and subtitles for video accessibility, ensuring fundamental rights. The introduction of a universal knowledge assimilation tool is driven by the rapidly expanding education industry, with the  global  e-learning  market  expected  to  reach  around

$400 billion by 2026, doubling its size from approximately $200 billion in 2019. Notably, the learning management system (LMS) market alone generated over $18 billion in revenue in 2019.[9]

## C. Voice Dubbing and Voice Clonning

Voice dubbing plays a crucial role in education, especially  in  India's  multilingual  environment.  Providing content in regional languages improves student accessibility and comprehension. Technologies like Retrieval-based Voice Conversion  (RVC)  replicate  educators'  voices,  preserving their  intonations  and  emotions  for  authenticity,  while  silero models  for  Text-to-Speech  (TTS)  synthesis  ensure  natural, contextually  accurate  audio.  These  solutions  offer  scalable, high-quality  dubbing,  allowing  educators  to  reach  wider audiences without compromising quality. This research addresses  past  challenges  in  domain-specific  solutions  and language accessibility, particularly for hearing-impaired individuals, by developing an interactive platform that supports personalized, multilingual learning. Using NLP and deep learning (DL), the platform enhances concept retention and breaks language barriers, making education more inclusive.

## II. RELATED WORKS

The  paper  proposes  an  automatic  subtitle  generation and semantic video summarization technique utilizing speech  recognition  and  NLP-based  text  summarization algorithms.  It  introduces  five  summarization  methodsLuhn's,  LSA,  Text  Rank,  Lex  Rank,  and  Edmundson's algorithms-and  demonstrates  their  effectiveness  through experimental results, enhancing video navigation and accessibility  on  platforms  like  YouTube  and  Dailymotion in  the  era  of  big  data  [10].  The  goal  was  to  develop  an LDA-based subtitle  summarization  model  for  educational videos, employing dataset expansion through human summaries, followed by LDA for extractive summarization.  Performance  comparisons  showed  LDA's superiority  in  ROUGE scores and human evaluation over TF-IDF  and  LSA  models.  Future  work  may  address challenges with topics rich in numbers and verbs, focusing on length control and punctuation improvements [11]. The study examines subtitle segmentation parameters like BLEUbr and a new metric, Sigma, highlighting sensitivities  to  classification  noise  and  estimating  system results.  Limitations  include  challenges  in  distinguishing homogeneous production and biases from alignment algorithms. Future work will involve developing balanced metrics and validating human decision links for improved subtitle segmentation assessment [12]. This research introduces a Python-based approach for efficient YouTube video  summarization  using  the  YouTube  Transcript  API and BERT algorithms, including extractive summarization and language translation, benefiting teaching, patent research, and information extraction [13]. It compares AIbased translation approaches with traditional machine translation,  showing  that  AI  translation  is  faster,  more affordable, reliable, and accurate, highlighting its potential to enhance classroom learning [14]. An Android-based API powered  by  Firebase  provides  a  solution  to  language barriers,  enabling  users  to  translate  scanned  text  images offline  using  OCR  and  ML  Kit  technologies,  improving user engagement [15]. The study aimed to generate computer-based exam  questions aligned with learning goals using NLP tools like SpaCy and NLTK, with future plans  for  automating  answer  validation  [16].    Another method  used  NLP  to  extract  features  like  POS  tags  and synonyms, leveraging  an  Apache  Solar  server  for  Named Entity  Recognition  and  question  formation.  This  system was beneficial for single-word answers but faced limitations  with  similarly  named  proper  nouns  [17].  The research  involved  creating  a  Q&amp;A  system  for  a  cohesive learning environment by extracting semantic relations and calculating word  similarities, though  it struggled with multi-part  questions  [18].  The  paper  also  explores  sign language processing, addressing challenges in recognition, translation, and modeling through interdisciplinary collaboration  [19].  Finally,  it  presents  EDUZONE,  an educational  tool  that  enhances  online  learning  via  video summarization and digital human technology, facing challenges with latency and accuracy [20].

## III. PROPOSED SYSTEM

The system improves educational accessibility by automating video translation and dubbing in various Indian languages.  It  integrates  STT,  NLP,  and  voice  cloning  to generate  subtitles  and  audio.  The  process  includes  audio extraction, transcription, translation, and subtitle synchronization, while voice cloning ensures naturalsounding audio. Other features include content summarization,  question  generation,  and  ISL  transcription for hearing-impaired students.

Fig 1: Flowchart of Proposed System



## A. Subtitle Generation and Translation

The  subtitle  generation  starts  with  audio  extraction  via FFMPEG. Whisper and Wav2vec models convert speech to text, with Whisper  excelling in noisy conditions. GoogleTrans  handles  translation  into  Indian  languages using  Google's  neural  machine  translation.  Whisper  and MoviePy then sync the translated text with video timestamps, producing coherent subtitles for better comprehension.

## B. Video Summarization and Question-Answer Generation

Before Text Rank, BERT, and T5 integration, conventional  summarization  methods,  reliant  on  word frequency and rule-based approaches, struggled with contextual  comprehension  and  semantic  nuances,  often yielding  incoherent  summaries.  Thus,  a  Question  and Answering  system  was  developed  to  clear  any  specific doubts  that  the  user  has  in  the  video.  This  feature  was implemented keeping in mind the need of QA systems for educational videos, where the student can use this feature to  clear  his/her  doubts  or  might  revise  thus  providing him/her a one-stop solution to test the concepts.

## C. ISL(Indian Sign Language)Translation

With  over  70  million  deaf  individuals  and  200+  sign languages  worldwide,  communication  methods  are  crucial. Our prototype  focuses  on  helping  individuals  with  hearing disabilities, their families, professionals, and content creators. It starts by accepting .mp4 files or YouTube links, using Pytube to download and FFMPEG to extract audio as .mp3.  The  Whisper  library,  trained  on  680,000  hours  of data,  acts  as  the  ASR  system  for  multilingual  transcription and English translation. Whisper's encoder-decoder transformer architecture is illustrated in Fig 2.

Fig 2: The encoder-decoder transformer of Whisper (a STT) model



The Whisper ASR system creates subtitles with accurate  timestamps,  while  MoviePy  handles  burned-in subtitles.  GoogleTrans,  chosen  for  its  language  support, translates English into Indic languages using NMT models:



The  y^ represents the translated text in the target language,  with  X  as  the  input  text  and  y  as  the  possible translations, based on conditional probability. Subtitle summarization  uses  BART,  T5,  and  TextRank  algorithms, focusing on tokenization, encoding, and abstractive summarization.  Post-processing  ensures  coherence.  Fig  3 shows tokenization across these methods.

Fig 3: Tokenization of words in a sentence



The  model  is  pre-trained  on  tokens  "t,"  referencing  past tokens "k" to compute the current token. To enhance tasks like summarization, it is fine-tuned in a supervised manner to  maximize  the  probability  of  label  "y"  given  feature vectors ͳǦ .  By  combining  these,  an  equation  is  formed where lambda (λ) regulates the effect of language modeling. In  the  summarization  equations  for  BERT  and  T5, ܺ represents the input, ܻ the  summary, and ܲ the  conditional probability  of  generating  the  i-th  token  based  on  prior tokens. These equations maximize the conditional probability to generate a summary ܻ from text ܺ .



TextRank  tokenizes  text,  removes  stop  words,  builds  a similarity graph, and applies PageRank to select top sentences  for  extractive  summaries.  For  MCQs,  Sense2vec creates distractors using semantic word embeddings. WordNet's hypernyms provide abstract concepts (e.g., "India" →  "countries in Asia"). Using "lava" as the keyword, we generated relevant distractors based on similar embeddings. ('molten\_rock|NOUN',0.8014) and ('volcano|NOUN',0.7906). Methods like Sense2vec, WordNet, and ConceptNet initially  gave  incorrect  options. Fine-tuning  a  BERT  model  on  subtitles  improved  out-ofvocabulary  handling  using  WordPiece  tokenization,  where each  token  tᵢ  is  split  into  sub-word  units,  mathematically represented as: (Equation). The WordPiece tokenizer breaks tokens into sub-units S = (S₁, S₂, Sₙ), applying the tokenizer formula for each token:





In BERT-based question answering, token scores for answer start and end positions are obtained with 'torch.argmax(start\_scores)'  and  'torch.argmax(end\_scores)'. The identified span is sliced from the 'tokens' list and joined to form the answer.

## D. Voice Dubbing and Voice Clonning

Voice dubbing is achieved using Silero models for textto-speech  (TTS)  and  Retrieval-based  Voice  Conversion (RVC)  to  replicate  the  original  speaker's  tone  and  style, ensuring natural and engaging audio in translated videos.

PESQ Score = 4.5 + 0.1* (Subjective Listening Quality)



These techniques ensure that the dubbed audio maintains the original context and emotional tone, enhancing the overall viewing experience.

- /g120 Inferencing  Voice:  Analyze  voice  characteristics using ML algorithms.
- /g120 Vocal  Pitch  Estimation:  Isolate  pitch  of  vocal components in music
- /g120 MDX-NET  and  De-echo:  Reduce  reverberation for clearer audio.
- /g120 Deep  Invariant  Optimal  Quantization:  Optimize audio quantization to reduce noise.
- /g120 Median Filtering: Minimize breathiness and noise for better quality.
- /g120 Transpose:  Adjust  audio  pitch  for  correction  or manipulation.
- /g120 Cloned Audio: Create modified audio that resembles the original.

Fig 4: MDX-net, De-echo, DIOQ with median filtering in RVC



We  fine-tuned  ConceptNet,  BART,  and  WordNet  to enhance our Q&amp;A system. ConceptNet provides commonsense knowledge for interpreting nuanced questions.  BART  generates  accurate  answers  from  Q&amp;A datasets  using  its  transformer  architecture,  while  WordNet helps manage synonyms and disambiguate meanings. Together,  these  resources  improve  response  precision  and enrich the user learning experience.

## A. Model Tunning

In our research, we  fine-tuned Retrieval-based Voice Conversion  (RVC)  models  to  improve  their  performance. RVC uses  a  vast  voice  database  to  convert  source  voices into target voices while preserving content. By fine-tuning with diverse datasets, we've enhanced the model's ability to replicate  vocal  traits  like  tone  and  pitch,  ensuring  highquality voice cloning. We also integrated advanced algorithms  for  seamless  voice  adaptation,  allowing  realtime  processing  and  natural  speech  synthesis.  Optimizing hyperparameters and incorporating speaker-specific features enables personalized voice conversion, positioning our project as a robust tool for customizable voice outputs.

## B. Lip-Syncing with Wav2Lip

The system uses  Wav2Lip technology  with  GANs  to sync dubbed audio with lip movements, enhancing visual coherence in videos. This ensures authenticity in educational content, providing students with an engaging and seamless experience.

## F. RVC Voice Clonning

The F1F3syn measure quantifies breathiness in a voice signal. It begins by preparing the signal within a frequency range  of  100-1500  Hz  to  capture  relevant  harmonics  and normalizing the amplitude envelope for visual comparison. The measure is calculated by cross-correlating the amplitude envelopes of the first (F1) and third (F3) formants over a 25 ms segment. The synchronization index F1F3syn is derived, where higher values indicate modal voice quality and lower values suggest increased breathiness or creakiness.

ݎ݋ݐܿܽܨ ݏݏ݄݁݊݅ݐܽ݁ݎܤ ൌ ڄ ߙ ሺ ܨ ͵ െ ܨ ͳሻ ൅ ߚ

In  this  model, α and β serve  as  coefficients that adjust the influence of F1 and F3 on the perceived breathiness of a sound. Here, F1 refers to the first formant frequency, while F3 represents  the  third  formant  frequency.  The  average F1F3syn value was approximately 0.911, indicating predominantly  modal  voice  quality.  This  result  highlights the  effectiveness  of  F1F3syn  in  assessing  breathiness  and differentiating  between  modal  and  breathy/creaky  voice qualities. Thus, F1F3syn serves as a valuable parameter for evaluating  voice  quality  and  understanding  breathiness  in vocal productions.

## V. CONCLUSION

This  project  successfully  developed  a  multimodal  and multilingual platform to make education accessible for all students,  overcoming  language  barriers  and  supporting users with hearing impairments. However, limitations included restricted English language support for videos and ISL transcription for certain phrases. Future enhancements will  focus  on  expanding  subtitle  support  for  more  Indic languages, particularly Devanagari and Dravidian languages.  Additionally, plans  include implementing realtime human voice cloning for audio and developing a 3D model for ISL translation.

Sign language datasets are essential to developing many sign language technologies. In particular, datasets are required for training artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) systems. Though the idea of using AI/ML for sign languages is not new, technology has now advanced to a point where developing such sign language technologies is becoming increasingly tractable. This critical juncture provides an opportunity to be thoughtful about an array of Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Ethics (FATE) considerations. Sign language datasets typically contain recordings of people signing, which is highly personal. The rights and responsibilities of the parties involved in data collection and storage are also complex and involve individual data contributors, data collectors or owners, and data users who may interact through a variety of exchange and access mechanisms. Deaf community members (and signers, more generally) are also central stakeholders in any end applications of sign language data. The centrality of sign language to deaf culture identity, coupled with a history of oppression, makes usage by technologists particularly sensitive. This piece presents many
