X.  Yang  et  al.  (eds.), Proceedings  of  Ninth  International  Congress  on  Information  and Communication  Technology ,  Lecture  Notes  in  Networks  and  Systems  1054,

[https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-5035-1\_7](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-97-5035-1_7)

Recognizing these challenges, the VirtualSign project emerges as a groundbreaking  initiative  that  aims  to  enhance  communication  accessibility  for  deaf  students in  educational  settings.  Through  the  utilization  of  advanced  technology  and  machine learning,  VirtualSign  revolutionizes  the  way  individuals  can  access  information  in different  languages  [2-5].

The  primary  objective  of  the  VirtualSign  project  is  to  create  an  inclusive  environment  in  the  field  of  education  by  breaking  down  linguistic  barriers  and  fostering inclusivity. By  focusing  on  the  educational  sphere,  VirtualSign  strives  to  provide deaf  students  with  equal  opportunities  to  engage  and  enhance  learning  [6].

VirtualSign  offers  a  comprehensive  suite  of  tools  for  assisted  communication, empowering  deaf  students  to  overcome  communication  obstacles  and  actively  participate in educational  activities. These  tools leverage  state-of-the-art  technology  to bridge the gap between different languages and facilitate smooth and efficient communication.

By  harnessing  the  power  of  technology,  VirtualSign  demonstrates  the  transformative  potential  of  inclusive  education.  The  project  represents  a  significant  milestone  in leveraging  technology  to  foster  an  environment  where  every  individual,  regardless  of hearing  impairments,  can  fully  participate  and  benefit  from  educational  experiences.

Moreover,  the  following  paper  explores  (1)  the  theoretical  framework  and  background  of  this  project,  focusing  on  the  principles  of  sign  language,  the  concept  of inclusive  education  and  the  potential  of  assistive  technologies,  (2)  the  methodology of the project (i.e., concept and objectives), (3) the VirtualSign architecture and its  technological  foundations,  and  (4)  the  implementation  and  development  of  the VirtualSign  technology  in  other  areas  and  projects  that  demonstrate  its  versatility  and potential  impact  beyond  educational  settings.  It  highlights  real  case  studies  where VirtualSign  has  been  integrated  into.  These  practical  applications  demonstrate  the adaptability  and  scalability  of  VirtualSign  in  addressing  communication  barriers  and promoting  inclusivity  across  various  contexts.

## 2 Theoretical  Framework

Sign  languages,  including  Portuguese  Sign  Language  (LGP),  exhibit  distinct  characteristics  that  distinguish  them  from  spoken  languages.  They  can  be  classified  as either  oral-auditory  or  visual-spatial  languages,  depending  on  the  mode  of  communication  used  by  the  deaf  community.  Portuguese  Sign  Language,  like  other  sign languages,  possesses  its  own  unique  grammar  and  structure,  allowing  deaf  individuals in  Portugal  to  communicate  effectively  within  their  community  [3].

However, despite the increasing interest and recognition of Portuguese Sign Language,  there  remains  a  significant  challenge  in  providing  adequate  support  for the  deaf  community  to  access  written  information  in  sign  language.  This  limitation leads  to  educational  information  exclusion  for  disabled  individuals  who  rely  on  sign language  as  their  primary  means  of  communication,  which  must  be  overcome  by inclusive  education.

Inclusive  education  is  an  approach  to  education  that  aims  to  provide  equal  opportunities  and  support  for  all  learners,  regardless  [6,  7].  Its  core  principle  is  the  recognition that  every  student  deserves  to  be  included  in  mainstream  educational  environments and  actively  participate  in  learning  alongside  their  peers  [8].  Implementing  inclusive education  can  pose  challenges,  such  as  the  need  for  adequate  resources,  specialized support  services,  and  teacher  training.  However,  by  embracing  inclusive  education, educational  systems  can  create  environments  that  foster  equality,  and  empower  all students  to  thrive  and  enhance  their  academic  growth  and  achievement  [7].  One  such resource  is  assistive  technologies.

Assistive technologies have a profound impact on the learning experience of deaf  students,  providing  numerous  advantages.  These  technologies  offer  access  to information,  enhance  communication,  support  language  development,  and  provide academic  assistance,  all  while  fostering  inclusive  learning  environments.

One  notable  advantage  of  technology  is  its  automatic  captioning  and  transcription services,  which  convert  spoken  language  into  written  text.  This  feature  allows  deaf students  to  follow  lectures,  presentations,  and  multimedia  content,  improving  their reading  and  comprehension  skills  and  ensuring  crucial  information  is  accessible  to them.

Furthermore,  technology  offers  a  range  of  visual  learning  tools  that  cater  to  diverse learning preferences and  enhance  conceptual  understanding. These  tools include multimedia  presentations,  educational  videos  with  captions  or  sign  language  interpretation,  interactive  simulations,  and  visual  aids.  By  providing  multiple  modalities for  accessing  information,  technology  empowers  deaf  students  to  grasp  complex subjects  effectively.

Online learning platforms also contribute to the educational journey of deaf students  by  offering  flexible  and  accessible  education.  These  platforms  provide  a  wide range  of  educational  materials,  interactive  exercises,  and  assessments,  enabling  deaf students  to  learn  at  their  own  pace,  review  content  as  needed,  and  access  resources anytime,  anywhere.  Additionally,  discussion  forums  and  collaboration  features  foster peer  interaction  and  support,  creating  a  sense  of  community  within  the  online  learning environment.

By embracing  these assistive technologies, educational institutions can foster the  educational  and  personal  growth  of  deaf  students,  ensuring  equal  opportunities for  success.  The  integration  of  technology  breaks  down  barriers,  creating  inclusive learning  environments  where  deaf  students  can  fully  participate,  engage,  and  thrive in  their  academic  pursuits.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Concept

The  VirtualSign  project  overall  goal  was  the  creation  of  an  assistive  tool,  an  automatic  bidirectional  translator,  available  in  classrooms,  with  the  purpose  to  assist  deaf students  in  educational  settings  in  the  access  to  information  and  communication. Individuals  with  such  impairments  often  face  significant  challenges  when  it  comes to  communication  and  information.  By  recognizing  these  barriers,  the  VirtualSign project  has  emerged  as  a  groundbreaking  initiative  aiming  to  bridge  linguistic  barriers and  improve  communication  accessibility.

The  VirtualSign  project  focuses  on  leveraging  advanced  technology  to  enhance accessibility  for  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.  By  providing  real-time  sign language  interpretation  and  communication  support,  VirtualSign  enables  individuals to  effectively  engage,  and  access  information.

The  VirtualSign  project  focuses  on  enhancing  access  to  mainstream  education  for deaf  students  by  utilizing  VirtualSign  Technology.  Traditional  educational  methods often  struggle  to  meet  the  unique  needs  and  communication  requirements  of  deaf students.  By  integrating  sign  language  as  an  instructional  language,  the  project  aims  to transform  the  educational  experience,  making  educational  materials  more  accessible and  empowering  deaf  students  to  actively  participate  and  excel  in  their  studies.

By  promoting  the  recognition  and  usage  of  sign  language,  the  VirtualSign  project fosters  a  diverse  and  inclusive  environment  that  values  the  linguistic  and  cultural diversity  of  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.

Through  its multifaceted  approach, the VirtualSign project strives to  promote social  inclusion,  dismantle  communication  barriers,  and  create  equal  opportunities for  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.

## 3.2 Objectives

In  today's  society,  promoting  social  inclusion  and  equal  opportunities  for  people  with disabilities,  particularly  those  with  hearing  impairments,  has  become  a  key  concern. Effective  communication  and  access  to  information  are  often  hindered  by  linguistic barriers  faced  by  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.  Recognizing  this  challenge, the  VirtualSign  project  has  emerged  as  a  groundbreaking  initiative  aimed  at  bridging these  barriers  and  improving  communication  accessibility.  With  a  focus  on  promoting social  inclusion,  enhancing  communication,  and  addressing  the  needs  of  deaf  students in  education  settings,  the  VirtualSign  project  strives  to  create  an  environment  where individuals  with  hearing  impairments  have  equal  access,  opportunities,  and  the  ability to  actively  participate  in  society.  To  achieve  this,  the  following  objectives  are  pursued:

- Enhance  communication  accessibility: The VirtualSign project aims to break linguistic  barriers  and  enhance  communication  accessibility  for  individuals  with speech,  hearing,  and  visual  impairments.  By  leveraging  the  VirtualSign  Technology,  the  project  enables  real-time  sign  language  interpretation,  empowering individuals  to  engage  in  effective  communication.
- Promote  social  inclusion  and  equal  opportunities:  The  project  seeks  to  promote social inclusion by providing equal opportunities for people with disabilities, particularly those with hearing impairments. Through the implementation of VirtualSign  Technology,  the  project  aims  to  create  an  inclusive  environment  where individuals  can  actively  participate  in  social  interactions.
- Enhance  educational  experiences  for  deaf  students:  The  VirtualSign  project  recognizes  the  challenges  faced  by  deaf  students  in  educational  settings  and  aims  to enhance  their  educational  experiences.  By  providing  innovative  tools  and  platforms  that  integrate  sign  language  as  an  instructional  language,  the  project  fosters effective  communication  between  deaf  students,  teachers,  and  peers,  empowering them  to  actively  participate  and  excel  in  their  studies.
- Promote  recognition  and  usage  of  sign  language:  The  VirtualSign  project  aims  to promote  the  recognition  and  usage  of  sign  language,  acknowledging  its  importance  as  a  means  of  communication.  By  embracing  sign  language  as  an  integral part  of  society,  the  project  strives  to  foster  a  more  inclusive  and  diverse  environment  that  values  the  linguistic  and  cultural  diversity  of  individuals  with  hearing impairments.

Additionally,  the  project  pursues  the  following  specific  objectives  to  support  the implementation  of  the  above  goals:

- Develop  and  implement  an  accessible and user-friendly virtual platform: The VirtualSign project aims to create a virtual platform specifically designed to cater  to  the  needs  of  deaf  students.  This  platform  will  provide  seamless  access  to educational  resources,  communication  tools,  and  interactive  learning  experiences.
- Enhance  communication  capabilities:  The  project  seeks  to  improve  communication  for  deaf  students  by  incorporating  innovative  technologies  such  as  sign language recognition, real-time captioning, and video conferencing features. These  tools  will  facilitate  effective  communication  between  students,  teachers, and  peers.
- Provide comprehensive educational content: The VirtualSign project aims to develop  a  diverse  range  of  educational  content  that  is  specifically  tailored  to  the needs  of  deaf  students.  This  content  will  cover  various  subjects  and  educational levels,  ensuring  that  students  have  equal  access  to  quality  education.
- Foster  collaboration  and  social  interaction:  The  project  recognizes  the  importance of  social  interaction  and  collaboration  in  the  learning  process.  It  aims  to  create  a virtual  environment  that  encourages  deaf  students  to  actively  engage  with  their peers,  teachers,  and  the  broader  community,  fostering  a  sense  of  inclusivity.

- Empower educators and support professionals: The VirtualSign project will provide  training  and  resources  to  educators  and  support  professionals  to  effectively  utilize  the  virtual  translator.  This  will  ensure  that  teachers  are  equipped  with the  necessary  skills  and  knowledge  to  create  an  inclusive  learning  environment.
- Conduct  research  and  development:  The  project  will  actively  engage  in  research and  development  to  continuously  improve  the  virtual  platform,  communication technologies,  and  educational  content.  By  staying  at  the  forefront  of  advancements in  technology  and  education,  the  VirtualSign  project  can  adapt  and  evolve  to  meet the  evolving  needs  of  deaf  students.
- Advocate  for  policy  changes  and  awareness:  The  VirtualSign  project  will  actively advocate  for  policy  changes  at  educational  institutions  and  government  levels  to promote  the  inclusion  of  deaf  students.  Additionally,  it  will  raise  awareness  about the  challenges  faced  by  deaf  individuals  and  the  importance  of  equal  access  to education  and  society.

By pursuing these objectives, the VirtualSign project aims to empower  deaf students, bridge communication  gaps,  and  create  a more  inclusive and equitable educational  environment  for  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.

## 3.3 Sustainability  and  Development

This  section  serves  as  a  comprehensive  roadmap  for  sustaining  the  impact  and  continuous  development  of  the  VirtualSign  project.  To  ensure  its  long-term  success,  the project  has  strategically  outlined  various  approaches.  These  include  seeking  sustainable  funding  through  grants  and  partnerships  committed  to  accessibility  and  inclusion,  collaborating  with  global  educational  institutions  and  stakeholders,  and  actively engaging  the  community  of  users  for  ongoing  feedback  and  input.

Additionally,  the  VirtualSign  project  prioritizes  research  and  development,  allocating  resources  to  stay  at  the  forefront  of  technology  and  educational  methodologies.  The  scalability  and  adaptability  of  the  VirtualSign  platform  are  key  considerations,  ensuring  it  can  evolve  with  emerging  technologies  and  changing  educational environments.

Through  the  implementation  of  these  strategies,  the  VirtualSign  project  aims  to guarantee  the  sustainability  of  its  platform  and  contribute  to  the  long-term  success of  deaf  students  in  mainstream  education.

## 4 VirtualSign  Architecture

## 4.1 VirtualSign  Model

VirtualSign  aims to address the lack of adaptability in  educational organizations for deaf and hard of hearing individuals, ensuring they have equal educational opportunities.  The  project  includes  the  development  of  a  model  to  integrate  them into  mainstream  education,  an  animated  virtual  character  for  translating  text-to-sign language,  and  a  virtual  reality  environment  for  translating  Portuguese  Sign  Language to  Portuguese  text.  The  model  can  be  applied  in  various  fields  like  virtual  museums, web  pages,  and  services.  The  project  was  initiated  by  an  engineering  school  to  assist in  translating  educational  content  into  Portuguese  Sign  Language  for  undergraduate computer  science  degrees.

## 4.2 Automatic  Sign  Language  Recognition

Sign  language  communication  encompasses  a  combination  of  two-handed  gestures and  non-manual  signals.  However,  recognizing  sign  language  presents  inherent  challenges due to the diverse variations in signs, which  can  range from  global  body movements  to  intricate  finger  configurations.  Each  sign  requires  the  acquisition  of specific  information,  with  varying  levels  of  detail  [9].  Therefore,  striking  a  balance between  capturing  overall  motion  and  preserving  subtle  local  movements  becomes crucial.  Additionally,  effectively  handling  occlusions  is  essential  in  this  context.

The  process  of  sign  language  recognition  involves  multiple  steps,  including  hand, face,  and  body  part  tracking,  feature  extraction,  modeling,  analysis  of  time-varying signals,  and  integration  of  information  from  different  modalities.  To  facilitate  these tasks,  a  variety  of  sensors  are  employed  to  capture  a  wide  range  of  features.

Use  of  Depth  sensors .  The  introduction  of  the  Microsoft  Kinect  depth  sensor  revolutionized  technology  by  enabling  computers  to  'see.'  Depth  images  obtained  from Kinect  are  easier  for  computers  to  interpret  compared  to  conventional  color  images. Processing  depth  information  allows  for  more  accurate  object  recognition,  irrespective  of  color.  Depth  sensors  have  proven  to  be  a  robust  tracking  method,  and  the Kinect  SDK  provides  accurate  position  and  orientation  data  for  hands  [10].

Depth-based  Hand  Localization  and  Tracking .  To  capture  hand  gesture  data,  direct measures  from  a  data  glove  with  14  sensors,  such  as  the  5DT  Data  Glove  5  Ultra,  were initially  used.  The  5DT  Data  Glove  SDK  already  offered  basic  gesture  recognition for  15  hand  gestures.  However,  an  updated  version,  the  5DT  Ultra  17  gloves,  includes additional  gyroscope  and  accelerometer  components  situated  in  a  small  black  box atop  the  glove.  These  additions  enable  the  determination  of  hand  rotation,  which was  not  possible  with  the  original  model.  Also,  the  IFG  data  gloves,  developed  in collaboration  with  the  Instituto  Federal  de  Goiás  in  Brazil,  represent  a  newer  model being tested. Unlike the flexion sensor-based gloves, the IFG gloves solely rely on  nine  sensors,  each  containing  an  accelerometer  and  gyroscope.  These  sensors are  strategically  positioned  on  the  fingers,  wrist,  and  bottom  of  the  index  and  ring fingers.  While  the  IFG  gloves  offer  advantages  such  as  customization  potential  based on  feedback,  affordability,  and  the  potential  for  a  Kinect-free  version,  they  require additional  preprocessing  to  accurately  predict  hand  configurations  due  to  the  absence of  flexion  sensors.

Building  the  Avatar  and  Hand-Coding  Gestures .  The  aim  was  to  develop  a  bidirectional  translator  for  Portuguese  Sign  Language.  This  required  recognizing  signs  based on  body  motion,  translating  them  to  written  Portuguese,  and  simulating  body  motion representing  written  Portuguese.  An  avatar  was  built  using  a  hand-coding  approach that  defines  hand  shape,  orientation,  location,  and  movement  type  for  each  sign  in  the vocabulary.  Sign  labels  were  classified  by  comparing  recognized  components  with the  ideal  lexicon  categories.

Analysis  of  Non-manual  Signals .  Facial  recognition  software  like  FaceReader  typically  focuses  on  basic  emotions,  while  software  like  Faceshift  uses  depth  sensors  to accurately  extract  facial  features  and  animate  an  avatar.  Other  non-manual  signals, such as torso motion, can also be recognized using depth sensors. New  gesture recognition  devices,  such  as  Omek  Gasp  and  Leap  Motion,  provide  accurate  hand and  finger  tracking.

## 4.3 Text-to-Sign  Translation  and  VSSO  Configurator

The  TTS  translator  and  VSSO  are  online  tools  developed  using  Unity  and  WebGL technologies,  ensuring  compatibility  across  different  web  browsers.  Users  can  conveniently  access  these  tools  from  any  location.  The  TTS  translator  enables  users  to  input text  and  instantly  view  the  corresponding  sign  language  gestures  performed  by  a  3D avatar.  Currently,  the  project  supports  different  European  sign  languages,  offering  a broad  range  of  accessibility.

The  VSSO  configurator  serves  as  a  tool  for  building  the  sign  language  lexicon  used in  the  project.  Deaf  individuals  and  sign  language  interpreters  actively  contribute  to this  process  by  adding  and  validating  words  through  an  intuitive  interface  reminiscent  of  a  3D  animation  tool.  The  configurator  allows  manipulation  of  the  avatar's body, head, arms, facial expressions, and hand  configurations. Expert validators, well-versed  in  sign  language,  ensure  the  accuracy  of  the  signs  created  by  editors. Additionally,  the  configurator  provides  a  context  feature  to  address  any  ambiguities that  may  arise  during  translation,  further  enhancing  the  quality  and  precision  of  the translations.

Fig.  1 Sign-to-text  translator  structure  and  triggers



## 4.4 Sign-to-Text  Translation

The  sign-to-text  translator  requires  the  use  of  data  gloves  and  a  Kinect  sensor.  A specialized  hand-capture  application  is  employed  to  generate  datasets  for  classification,  while  the  sign-to-text  translator  application  performs  the  actual  translation process.  The  system  utilizes  the  data  gloves,  equipped  with  flexion  sensors  and  a gyroscope,  to  capture  hand  movements,  along  with  the  Microsoft  Kinect  sensor  for detecting  both  hand  and  body  movements.

The  sign-to-text  translation  tool  generates  a  translation  graph  based  on  the  established  lexicon.  Triggers,  such  as  changes  in  hand  configuration,  hand  rotation,  and body  movement,  are  employed  to  match  gestures  to  words  in  real-time  translation. The  tool  continuously  monitors  user  input  from  the  data  gloves  and  Kinect  sensor, activating  the  appropriate  triggers  to  ensure  accurate  and  timely  translations  (Fig.  1).

## 4.5 PowerPoint  Add-On

To  enhance  accessibility  and  inclusivity  in  educational  presentations,  a  PowerPoint add-on has been developed specifically for text-to-sign translation. This add-on empowers  users  to  select  text  directly  from  a  slide,  choose  the  desired  sign  language, and  receive  a  video  presentation  showcasing  the  3D  avatar  performing  the  translation  in  real  time.  This  feature  greatly  benefits  teachers  and  students  by  seamlessly integrating  sign  language  accessibility  into  their  presentations,  promoting  effective communication  for  individuals  with  hearing  impairments.

## 5 Enhancing  the  VirtualSign  Technology:  Revolutionizing Communication  and  Accessibility

The  VirtualSign  technology  has  emerged  as  a  powerful  tool  to  cater  to  the  specific needs  of  deaf  individuals  in  various  projects,  recognizing  the  challenges  faced  by deaf individuals in educational  settings and public spaces. These  initiatives have focused on leveraging this technology to  promote inclusion and accessibility in education,  cultural  tourism,  and  technical  knowledge  dissemination.  By  integrating sign language  automatic  translation technology, these projects aim to bridge the communication  gap  between  deaf  and  non-deaf  individuals,  provide  equal  learning opportunities,  and  enhance  the  overall  experiences  of  deaf  individuals  in  different domains.

Various  projects  have  harnessed  the  VirtualSign  technology  to  address  the  needs of  deaf  individuals  in  different  contexts.  In  one  project,  a  pedagogical  model  was proposed  to deliver inclusive educational  materials  for the  deaf  through  Massive Online  Open  Courses  (MOOCs)  integrated  with  sign  language  automatic  translation  technology.  This model  was  implemented  in  a  course  on  digital literacy for schoolteachers,  which  underwent  evaluation  to  assess  its  inclusiveness  and  value  for deaf  students.  The  positive  results  encouraged  the  authors  to  extend  the  pedagogical model  to  create  multilingual  MOOCs,  including  Portuguese,  Brazilian  Portuguese, LGP,  and  Libras  sign  languages.  The  VirtualSign  technology  played  a  crucial  role  in providing  sign  language  accessibility  through  a  3D  avatar,  enabling  translation  from spoken  language  to  sign  language  and  vice  versa.  Additionally,  an  audio  add-on  was included  to  benefit  blind  users  [11].

The  Inclusive  Cultural  Heritage  Tourism  (ICHT)  project,  on  the  other  hand,  is geared  toward  inclusive  cultural  tourism  and  addresses  the  needs  of  deaf  tourists visiting  cultural  heritage  spots.  The  system  integrates  an  online  platform  and  an  automatic  bidirectional  sign  language  translator  (ATT)  for  touristic  activities.  The  ATT translator,  based  on  the  VirtualSign  technology,  enables  communication  between deaf  and  non-deaf  users  in  various  sign  languages  and  spoken  languages.  The  ICHT system  also  includes  an  informatics  system  installed  on-site  at  cultural  heritage  destinations,  providing  information,  ludic  activities,  and  bilingual  interfaces  (avatar  and hologram)  in  different  languages  [12-15].

Recognizing  the  specific  challenges  faced  by  deaf  students  in  education,  the  TechWhiz  project  sought  to  enhance  their  learning  experience.  The  TechWhiz  platform focuses  on  providing  equal  access  to  education  for  deaf  students  by  developing  a semiautomatic  glossary/dictionary  in  sign  language.  This  glossary  aims  to  explain technical  and  scientific  concepts  to  deaf  students,  filling  the  gap  that  often  arises  when sign  language  interpreters  are  not  available.  The  TechWhiz  platform  utilizes  artificial intelligence,  web  scraping,  and  3D  animation  technologies  to  offer  explanations  in sign  language  for  technical  terms  and  concepts  [16].

The  Assisted  Communication  for  Education  (ACE)  and  the  International  Assisted Communication  for  Education  (I-ACE)  projects  aim  to  promote  access  to  education and  citizenship  for  individuals  who  are  deaf  or  blind  [1,  17,  18].

The  ACE  project  focuses  on  enabling  collaborations  between  different  user  types and interactions through various architectures such as collaborative art, serious games,  and  virtual  classrooms.  It  acknowledges  the  creativity  of  blind  individuals and  seeks  to  leverage  it  through  digital  games  and  tools.  Serious  games  have  been developed  for  both  deaf  and  blind  users,  promoting  cooperation  and  communication [1,  17].

The  I-ACE  project  specifically  addresses  the  needs  of  deaf  students  in  education and  citizenship.  It  recognizes  that  access  to  education  is  severely  compromised  for  the deaf  and  hearing  impaired.  The  I-ACE  project  aims  to  establish  an  innovative  infrastructure  that  supports  live  assisted  communication  between  conventional  classrooms and  deaf  students,  as  well  as  between  deaf  and  non-deaf  individuals.  By  bridging this  communication  gap,  the  project  strives  to  improve  integration,  education,  and overall  quality  of  life  for  deaf  students  [18].

Moreover,  the  ACE  and  I-ACE  projects  emphasize  the  importance  of  increasing digital  literacy  among  deaf  and  blind  individuals,  enhancing  their  communication competences  through  digital  arts,  and  providing  inclusive  learning  environments.  By leveraging  technology  and  innovative  approaches,  these  projects  aim  to  empower individuals  with  disabilities,  enhance  their  learning  experiences,  and  promote  equal opportunities  for  education  and  participation  in  society.

All  of  these  projects  leveraged  the  VirtualSign  technology  developed  by  the  Polytechnic  Institute  of  Porto,  which  facilitated  the  translation  between  spoken  and  sign languages.  The  VirtualSign  3D  avatar  and  its  translation  infrastructure  served  as  the foundation  for  sign  language  accessibility  in  both  the  pedagogical  MOOCs  and  the TechWhiz  glossary.  The  ICHT  project  expanded  on  this  technology  to  develop  an innovative  solution  for  inclusive  tourism,  using  computer  vision,  machine  translation,  holography,  and  3D  animations  to  create  a  unique  user  interface  for  deaf  and non-deaf  users.

By harnessing the VirtualSign technology, these projects aimed  to bridge the communication  gap  between  deaf  and  non-deaf  individuals,  promote  inclusion  in education  and  tourism,  and  facilitate  access  to  cultural  heritage  sites  for  the  deaf.

## 6 Conclusions

The  integration  of  technology  plays  a  crucial  role  in  empowering  deaf  students  by granting  access  to  information,  fostering  communication,  and  expanding  educational resources.  The  VirtualSign  system  revolutionizes  communication  by  enabling  individuals  with  different  languages  to  interact,  bridging  the  gap  between  deaf  and  nondeaf  individuals  worldwide.  Through  machine  learning  and  advanced  technology like  Kinect  and  5dt  Gloves,  VirtualSign  achieves  high  accuracy  in  recognizing  sign language.  With  a  strong  focus  on  promoting  social  inclusion  and  meeting  the  needs of  deaf  students  in  educational  settings,  the  project  aims  to  create  an  environment where  individuals  with  hearing  impairments  have  equal  access  and  opportunities.  By implementing  VirtualSign  in  educational  institutions,  communication  between  deaf and  non-deaf  individuals  can  be  greatly  enhanced.

Future  plans  for  VirtualSign  in  education  involve  developing  a  gloveless  system with the same precision in gesture-to-text translation, making the technology more accessible in classrooms. The project also aims to create an intermediate semantic  system  that  seamlessly  bridges  sign  language  and  written  text,  facilitating communication  between  deaf  and  non-deaf  individuals.

The  VirtualSign  system  serves  as the foundation  for other innovative projects aimed  at  enhancing  the  educational experience  of deaf students, but  also  among other  domains,  such  as  cultural  tourism.  By  leveraging  the  success  of  VirtualSign, these  projects  build  upon  its  principles  of  inclusivity  and  accessibility,  and  fosters communication.

Overall,  the  VirtualSign  project  is  dedicated  to  creating  an  inclusive  and  accessible  learning  environment,  enabling  deaf  students  to  fully  engage,  communicate,  and express  themselves  in  educational  activities.  By  leveraging  innovative  technology, VirtualSign  promotes  equal  opportunities  and  social  inclusion  in  education.  It  represents  a  significant  advancement  in  assisted  communication,  fostering  inclusivity  and enhancing  the  educational  experience  in  any  area  of  study  for  individuals  with  hearing impairments.

## Visual Kids: Interactive Learning Application for Hearing-Impaired Primary School Kids in Sri Lanka

## Dodandeniya J.M.D.G.K.M

Department of Information Technology Faculty of Computing Sri Lanka Institute of Information

Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka it20089672@my.sliit.lk

## Dela W.W.M.R.T.I.W

Department of Information Technology Faculty of Computing Sri Lanka Institute of Information

Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka it20005412@my.sliit.lk

## Dayananda G.A.I.P

Department of Information Technology Faculty of Computing Sri Lanka Institute of Information

Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka it20126810@my.sliit.lk

## Dinuka R. Wijendra

Department of Information Technology Faculty of Computing Sri Lanka Institute of Information

Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka dinuka.w@sliit.lk

Abstract -E-learning is one of the most common methods used for educational purposes. However, most e-learning environments are not particularly useful for students with hearing impairments due to their lack of adaptability. 'Visual Kids' is an e-learning application that provides deaf students with an accessible learning experience through video sign language tutorials, visual aids, and interactive activities. According to the primary educational curriculum, this platform will show students how to write letters and numbers step-by-step. Also, this application includes a gamified learning environment with interactive games and quizzes that make learning fun and enjoyable. This application provides the capability of teaching letters and numbers using sign language, and it recognizes the sign language, handwritten letters and numbers that students provide. While answering the game-based questions, the student's facial expressions can change to happy, sad, or angry. Their expressions can be identified using face recognition technology. Screening results from the models built in this research provided an accuracy of 96%, 98%, and 98% for sign language recognition, identifying handwritten letters and numbers, and identifying emotions using facial expressions, respectively. This application aims to improve educational outcomes for deaf primary pupils and support their academic and social progress.

Index Terms -Hearing Impaired students, Sign language, Elearning application, Face Emotion Recognition, Game-Based Learning, Handwritten Recognition

## I. INTRODUCTION

Hearing is the ability to perceive and interpret sound waves in the environment. Hearing allows us to sense and understand the auditory stimuli around us, which plays a crucial role in communication, learning, and our overall perception of the world. However, due to hearing problems, some groups of people are unable to listen. This will eventually make it

difficult for them to share their ideas with others and get the education they need.

Hearing impairment (HI) or hearing loss is an inability to hear. Hearing loss may be mild, moderate, severe, or profound [1]. The condition affects one or both ears and causes difficulty listening to conversational speech or loud noises. Hearing loss can be due to different causes, such as childhood or infant hearing loss, a variety of infections, such as chronic ear infections, certain toxins or medications, noise-induced hearing loss, and ageing-related hearing loss. Depending on the severity of the hearing loss, it can be temporary or permanent [1]. As a result, this deafness can have a significant impact on an individual's daily life, affecting their ability to communicate and participate in activities.

In recent years, hearing loss has become a major issue in many nations. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that over 466 million individuals worldwide have hearing issues, per the article [1]. 432 million of these 466 million people are adults, and 34 million are kids. Similar to other countries in the world, Sri Lanka also suffers from a hearing disability. According to the article, the WHO estimates that 9% of Sri Lankans have hearing problems [2]. The main problem that should be considered is that many children are part of this deaf community, while there are school-going children among them. In Sri Lanka, 4% of primary school students have hearing loss disabilities [3]. These children are exposed to different barriers and challenges when obtaining an education. Societal attitudes, a lack of understanding, a lack of access to tools for education and essential services, a shortage of specialized teaching and learning resources and assistive devices, limited access to training tools, and communication issues are some of the challenges these students face in learning [4]. In general, these barriers arise from not being able to communicate with each other and not being capable of learning very quickly like other children.

The usage of technology within the education department has become more vital with each passing year. The E-Learning environment is one of the most popular technical approaches used. In education, e-learning environments are used by a wide variety of students, including those who are hearing impaired. However, the Sri Lankan deaf community has access to only limited applications and research designed specifically for them. The previous applications for hearing-impaired people were only to help them recognize sign language [11,12]. Those applications could not help children learn various kinds of subjects, as in public schools. Without an online tutoring application for children with hearing impairments, these children will increasingly lag behind normal children.

This research focuses on studying and developing an elearning application for primary students with hearing impairments, specifically targeting children in the age range of 5 to 10 years old. This research aims to help these students learn basic letters and numbers using sign language, as well as to facilitate easier letter and number writing. The research seeks to create an e-learning application designed for the convenience of hearing-impaired primary students, allowing them to independently enhance their knowledge without the need for constant guidance from teachers or parents. For this research, chose hearing-impaired primary students because they are in a crucial stage of language development, making early sign language intervention beneficial for their language skills and overall well-being. Primary school students with hearing impairments may also be more motivated to learn than older students, as they are still developing their language skills and may be eager to learn a new way to communicate.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

The advancement of technology has a better way for innovative educational approaches, including e-learning, which has the potential to enhance the learning experiences of students with diverse needs [5]. In the case of hearing-impaired children, e-learning applications can offer valuable support in their educational journey. Some authors have worked in the past to provide solutions to avoid learning difficulties by creating various e-learning applications using different technologies to teach hearing-impaired children.

In the hearing-impaired kid's project, one of the objectives is teaching English letters and numbers using sign language [6]. There are several previous studies that have addressed the importance of teaching sign language to hearing-impaired children. There is research on e-learning environments specifically designed for hearing-impaired students, and the study emphasized the significance of incorporating sign language into the curriculum to facilitate communication and language development [6].

Another study, which demonstrated a system for interpreting sign language in order to assist deaf and hearing people, shows that technology can be used to aid their acquisition of sign language [7]. According to the teaching sign language function, the application provides video tutorials about sign language for hearing-impaired kids and allows them to practice English and mathematics using hand gestures. Aligning with the objective, which is identifying letters and numbers. According to this function, get an analysis of students' letter and number writing accuracy.

Another objective of the research is to provide a platform for recall and practice lessons using gamification activities, while students doing the activities on the gamification platform suggest the best way to practice student activities using facial emotion recognition technology. Gamification has gained recognition as an effective approach in educational settings. Another study states how empirical evidence on the impact of gamification in teaching and learning has been systematically reviewed [8]. Their findings indicated positive outcomes, including increased motivation and engagement.

There are several research have for facial recognition technology and teaching in classroom activities. There is research for the Student Emotion Recognition System (SERS) to improve online learning through the measurement of learner concentration [9]. By utilizing facial recognition technology, the application can gauge the child's engagement and attention levels. And another study mentions students' facial expressions during a lecture [10]. Previous studies have highlighted the importance of teaching sign language to facilitate communication and language development. Furthermore, the incorporation of English letters and numbers, learning activity games, and facial recognition techniques can significantly enhance the learning experiences of hearing-impaired children. However, further research and development are necessary to implement and evaluate the effectiveness of such an e-learning application in Sri Lanka's context.

Previous research has shown the potential of e-learning applications to support the educational journey of hearingimpaired children. However, there is a research gap in the development of e-learning applications that combine sign language, gamification activities, and facial emotion recognition technology to provide a comprehensive and engaging learning experience for hearing-impaired children in Sri Lanka. Existing e-learning applications for these children typically focus on teaching sign language or delivering educational content through various modalities but lack integration of these elements. This study aims to bridge these gaps by developing an e-learning application specifically designed for hearing-impaired children in Sri Lanka that incorporates all of these components and assesses its effectiveness in enhancing learning outcomes.

## III. METHODOLOGY

In this research, an E-Learning system for hearing-impaired primary school students to learn letters and numbers through the use of four key functionalities is presented. They are, 1. Sign Language Recognition, 2. Identify the handwritten letters and numbers, 3. Identifying emotions using facial expressions, 4. Gamified learning environment.

Fig. 1. System overview



## A. Sign Language Recognition

This application allows hearing-impaired students opportunities to learn letters and numbers using sign language, and it can also be a great opportunity for the user to learn and improve their knowledge of sign language. In this application, used the American Sign Language (ASL) alphabet (A-Z) and numbers (0-9). This e-learning platform provides video lessons and interactive images to teach sign language. After being given basic lessons, such as alphabet letters in ASL, the system will give a test to check their knowledge of what they have studied so far. To face the test, a student requires only a personal computer, webcam, and internet connection. After the task begins, the system displays the letter or number of the alphabet on the screen and asks the student to indicate the correct sign language for that letter. The user should do that in front of the webcam. If the user's motion is correct, it is saved, and the user moves on to the next task; however, if the user's motion is incorrect, the student is requested to repeat the task again. 'Fig. 2' shows how the system detects the sign of the user.

Fig. 2. Recognize the hand sign



All the images were taken under low-resolution laptop webcams to get the low-resolution images based on training purposes [11]. Furthermore, this model can be used to identify images in real-time with low latency. For successful model training, 750 sign images were collected, and all the images were divided into train and test datasets. Then, for trains and test image datasets, the tested individual images have been converted to CSV (Comma Separated Value) files. Using the CSV files, the model is started to train using the TensorFlow model trainer and Keras library with the CNN (Convolutional Neural Networks) configuration. A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a type of deep learning algorithm that is widely used for image recognition and analysis purposes [15]. After successfully training the model, the webcam opens and detects images using the pre-trained model. Once the image detection is over, with an accuracy 96%, the image will be sent through an API to the image classifier for further classification [11, 12].

In the intricate process of image classification within a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier, several steps are involved. The first step is pooling, a critical layer in the network's architecture. During pooling, the image is subjected to a series of convolutional layers, each equipped with specialized kernels. These convolutional layers serve to capture important visual patterns and features within the image. Simultaneously, they contribute to the reduction of the image's dimensionality, which is crucial for efficient processing. This process continues with the addition of multiple convolutional layers, with pooling being applied iteratively until the desired level of filtration is achieved. Once this intricate feature extraction is complete, the network then flattens the resulting feature maps into a one-dimensional vector. Subsequently, this vector is passed through a fully connected layer, which employs complex computations to map the features to a specific output class. To determine the class, an activation function is applied, enabling the model to identify the predicted sign letter. Once the sign letter is identified, it is seamlessly transmitted to the Text and Audio Generator section through an API, where it can be converted into the corresponding text or audio representation, facilitating seamless communication for individuals using sign language [11, 14].

## B. Identify the handwritten letters and numbers

Identifying letters and numbers are necessary for this component. There are three categories for both letters and numbers. Numbers and letters are taught to students first. Here, the digits teach the numerals from 1 to 10, and the letters teach the English alphabet from A to Z. Second, they must use sticks to create numbers and letters. At that point, kids will be certain that they grasp the letter or number. Then, students can type letters on the computer screen. Determine whether a digit is right or incorrect after children have written letters.

Use the SVC (Support Vector Clustering) technique to recognize the handwritten text and digits entered by the users. This is constructed by SVM (Support Vector Machine). SVM is useful for a variety of tasks, including regression and classification. Using a kernel function in SVC converts data points from the data space to the high dimensional feature space. Using the support vector domain description technique, the kernel's feature space algorithm determines the shortest range that fully encompasses the image of the outcomes. A series of contours that encircle the data points are produced when this range is remapped into the data space. Such contours are interpreted by the SVC as cluster borders, and the points they cover are connected to the same cluster [17].

To identify the numbers, a total of 1000 images were used. To fit the model and determine its accuracy, the system used the Support Vector Clustering algorithm. This approach seeks to arrange data more meaningfully by categorizing it according to specific criteria [16].

## C. Identifying emotions using the facial expression

This study aimed to use facial recognition technology to select the best learning method for students with hearing loss. The participants of the study were 20 students with hearing loss, aged between 5 and 10 years. The participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups, each group playing a different educational game. The games were engaging activities, and students were able to visually identify pictures and select the appropriate word for each image. They will also be able to practice and recall math operations using visual aids, such as graphics and pictures, to enhance their understanding of math operations. The front camera on the device will be automatically accessible by the app when a student begins to play the game in order to capture the student's face and record their facial expressions for the duration of the activity. The application used trained models, such as facial emotion detection models, for analyzing students' facial expressions and emotions. It will primarily identify five emotions: happy, sad, angry, surprised, and neutral. 'Fig. 3' shows how to detect the user's emotions. The application also recorded the duration of each emotion and the number of times the student switched to another game.

(a) Emotion - Happy





(b) Emotion-Sad

Fig. 3. Sample Emotion Analysis

More than 5,000 photos of kids with various facial expressions between the ages of 5 and 10 were used to construct the dataset for facial emotion identification. The dataset includes a collection of facial expression pictures representing the five basic emotions of happiness, sadness, anger, surprise, and neutrality. The dataset's images were used to train the model. CNN was used to train this model. CNN was chosen for this model's training because it offers a very high level of accuracy in picture categorization and because it does so automatically and without human supervision. When thousands of features need to be retrieved, it is therefore suitable. The sequential model receives the preprocessed images in this research paper. In the model, the fundamental components are the convolutional network, max pool layer, dropout layer, and dense layer networks. The preprocessed photos are fed into the convolution layer and the max pool layer. The convolution layer creates a convolution kernel that is convolved with the layer input, resulting in a tensor of outputs. Following the convolution layers, a max pooling layer with a pool size of 2x2 is added. This layer down-samples the input along its spatial dimensions (height and width) by selecting the maximum value over an input window for each channel of the input [18]. The CNN model has been trained to recognize the five primary emotions of surprise, anger, sadness, neutral and happiness [13].

## D. Gamified learning environment

The component we've developed facilitates a gamified learning environment for hearing-impaired primary students to engage in interactive games. The system utilizing HumanComputer Interaction (HCI) theory, aims to enhance the effective learning of letters and numbers. Given that children may not always be interested in traditional learning, this interactive environment is designed to teach lessons more engagingly. The games within this web-based learning environment feature visually appealing graphics, colors, and images, ensuring an attractive and interactive backdrop for learning. The user interface is designed with simplicity in mind, making it easy for children to navigate and use.

The system is web-based and applies Motivational Design principles, incorporating game elements like points, badges, and leaderboards to motivate students. An image is initially provided in each game, and the student must supply the correct letters corresponding to the picture. In case of an accurate answer, a confirmation message appears, otherwise, an incorrect answer notification is displayed. The game also features number-related activities and a letter-matching exercise, providing a variety of ways for students to practice and reinforce their knowledge.

Fig. 4. Sample game base learning interfaces (a) Interface for learning numbers (b) Interface for learning letters



The component we've developed employs a User-Centered Design (UCD) approach, taking into account the specific needs, preferences, and contexts of hearing-impaired primary students. We've designed this component to provide an educational gamified learning environment, leveraging cutting-edge technologies like React and Python as depicted in 'Fig. 4'

## IV. RESULT &amp; DISCUSSION

This section elaborates on the experiment outcomes for each model. This research aims to introduce a more effective Elearning platform for hearing-impaired primary school children.

In times of crisis, hearing-impaired students need an effective way to continue their education. It would not be effective for those with hearing impairment to use an online teaching model, where teachers speak, and students listen. Therefore, as an option for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, the e-learning platform has been proposed to support them in learning letters and numbers with proper instructions Python is used for the application's backend, and the front end of the application is built using React, an SQLite database, Flask, and TensorFlow. Machine learning concepts and algorithms, image processing, face recognition techniques and gamification environments have been used in the research.

## A. Sign Language Recognition

CNN is used for image processing and recognition. The alphabet and the numbers [1-10] were the two categories that were selected for training. To detect the alphabet, the CNN model was trained with 26 classes where each class has 750 images. From the data set, 80% of the samples were used for training and 20% of the samples were used for testing purposes. For the test input data, the CNN model achieved an overall 96% accuracy as shown in 'Fig. 5' and 0.1251 test error in the training process with 50 epochs of the model. 'Fig. 6' presents the Precision, Recall, F1 score, and accuracy for each letter in the trained model's classification.

Fig. 5. Training and Validation Accuracy graph of letter Recognition



Using the MNIST number dataset, CNN was trained to recognize the numbers with an accuracy of 97%. For improved training, the epochs were set to 50, and 'Fig. 7' displays the training and validation accuracy.

Fig. 6. Model accuracy



Fig. 7. Training and Validation Accuracy graph of Numbers Recognition



## B. Identify the handwritten letters and numbers

More than 1,000 letters and numbers were collected for each letter and number for recognition. Machine learning is used to identify the numbers and letters that children write. This dataset was split into two sets 20% was utilized for testing and 80% for training. The Support Vector Clustering algorithm has been applied to the model training process to fit it and verify its accuracy. For the test input data, the SVM model achieved above 98% accuracy.

## C. Identifying emotions using the facial expression

The dataset collection consisted of more than 5,000 facial expression images of students, which were used to train a CNN model with a resulting accuracy of 98% and a loss of 2%, as depicted in 'Fig. 8' The accuracy can be improved by feeding more training data to the neural network. The model is capable of detecting five common emotions among students, including surprise, anger, sadness, neutral and happiness.

## D. Gamified learning environment

According to the gamified learning environment, when a child completes a level successfully, he is unlocked to the next level and the child gets a reward according to the points. 'Fig. 9' shows the result of the game.

Fig. 8. Loss and Validation Accuracy graph of Face emotion detection



Fig. 9. Results of the game



## V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

In Sri Lanka, there is a shortage of E-learning applications developed for hearing-impaired students to learn sign language, basic letters, and numbers more easily. The study's output was the creation of the 'Visual Kids' e-learning platform, which offers primary school-aged children with hearing impairments in Sri Lanka a successful learning environment for learning letters and numbers.

The system was built using technologies like React, SQLite, Flask, TensorFlow, and Python, incorporating machine learning and image processing techniques. The evaluation of the sign language recognition model showed 96% accuracy in detecting alphabet signs and 97% accuracy for number signs. The handwriting recognition model achieved 98% accuracy. The facial emotion recognition model can detect five emotions with 98% accuracy.

By leveraging technology to create an accessible, interactive, and adaptable environment, this e-learning platform shows the potential to significantly enhance educational outcomes for hearing-impaired students. It can facilitate independent learning and provide engagement analytics to teachers.

However, more extensive testing and feedback from students and teachers should be conducted to further refine the system. Additional features could also be incorporated, such as expanding the curriculum beyond letters and numbers, adding more sign languages, and extending it to higher grade levels. Overall, this study provides a critical proof of concept and a starting point for creating technologically-enabled strategies to support inclusive education for Sri Lankans with hearing disabilities.
